01

Scaling

Picture this

You launch your app on a single machine: the web app, the database and the cache all share one box, like a food truck where one cook takes orders, grills, and washes dishes. It works beautifully for a hundred friends. Then a post goes viral and a million strangers show up at once. The CPU pins at 100%, the database starts queuing reads behind writes, and if that one box reboots, your entire product vanishes from the internet. This chapter is the story of turning that food truck into a restaurant chain, one deliberate step at a time.

1 Macro Structure & Dependency Map

From 10,000 feet, scaling is four moves repeated at every tier: separate the parts, copy them, move hot data closer, and decouple what does not need to wait. Read the map top to bottom; each hub unlocks the ones beneath it.

  • Separation of tiers — you cannot scale a part independently until it lives on its own machine
    • Single server: DNS resolves api.mysite.com to one IP; HTTP returns HTML or JSON
      • Traffic from web apps (server-side Python/Java, client-side JS/HTML) and mobile apps (HTTP + JSON)
    • Dedicated database server
      • SQL (MySQL, PostgreSQL) vs NoSQL (key-value, graph, column, document)
      • NoSQL when you need super-low latency, unstructured data, only serialization, or massive volume
  • Horizontal scaling + redundancy — adding machines instead of bigger machines is the only path past hardware limits and single points of failure
    • Load balancer spreads traffic; reroutes if a server dies
    • Stateless web tier: session data moves to a shared store, enabling auto-scaling
    • Database replication: master takes writes, slaves take reads
      • Failover: slave promoted to master; data recovery scripts, multi-master, circular replication
    • Multi-data center: GeoDNS routing, data replication across centers
      • Traffic redirection tools, data synchronization, automated deployment
  • Caching layers — memory is far faster than disk, so every repeated read you absorb early protects the database
    • Cache tier: read-heavy, rarely-modified data
      • Expiration, consistency, SPOF mitigation, LRU eviction
    • CDN: static assets (images, CSS, JS) on geographically distributed servers
      • Cost, cache expiry, CDN fallback, file invalidation
  • Decoupling & data partitioning — at the largest scale, components must stop waiting on each other and data must stop living in one place
    • Message queue: producers publish, consumers process asynchronously
    • Sharding by a key such as user_id
      • Resharding (consistent hashing), celebrity problem, joins and de-normalization
    • Logging, metrics, automation to see and steer the whole machine

Separation comes first because it is the precondition for everything else: you cannot put a load balancer in front of a web tier that still owns the database. Horizontal scaling is the spine, but it only works once servers are stateless and data is replicated. Caching then shields the data tier, and decoupling plus sharding carry you from millions of users into tens of millions.

2 Black-Box Cause & Effect Flow

Treat each layer as a sealed box: something goes in, something comes out, and the output of one is the input of the next. The order below is the order a request actually meets them.

DNS / GeoDNS

Input: A domain name such as api.mysite.com plus the user's location.

Output: The IP address of the nearest data center's entry point.

The phone book of the internet; with GeoDNS it is a phone book that hands you the number of the branch closest to your house.

→ feeds into: CDN (for static files) and the load balancer (for dynamic requests)

CDN

Input: A request for a static asset: an image, a CSS file, a JavaScript bundle.

Output: The asset from the nearest edge server, or, on a miss, a fetch from the origin that is then cached.

Vending machines placed in every neighborhood so people stop driving to the central warehouse for a soda.

→ feeds into: the browser renders the page shell; dynamic calls continue to the load balancer

Load balancer

Input: Every dynamic HTTP request hitting the public IP.

Output: The same request forwarded to one healthy web server in the pool.

A host at the restaurant door seating guests at whichever table is free, and quietly skipping a waiter who has gone home sick.

→ feeds into: stateless web servers

Stateless web server

Input: A request plus a session ID; session data is fetched from a shared store.

Output: Business logic executed; reads go to cache/DB, slow side-work goes to a queue.

An interchangeable waiter who keeps no notes in a pocket; every order is written on the shared board, so any waiter can serve any guest.

→ feeds into: cache, database, message queue

Cache tier

Input: A key for frequently read, rarely modified data.

Output: The value from memory (hit), or nothing (miss), in which case the server reads the DB and fills the cache.

The spice rack beside the stove: the cook grabs salt in a second instead of walking to the basement pantry.

→ feeds into: on a miss, the database

Replicated, sharded database

Input: Writes (insert, update, delete) and reads, each routed by a sharding key like user_id.

Output: Writes land on the master of the right shard; reads are served by its slaves.

A library split into several buildings by surname; in each building, one head librarian updates the catalog while many assistants answer questions from copies.

→ feeds into: the response returned to the web server

Message queue + workers

Input: Messages published by producers, e.g. "process this photo".

Output: Consumers pull messages and perform the work asynchronously, at their own pace.

The ticket rail in a kitchen: waiters clip orders and walk away; cooks pull tickets when their hands are free.

→ feeds into: background results, observed via logging and metrics

Follow one request

  1. A user in Europe opens your app. GeoDNS resolves api.mysite.com to the European data center rather than the US one.
  2. The page's logo, CSS and JavaScript are fetched from a nearby CDN edge; they were cached there after the first visitor's miss hit the origin.
  3. The app then calls GET /feed. The load balancer receives it on its public IP and forwards it to Server 2, because Server 1 just failed a health check.
  4. Server 2 holds no memory of this user. It reads the session from the shared NoSQL store using the session ID, so it does not matter which server answered last time.
  5. It asks the cache for the user's profile: a hit, returned from memory in a fraction of the time a disk read would take.
  6. The feed items are a miss. The server hashes user_id to find shard 2 and reads from one of that shard's slave replicas, then writes the result into the cache with an expiry.
  7. The user also uploads a photo. The server writes the metadata to shard 2's master, then publishes a "resize photo" message to the queue and responds immediately.
  8. A worker picks up the message seconds later and creates thumbnails; logs and metrics record the latency and error rate of every step for the dashboards.

3 Purpose & Concept Beacons

Scaling is not one big leap but an iterative sequence of removing the current bottleneck and single point of failure. The five takeaways: keep the web tier stateless, build redundancy at every tier, cache aggressively, shard the data tier, and decouple components.

Mental picture

Think of growing a single food truck into a national restaurant chain. The host at the door who seats guests is the load balancer; the interchangeable waiters who carry no private notes are the stateless web servers, and the shared order board is the session store. The spice rack by the stove is the cache, and the vending machines in every neighborhood are the CDN. The head chef who alone changes the recipe book while sous-chefs read copies is master-slave replication; splitting the recipe book into volumes by dish is sharding. The ticket rail between waiters and cooks is the message queue, and opening branches in other cities, with GeoDNS as the signpost, is the multi-data center setup.

Vertical scaling (scale up)Bigger CPU/RAM on one box: simple, but capped by hardware, costly, and still a single point of failure.
Horizontal scaling (scale out)More servers in a pool behind a load balancer; the default choice for large-scale systems.
Load balancerDistributes traffic across servers; gives redundancy (reroute on failure) and scalability (add servers on spikes).
Master-slave replicationWrites to the master, reads from many slaves; you see it whenever reads far outnumber writes.
Slave promotionIf the master dies a slave becomes master; it may be stale, so recovery scripts fill the gap.
Cache (LRU eviction)In-memory store for read-often, write-rarely data; when full, the least recently used item is evicted.
CDNGeographically distributed cache for static content; you pay per transfer and must plan fallback and invalidation.
Stateless web tierSession data lives in a shared store, so any server can handle any request and auto-scaling becomes trivial.
GeoDNSResolves a domain to the nearest data center, cutting latency and enabling failover between regions.
Message queueDurable buffer between producers and consumers; signals asynchronous work and independent scaling of each side.
Sharding keyThe field (e.g. user_id) that decides which shard holds a row; must spread data evenly.
Celebrity problemOne hot key overloads one shard; the fix may be a dedicated shard per celebrity.

4 Opportunistic Drilling

Four ideas carry most of the weight in interviews and later chapters: the load balancer, replication, statelessness, and sharding. Master these and the rest of the chapter reads like variations on a theme.

Load balancer: redundancy and elasticity in one box

Without a load balancer, users connect straight to one web server. If that server goes offline, the site is down; if traffic doubles, the server chokes. Placing a load balancer in front changes the contract: users talk only to the balancer's public IP, and the web servers sit behind it on private IPs.

Two benefits fall out immediately. Redundancy: if Server 1 goes offline, all traffic is routed to Server 2. Scalability: if traffic grows rapidly, you add Server 3, 4, 5 to the pool and the balancer starts using them.

Vertical scalingHorizontal scaling
HowAdd CPU/RAM to one serverAdd more servers behind a load balancer
LimitHard hardware ceilingPractically unbounded
FailureOne box = single point of failureRedundant; traffic rerouted
CostHigh overall cost at the top endCommodity machines added incrementally

Database replication: one writer, many readers

Most applications read far more than they write, so the master-slave model splits the work accordingly. All data-modifying commands (insert, update, delete) go to the master. Copies of the data flow to slaves, which serve reads in parallel. That is why a system usually has many more slaves than masters.

The payoff is threefold: better performance through parallel reads, reliability because data survives the loss of a server, and high availability because the site stays up when a database dies.

  1. One slave, and it dies: reads go temporarily to the master until a replacement slave is added.
  2. Several slaves, one dies: reads are redirected to the other healthy slaves and a new server replaces the dead one.
  3. Master dies: a slave is promoted to master and a new slave is added for replication.
  4. Promoted slave was behind: missing data is filled by data recovery scripts; multi-master and circular replication are alternative setups.
Common trap: assuming slave promotion is lossless. In production the promoted slave may not be up to date, so you must mention recovery scripts or a stronger replication scheme.

Stateless web tier: the key that unlocks auto-scaling

A stateful server remembers a user's session in its own memory. That forces every request from that user back to the same server (sticky sessions), which makes adding or removing servers painful and failures destructive: the session dies with the box.

The fix is to move session data out to a shared data store, shared by every server. Now every web server is interchangeable. The load balancer can send any request anywhere, and servers can be auto-scaled up and down with traffic.

Gains

Easy horizontal scaling, painless auto-scaling, and a server crash no longer logs users out.

Costs

Every request needs a lookup in the shared store, which itself must be fast and redundant.

Sharding: splitting the data tier itself

Eventually even a replicated master cannot hold all the data or absorb all the writes. Vertical scaling of the database has physical and cost limits and heightens single-point-of-failure risk. Sharding splits one large database into smaller shards. Each shard has the same schema, but the rows on each are unique to it.

A sharding key decides the placement, for example a function of user_id picks which of four shards holds a user. The single most important decision is choosing a key that spreads data evenly.

ChallengeWhat goes wrongRemedy in the notes
ReshardingA shard fills up from growth, or uneven distribution exhausts some shards fasterConsistent hashing
Celebrity (hotspot)Excessive access to one key overloads its shardAllocate a shard per celebrity
JoinsJoins across shards are hardDe-normalize so queries hit a single table
Common trap: picking a key that looks unique but clusters traffic, such as a timestamp. Evenness of both data and load is what makes a sharding key good.

Test yourself

Write your answer in the margin with your stylus first, then tap to reveal.

Why must the web tier be made stateless before you can auto-scale it?

A stateful server holds session data in its own memory, so a user's requests must keep returning to that same server. Adding or removing servers would then break sessions. Moving session data into a shared store makes every server interchangeable, so the load balancer can route anywhere and servers can come and go freely.

What happens if the master database goes offline?

A slave is promoted to be the new master and a new slave is added. Because the promoted slave may not be fully up to date, missing data must be recovered with data recovery scripts; multi-master or circular replication can help.

Compare vertical and horizontal scaling.

Vertical scaling adds CPU and RAM to one machine: simple but capped by hardware, expensive, and without redundancy. Horizontal scaling adds more machines behind a load balancer, giving redundancy and near-unlimited growth, which is why large systems prefer it.

When is a cache the right tool, and what policy removes items when it is full?

Use a cache when data is read frequently but modified infrequently. When the cache is full, an eviction policy frees memory; LRU (least recently used) is the most popular. Also plan expiration, consistency with the data store, and multiple cache servers to avoid a single point of failure.

What happens to users if the CDN has a temporary outage?

Clients should detect the problem and fall back to requesting the static resources directly from the origin server. Without that fallback, pages would load without images, CSS or scripts.

Why does sharding make joins hard, and what is the usual workaround?

Related rows may live on different shards on different servers, so a single join query cannot see them all. The common workaround is to de-normalize the data so queries can be answered from a single table on one shard.

What does a message queue buy you compared to a direct call?

Producers publish a message and move on; consumers process it asynchronously when they are ready. The queue buffers bursts and decouples the two sides, so each can scale and fail independently.

Introduction

Scaling a system to support millions of users is a complex, iterative journey requiring refinement and optimization. This chapter outlines how to begin with a single server setup and scale the architecture step by step to handle millions of users.

Section 1: Single Server Setup

Initially, all components (web app, database, cache) run on a single server.

Request Flow

  1. Users access the application via domain names (e.g., api.mysite.com), resolved to IP addresses using DNS.
  2. IP address of the web-server is returned to the browser or mobile app.
  3. HTTP requests are sent to the web server, which returns HTML or JSON responses.

Traffic Sources

  1. Web Applications: Use server-side languages (e.g., Python, Java) for business logic and client-side languages (e.g., JavaScript, HTML) for presentation.
  2. Mobile Applications: Communicate with the web server using HTTP and JSON for lightweight data exchange.

Section 2: Database Separation

As the user base grows, the database is moved to a dedicated server to allow independent scaling of web and database tiers.

Database Choices

  1. Relational Databases (SQL): Structured data stored in tables. Examples: MySQL, PostgreSQL.
  2. Non-Relational Databases (NoSQL): Suitable for unstructured data or low-latency requirements. Categories include:
    • Key-Value Stores
    • Graph Databases
    • Column Stores
    • Document Stores
  • Non-relational databases might be the right choice if:
    • application requires super-low latency.
    • data is unstructured, or there is no relational data.
    • only need to serialize and deserialize data (JSON, XML, YAML, etc.).
    • need to store a massive amount of data.

Section 3: Vertical vs Horizontal Scaling

Vertical Scaling

  • Adds more resources (CPU, RAM) to existing servers.
  • Limited by hardware constraints and lacks redundancy.

Horizontal Scaling

  • Adds more servers to the pool, making it more suitable for large-scale systems.
  • A load balancer is used to handle the request routing between the servers.

Section 4: Load Balancer

A load balancer distributes traffic among multiple servers. Benefits include:

  1. Redundancy: If a server goes offline, traffic is rerouted.
    • If server 1 goes offline, all the traffic will be routed to server 2.
  2. Scalability: Easily add servers to handle traffic spikes.
    • If the website traffic grows rapidly, subsequent servers can be added to handle the additional traffic.

Section 5: Database Replication

Master-Slave Model

  • Master Database: Handles write operations.
    • All the data-modifying commands like insert, delete, or update must be sent to the master database.
  • Slave Databases: Handle read operations, improving performance and reliability.
    • Since the ratio of reads to writes is higher in most applications; thus, the number of slave databases in a system is usually larger than the number of master databases.

Benefits

  1. Improved performance through parallel read operations.
  2. High availability and data reliability through redundancy.

Failure Handling

  • If only one slave database is available and it goes offline, read operations will be directed to the master database temporarily.
  • In case multiple slave databases are available, read operations are redirected to other healthy slave databases and a new server will replace the old one.
  • If the master database goes offline, a slave database will be promoted to be the new master.
  • In production system the chosen slave database might not be up to date, hence data needs to be updated by running data recovery scripts (methods like multi-masters and circular replication could help).

Section 6: Caching

A cache stores frequently accessed data in memory to reduce database load. The cache tier is a temporary data store layer, much faster than the database.

Caching considerations

  1. Use case: Consider using cache when data is read frequently but modified infrequently.
  2. Expiration Policies: Once cached data is expired, it is removed from the cache. When there is no expiration policy, cached data will be stored in the memory permanently.
  3. Consistency: This means keeping the data store and the cache in sync. Inconsistency can happen because data-modifying operations on the data store and cache are not in a single transaction.
  4. Mitigating failures: A single cache server represents a potential single point of failure, multiple cache servers across different data centers are recommended to avoid SPOF.
  5. Eviction Policies: Once the cache is full, items need to be evicted to free up memory. LRU is the most popular cache eviction policy.

Section 7: Content Delivery Network (CDN)

A CDN improves load times by caching static content (images, CSS, JavaScript) on geographically distributed servers.

Workflow

  1. User requests content from the nearest CDN server.
  2. If unavailable, content is fetched from the origin server and cached.

CDN considerations

  1. Cost: CDNs are run by third-party providers which charge for data transfers in and out of the CDN.
  2. Cache Expiry: The cache expiry time should neither be too long nor too short.
  3. CDN fallback: If there is a temporary CDN outage, clients should be able to detect the problem and request resources from the origin.
  4. Invalidating files: If files are updated the cache should be invalidated to point to the updated files.

Section 8: Stateless Web Tier

By moving session data to a shared datastore, web servers become stateless. This allows:

  1. Easier horizontal scaling.
  2. Auto-scaling based on traffic.

Section 9: Multi-Data Center Setup

Deploying across multiple data centers improves availability and reduces latency. Strategies include:

  1. GeoDNS Routing: Direct users to the nearest data center.
  2. Data Replication: Synchronize data across centers to prevent inconsistencies.

Key considerations

  • Traffic redirection: Effective tools are needed to direct traffic to the correct data center.
  • Data synchronization: A common strategy is to replicate data across multiple data centers.
  • Test and deployment: Automated deployment tools are vital to keep services consistent through all the data centers.

Section 10: Message Queue

A message queue is a durable component, stored in memory, that supports asynchronous communication. It serves as a buffer and distributes asynchronous requests.

  • Input services, called producers/publishers, create messages, and publish them to a message queue.
  • Other services called consumers/subscribers, connect to the queue, and perform actions defined by the messages.

Section 11: Logging, Metrics, and Automation

Importance

  1. Logging: Tracks errors and system health.
  2. Metrics: Provides insights into performance and user activity.
  3. Automation: Streamlines testing, deployment, and scaling.

Section 12: Database Scaling

Vertical Scaling

  • Adds hardware resources but has physical and cost limitations.
  • Has multiple drawbacks:
    • Greater risk of single point of failures.
    • Overall cost of vertical scaling is high

Horizontal Scaling (Sharding)

  • Divides data across multiple shards using keys (e.g., user_id).
    • Sharding separates large databases into smaller, more easily managed parts called shards.
    • Each shard shares the same schema, though the actual data on each shard is unique to the shard.
  • Sharding key is critical when implementing a sharding strategy. When choosing a sharding key it is important to choose a key that can evenly distribute data.

Challenges

  1. Resharding data: Resharding data is needed when:
    • Single shard could no longer hold more data due to rapid growth.
    • Certain shards might experience shard exhaustion faster than others due to uneven data distribution.
    • Consistent Hashing is used to overcome these problems
  2. Celebrity problem: Excessive access to a specific shard could cause server overload.
    • To solve this problem, we may need to allocate a shard for each celebrity.
  3. Join and de-normalization: Once a database has been sharded across multiple servers, it is hard to perform join operations across database shards.
    • A common workaround is to de-normalize the database so that queries can be performed in a single table.

Conclusion

Key Takeaways

  1. Keep the web tier stateless.
  2. Build redundancy at every tier.
  3. Use caching and CDNs to optimize performance.
  4. Scale the data tier with sharding.
  5. Decouple components for flexibility.

This chapter provides a solid foundation for building scalable systems that can handle millions of users.

02

Back-of-Envelope Estimation

Picture this

Ten minutes into a design interview, the interviewer leans back and asks: "So how much storage will this need in five years?" There is no calculator, no spreadsheet, just a marker and a whiteboard. A candidate who freezes, or who spends five minutes dividing 99,987 by 9.1 to four decimal places, loses the room. A candidate who says "about 150 million daily users, two posts each, 10% with a 1 MB photo, so roughly 30 TB a day and about 55 PB over five years" wins it. Back-of-the-envelope estimation is that second candidate's skill: fast, rough, clearly reasoned numbers that tell you whether a design can survive reality.

1 Macro Structure & Dependency Map

The chapter has three reference tables you memorize and one method you practice. Read the map as "facts on the left, technique on the right": the facts feed the technique.

  • Powers of two (data volume) — every storage and bandwidth number is expressed in these units
    • 2^10 is about a thousand (KB), 2^20 a million (MB), 2^30 a billion (GB), 2^40 a trillion (TB), 2^50 a quadrillion (PB)
      • Exact byte counts (1,024 vs 1,000) rarely matter at this precision
  • Latency numbers — they tell you which operations are cheap and which will dominate response time
    • Memory is fast (100 ns), disk is slow (HDD seek 10 ms)
      • L1 0.5 ns, L2 7 ns, SSD random read 150 µs
    • Network: round trip in a data center 500 µs, inter-region 150 ms
      • Compress data before sending it over the internet
  • Availability in nines — the language of SLAs and downtime budgets
    • 99% about 3.65 days/year; 99.9% about 8.8 hours; 99.99% about 52 minutes
      • 99.999% about 5.3 minutes; 99.9999% about 31.56 seconds
    • Amazon, Google, Microsoft target SLAs of 99.9% or higher
  • The estimation method — assumptions in, QPS and storage out; this is what the interviewer actually scores
    • Worked example: Twitter QPS and media storage
    • Tips: round aggressively, write assumptions down, label units
      • Common targets: QPS, peak QPS, storage, cache, number of servers

The first three hubs are reference facts; the fourth is the skill that uses them. Powers of two let you convert "150 million times 1 MB" into terabytes without panicking, latency numbers tell you whether a design's hot path can hit memory or must hit disk, and nines translate a vague "highly available" into minutes of downtime. The method stitches them together, and it is the process, not the precision, that is being evaluated.

2 Black-Box Cause & Effect Flow

An estimate is a small pipeline: each stage takes the previous stage's number, multiplies or divides by one assumption, and passes a new number on. Keep every box simple and every unit labeled.

Assumptions

Input: The problem statement plus answers to your clarifying questions.

Output: A short written list: 300M MAU, 50% daily active, 2 tweets/user/day, 10% with media, 5-year retention.

The ingredients list on a recipe card; if it is not written down, nobody can check your cooking.

→ feeds into: DAU calculation

Daily active users

Input: MAU and the daily-active percentage.

Output: DAU = 300M x 50% = 150M.

Of everyone with a gym membership, how many actually walk through the door today.

→ feeds into: QPS and storage

Average QPS

Input: DAU x actions per user per day, divided by 24 hours x 3,600 seconds.

Output: 150M x 2 / 86,400 is about 3,500 tweets per second.

Spreading a day's worth of traffic evenly across every second, like pouring a bucket through a funnel at a constant rate.

→ feeds into: peak QPS

Peak QPS

Input: Average QPS and a peak multiplier (2x in the notes).

Output: 2 x 3,500 is about 7,000 QPS.

Traffic is never flat; the funnel must be wide enough for the evening rush, not just the average.

→ feeds into: number of servers, cache sizing

Daily storage

Input: DAU x tweets/day x media fraction x media size.

Output: 150M x 2 x 10% x 1 MB = 30 TB per day.

How many boxes the moving truck must carry every single day.

→ feeds into: long-term storage

Retention storage

Input: Daily storage x 365 x retention years.

Output: 30 TB x 365 x 5 is about 55 PB.

The size of the warehouse you need once five years of daily deliveries have piled up.

→ feeds into: design decisions (sharding, object storage, cost)

Follow one estimate

  1. Write the assumptions on the board: 300 million MAU, 50% use it daily, 2 tweets per user per day, 10% of tweets contain media, keep data for 5 years.
  2. DAU: 300M x 0.5 = 150M. Say it out loud and write the unit: "150 million users per day".
  3. Tweets per day: 150M x 2 = 300M tweets/day.
  4. Average QPS: 300M / 86,400 seconds. Round 86,400 to about 100,000 for a sanity check (3,000), then state the notes' figure of about 3,500 tweets/s.
  5. Peak QPS: double it, about 7,000 tweets/s. This is the number the write path must survive.
  6. Note the per-tweet sizes: tweet_id 64 bytes, text 140 bytes, media 1 MB. The media dwarfs the rest, so it drives storage.
  7. Media per day: 300M tweets x 10% = 30M media tweets x 1 MB = 30M MB = 30 TB/day.
  8. Five years: 30 TB x 365 is about 11 PB per year; x 5 is about 55 PB. Circle it and tell the interviewer what it implies for the storage design.

3 Purpose & Concept Beacons

Estimation is a thought experiment that checks whether a design can meet its requirements, using a handful of memorized benchmarks. In Jeff Dean's framing, the goal is judgment, not arithmetic precision.

Mental picture

Think of an architect sketching a bridge on a napkin before any engineer runs a simulation. The assumptions are the expected cars per hour and their weight; the powers of two are the ruler markings that let the architect write tons instead of counting kilograms. The latency table is the knowledge that steel is strong and wood is weak, telling the architect which material belongs on the load-bearing span, just as memory belongs on a hot path and disk seeks do not. The nines are the promise of how many days a year the bridge may close for repairs. The napkin number will not be exact, but it instantly tells you whether you need a footbridge or a suspension bridge.

2^10 / 2^20 / 2^30 / 2^40 / 2^50KB, MB, GB, TB, PB: roughly thousand, million, billion, trillion, quadrillion bytes.
Main memory 100 nsMemory access is the cheap path; anything hot should live here (caches).
HDD seek 10 msAbout 100,000 times slower than memory: avoid disk seeks whenever possible.
SSD random read 150 µsMuch faster than HDD, still far slower than memory.
DC round trip 500 µs vs inter-region 150 msCrossing regions costs about 300 times a local round trip; keep chatty calls local and compress what travels.
99.9% (three nines)About 8.8 hours of downtime a year; the typical cloud SLA floor.
99.99% (four nines)About 52 minutes a year; each extra nine cuts downtime roughly tenfold.
QPS = DAU x actions / 86,400Turns daily behavior into per-second load; the first number most designs need.
Peak QPS = 2 x QPSSize for spikes, not averages.
Storage = DAU x items x fraction x sizeMultiply by 365 x years for retention; the biggest object (media) usually dominates.
Round, write, labelApproximate freely, document assumptions, always attach units.

4 Opportunistic Drilling

The worked Twitter estimate, the latency ladder and the nines are what interviewers probe most. Drill them until you can reproduce each from memory in under a minute.

Powers of two: the units that make big numbers tame

Storage math is multiplication of big numbers, and big numbers are only manageable if you can map them onto units instantly. Each step of 2^10 is roughly a factor of a thousand, and each has a name: kilobyte, megabyte, gigabyte, terabyte, petabyte.

That lets you think "30 million megabytes" and immediately say "30 terabytes", because a million MB is a TB. The 1,024-versus-1,000 difference is noise at this level of precision.

The latency ladder: where time actually goes

The absolute numbers matter less than the ratios. Memory is measured in nanoseconds, SSDs in microseconds, spinning disks in milliseconds, and cross-region networks in hundreds of milliseconds. Each jump is orders of magnitude, not percentages.

OperationLatency (2020)What it tells you
L1 cache0.5 nsEffectively free
L2 cache7 nsStill trivially fast
Main memory100 nsThe target for hot data
SSD random read150 µsAbout 1,500x memory
Round trip in data center500 µsEvery internal service call costs this
HDD random seek10 msAbout 100,000x memory; avoid
Inter-region round trip150 msUsers feel this; route them nearby

Three design rules fall out: memory is fast and disk is slow, so cache; avoid disk seeks; and compress data before sending it over the internet, since bandwidth and distance are expensive.

Common trap: mixing up µs and ms. A 150 µs SSD read and a 150 ms inter-region hop differ by a factor of a thousand; label units every time.

Availability in nines: turning promises into minutes

"Highly available" means nothing until you put a number on it. Each added nine divides allowed downtime by about ten: two nines allow about 3.65 days a year, three nines about 8.8 hours, four about 52 minutes, five about 5.3 minutes, six about 31.56 seconds.

An SLA (Service Level Agreement) is the formal promise. Major cloud providers such as Amazon, Google and Microsoft set theirs at 99.9% or higher, so a design built on them inherits roughly that ceiling unless it adds its own redundancy.

AvailabilityDowntime per year
99%~3.65 days
99.9%~8.8 hours
99.99%~52 minutes
99.999%~5.3 minutes
99.9999%~31.56 seconds

The Twitter estimate: the template for every estimate

Almost every estimation question follows the same skeleton: users to active users, active users to actions per second, actions to bytes, bytes to total storage over time. Memorize this one example and you can re-skin it for any product.

  1. DAU = 300M MAU x 50% = 150M.
  2. Tweet QPS = 150M x 2 / 24 h / 3,600 s, about 3,500.
  3. Peak QPS = 2 x 3,500, about 7,000.
  4. Media per day = 150M x 2 x 10% x 1 MB = 30 TB.
  5. Five-year media = 30 TB x 365 x 5, about 55 PB.
Gains

Rounding (e.g. 99,987 / 9.1 becomes 100,000 / 10 = 10,000) keeps you fast and keeps the interviewer following your reasoning.

Costs

The answer is only as good as the written assumptions; an unstated assumption makes a correct calculation look wrong.

Common trap: chasing precision. The interviewer is scoring the process: clear assumptions, labeled units, sensible rounding, and a conclusion about what the number means for the design.

Test yourself

Work each one in the margin with your stylus before you peek.

With 300M MAU, 50% DAU and 2 tweets per user per day, what are average and peak tweet QPS?

DAU is 150M, so 300M tweets per day. Dividing by 86,400 seconds gives about 3,500 QPS on average, and doubling for peak gives about 7,000 QPS.

How did the notes reach about 55 PB of media storage over five years?

150M DAU x 2 tweets x 10% with media x 1 MB = 30 TB per day. Then 30 TB x 365 days x 5 years is about 55 PB.

Why does the latency table push designs toward caching?

Main memory access is about 100 ns while an HDD seek is about 10 ms, roughly 100,000 times slower. Keeping hot data in memory and avoiding disk seeks is therefore the biggest single lever on response time.

Compare 99.9% and 99.99% availability in yearly downtime.

99.9% allows about 8.8 hours of downtime per year; 99.99% allows about 52 minutes. One extra nine cuts permitted downtime by roughly a factor of ten.

What happens if you forget to write down your assumptions?

Neither you nor the interviewer can trace where a number came from, so errors are hard to catch and a correct calculation can look arbitrary. Written assumptions also let you revisit the estimate later when requirements change.

Why compress data before sending it over the internet?

Network transfer, especially across regions at about 150 ms per round trip, is slow and bandwidth is limited. Compressing reduces the bytes on the wire, saving bandwidth and transfer time.

Name the five common estimation scenarios the notes list.

QPS (traffic intensity), peak QPS (spikes), storage requirements, cache requirements (memory needed for caching), and number of servers (hardware based on workload).

Introduction

Back-of-the-envelope estimation is a crucial skill in system design interviews. It involves making quick, rough calculations to assess system capacity or performance. According to Jeff Dean, Google Senior Fellow, these estimates help evaluate whether designs meet requirements through thought experiments and common performance benchmarks.

This chapter covers key concepts, methodologies, and examples to build proficiency in scalability and estimation.

Section 1: Key Concepts

Power of Two

Understanding data volume in terms of powers of two is fundamental:

This knowledge helps in performing accurate storage and bandwidth calculations.

Latency Numbers Every Programmer Should Know

Latency numbers represent the time taken for various operations in computing systems. These provide insights into relative performance:

OperationLatency (2020)
L1 Cache Access0.5 ns
L2 Cache Access7 ns
Main Memory Access100 ns
SSD Random Read150 µs
HDD Random Seek10 ms
Round-Trip in Data Center500 µs
Inter-Region Data Center150 ms

Key Insights:

  • Memory is fast, disk is slow.
  • Avoid disk seeks whenever possible.
  • Compress data before transmitting over the internet to save bandwidth.

Availability Numbers

High availability (HA) ensures minimal downtime. Availability is expressed in nines:

  • 99% (Two Nines): ~3.65 days/year of downtime
  • 99.9% (Three Nines): ~8.8 hours/year of downtime
  • 99.99% (Four Nines): ~52 minutes/year of downtime
  • 99.999% (Five Nines): ~5.3 minutes/year of downtime
  • 99.9999% (Six Nines): ~31.56 seconds/year of downtime

Cloud providers like Amazon, Google, and Microsoft aim for SLAs (Service Level Agreements) of 99.9% or higher.

Section 2: Example Estimation - Twitter QPS and Storage Requirements

Assumptions

  • 300 million monthly active users (MAU).
  • 50% daily active users (DAU).
  • Average tweets/user/day: 2.
  • 10% of tweets contain media.
  • Data retention: 5 years.

Estimations

  1. Query Per Second (QPS):
    • DAU = 300M x 50% = 150M
    • Tweets QPS = 150M x 2 tweets / 24 hour / 3600 seconds = ~3500
    • Peak QPS = 2 x 3500 = ~7000
  2. Media Storage:
    • Tweet Size Components:
      • tweet_id: 64 bytes
      • text: 140 bytes
      • media: 1 MB
    • Daily Media Storage: 150M x 2 x 10% x 1MB = 30TB per day
    • 5-Year Storage: 30TB x 365 x 5 = ~55PB

Section 3: Tips for Effective Estimation

1. Rounding and Approximation

Precision is not critical; focus on the process. Simplify complex calculations using round numbers. For example: 99987 / 9.1 can be approximated as 100,000 / 10 = 10,000.

2. Write Down Assumptions

Document assumptions clearly for future reference.

3. Label Units

Avoid ambiguity by labeling units (e.g., 5 MB instead of 5).

4. Common Estimation Scenarios

  • QPS (Queries Per Second): Measure traffic intensity.
  • Peak QPS: Account for traffic spikes.
  • Storage Requirements: Estimate total data needs.
  • Cache Requirements: Evaluate memory requirements for caching.
  • Number of Servers: Calculate hardware needs based on workload.
03

System Design Framework

Picture this

The interviewer says six words, "Design a news feed system," and then goes quiet. The clock starts: 45 minutes. One candidate grabs the marker and starts drawing Kafka clusters before knowing whether the feed even has videos. Another asks four sharp questions, sketches five boxes, checks the numbers, and then invites the interviewer to pick which box to open up. Same knowledge, very different outcome. This chapter is the playbook that turns a vague prompt into a structured, collaborative 45 minutes.

1 Macro Structure & Dependency Map

The framework is four steps in strict order, wrapped in communication habits and a time budget. Each step's output is the next step's raw material, so skipping one leaves the next without a foundation.

  • Step 1: Understand the problem & scope — every later decision depends on knowing what is being built and at what scale
    • Ask clarifying questions: key features, scale, web vs mobile, existing constraints
      • News feed examples: mobile or web? how many friends? images and videos? reverse chronological?
    • Document assumptions on the whiteboard
  • Step 2: High-level design & buy-in — the blueprint you and the interviewer agree on before investing in details
    • Box diagram: clients, APIs, databases, caches, CDNs
    • Back-of-the-envelope check against scale constraints
    • Walk through use cases to catch edge cases
      • News feed split: feed publishing flow and feed retrieval flow
  • Step 3: Design deep dive — where you prove depth on the parts that matter most
    • Prioritize key components; discuss bottlenecks; avoid over-engineering
      • URL shortener: hash function; chat: latency and online/offline status; news feed: publishing and retrieval
  • Step 4: Wrap-up — shows self-awareness and forward thinking
    • Identify bottlenecks, recap decisions and trade-offs
    • Propose enhancements
      • Scaling from 1 million to 10 million users; error handling for server failures and network issues
  • Cross-cutting habits — the interview grades collaboration and communication, not just the diagram
    • Dos: ask, communicate, iterate, stay flexible, focus on critical parts
    • Don'ts: premature solutions, going silent, over-engineering
    • Time: 3-10 / 10-15 / 10-25 / 3-5 minutes

The four steps form a chain: scope produces requirements, requirements shape the blueprint, the agreed blueprint tells you where to dive, and the dive gives you material to reflect on in the wrap-up. The habits hub runs alongside all four, because the interviewer is evaluating how you handle ambiguity and collaborate just as much as the final architecture.

2 Black-Box Cause & Effect Flow

Treat each step as a machine with a clear input and a deliverable output. If you cannot name the output of a step, you have not finished it.

Clarifying questions

Input: A vague prompt such as "Design a news feed system".

Output: A short list of features, scale, platforms and constraints.

A tailor measuring you before cutting any cloth.

→ feeds into: written assumptions

Documented assumptions

Input: The answers you received plus reasonable guesses where the interviewer left it to you.

Output: A visible reference list on the whiteboard.

A contract pinned to the wall; both sides can point to it when a later decision is questioned.

→ feeds into: the high-level blueprint and the estimates

High-level blueprint

Input: Requirements and assumptions.

Output: A box diagram of clients, APIs, databases, caches and CDNs, split into main flows.

An architect's floor plan: rooms and doors, no furniture yet.

→ feeds into: estimation check and use-case walkthrough

Estimates + use-case walkthrough

Input: The blueprint and the scale assumptions.

Output: Confidence that the design meets scale, plus a list of edge cases, and the interviewer's buy-in.

Walking through the floor plan pretending to be a resident at rush hour to see where people collide.

→ feeds into: choice of deep-dive targets

Deep dive

Input: The agreed blueprint and the components most relevant to this problem.

Output: Detailed design of 1-3 critical components, with bottlenecks and solutions.

Opening one wall to show the plumbing, not re-tiling every bathroom.

→ feeds into: wrap-up

Wrap-up

Input: The complete design and remaining minutes.

Output: Bottlenecks named, decisions and trade-offs recapped, enhancements proposed.

The final walkthrough with the client, including an honest list of what you would improve with more budget.

→ feeds into: the interviewer's overall impression

Follow one interview

  1. Minute 0: the prompt is "Design a news feed system." You resist the urge to draw and pick up the marker only to write "Questions".
  2. Minutes 1-6: you ask whether it is a mobile app, web app or both; how many friends a user can have; whether the feed includes images and videos; and whether it is sorted in reverse chronological order. You write each answer down as an assumption.
  3. Minutes 7-12: you draw boxes for clients, an API layer, databases, a cache and a CDN, and split the design into two flows: feed publishing and feed retrieval.
  4. Minutes 13-18: you run a quick back-of-the-envelope estimate to show the design can handle the scale, and walk through "a user posts a photo" end to end to surface edge cases. You ask, "Does this look reasonable before I go deeper?"
  5. Minutes 19-40: with the interviewer's nod, you deep dive into the feed publishing and retrieval processes, naming bottlenecks and how you would relieve them, while talking through your reasoning out loud.
  6. When the interviewer suggests an alternative, you treat it as a teammate's idea, compare it honestly, and adjust.
  7. Minutes 41-45: you recap the major decisions and trade-offs, name the remaining bottlenecks, and propose next steps: what changes to go from 1 million to 10 million users, and how you would handle server failures and network issues.

3 Purpose & Concept Beacons

A system design interview simulates real-world problem solving under ambiguity. The 4-step framework gives you a repeatable path that shows technical depth, collaboration and communication in 45 minutes.

Mental picture

Think of commissioning a house with a client. First you interview the client about family size, budget and style; that is Step 1, scope and assumptions. Then you sketch a floor plan and get the client to sign off before ordering bricks; that is Step 2, the high-level design and buy-in. Next you detail the kitchen and plumbing, the rooms that make or break the house, rather than choosing doorknobs; that is Step 3, the deep dive into critical components. Finally you do a walkthrough, recapping choices and listing future upgrades; that is Step 4, the wrap-up. Throughout, the client is a partner in the room, which is exactly how you should treat the interviewer.

4-step frameworkScope, high-level design, deep dive, wrap-up: always in this order.
Clarifying questionsFeatures, scale, platform, constraints; they prevent solving the wrong problem.
Written assumptionsA shared reference that makes every later number and decision traceable.
Buy-inThe interviewer agrees with the blueprint before you invest time in details.
Box diagramClients, APIs, databases, caches, CDNs: the vocabulary of Step 2.
Back-of-the-envelope checkConfirms the blueprint can meet the stated scale.
Use-case walkthroughTracing real scenarios through the diagram to expose edge cases.
Deep-dive targetThe component most specific to the problem, e.g. the hash function for a URL shortener.
Over-engineeringAdding complexity the requirements do not demand; a red flag, not a bonus.
1M to 10M usersThe classic wrap-up follow-up: how would the design evolve at ten times the scale?
3-10 / 10-15 / 10-25 / 3-5Minutes per step in a 45-minute interview; the deep dive gets the largest share.

4 Opportunistic Drilling

Steps 1 and 2 are where most candidates lose points, the deep dive is where strong candidates earn them, and time management determines whether you even reach the wrap-up. Drill these.

Step 1: scope before solutions

The most common failure is jumping into a solution before understanding the problem. Interviewers treat that as a red flag because in real engineering, building the wrong thing is the most expensive mistake there is.

Good questions fall into four families: what are the most important features, what scale must the system handle, is it web, mobile or both, and are there existing technologies or constraints. Each answer should go on the whiteboard as an assumption so you and the interviewer share the same picture.

  1. Is it a mobile app, a web app, or both?
  2. How many friends can a user have?
  3. Should the feed include images and videos?
  4. Is the feed sorted in reverse chronological order?
Common trap: asking questions and then not writing the answers down. Five minutes later you cannot remember whether videos were in scope, and your design drifts.

Step 2: the blueprint and the buy-in

The goal is a high-level architecture that the interviewer agrees with. Draw simple boxes for the key components (clients, APIs, databases, caches, CDNs) and treat the interviewer as a teammate who can redirect you early and cheaply.

Two checks make the blueprint trustworthy: a back-of-the-envelope calculation to confirm it can handle the scale, and a walkthrough of concrete use cases to reveal edge cases. For a news feed, splitting the drawing into a feed publishing flow (writing posts and populating friends' feeds) and a feed retrieval flow (aggregating friends' posts in reverse chronological order) makes both checks easier.

Gains

Early agreement means your deep-dive time is spent on what the interviewer actually cares about, and mistakes are caught when they are cheap to fix.

Costs

Takes 10-15 minutes you might be tempted to spend on details; skimping here makes the deep dive feel unanchored.

Step 3: choosing where to dig

You cannot detail everything in 10-25 minutes, so the skill is prioritization. Focus on the components most relevant to this particular problem, discuss the bottlenecks they face, and propose concrete solutions.

ProblemNatural deep-dive focus
URL shortenerHash function design
Chat systemLatency reduction; online/offline status
News feedFeed publishing and retrieval processes

Balance is everything. Too shallow and you show no depth; too deep in an irrelevant corner and you over-engineer while the real bottleneck goes undiscussed.

Common trap: diving into a favorite technology rather than the problem's defining component. Ask yourself: "What would break first at scale?" and go there.

Time management and the wrap-up

In a 45-minute interview, budget roughly 3-10 minutes for scope, 10-15 for high-level design, 10-25 for the deep dive and 3-5 for the wrap-up. The ranges flex with the problem, but the deep dive should always get the biggest slice.

The wrap-up is short but valuable. Name the bottlenecks you know remain, recap the major decisions and their trade-offs, and propose enhancements: how the design would scale from 1 million to 10 million users, and how it handles server failures or network issues. It shows you can critique your own work.

DoDon't
Ask questions to clarify ambiguityDesign before understanding requirements
Communicate your thought processGo silent
Iterate with the interviewer as a collaboratorOver-engineer
Show flexibility and suggest alternatives
Focus on critical components

Test yourself

Jot your answer in the margin with your stylus, then open the card to check.

Why is jumping straight into a solution penalized?

Without clarifying requirements you may design the wrong system entirely. The interview evaluates how you handle ambiguity, and asking good questions first is the evidence of critical thinking the interviewer is looking for.

What are the four steps of the framework and their time budgets in a 45-minute interview?

Understand the problem and scope (3-10 minutes), propose a high-level design and get buy-in (10-15), design deep dive (10-25), and wrap-up (3-5).

What happens if you skip getting buy-in on the high-level design?

You risk spending the deep dive on areas the interviewer does not care about, or building on a blueprint they disagree with. Buy-in turns the interviewer into a collaborator and catches mistakes early, when they are cheap to fix.

How would you split a news feed design at the high level?

Into a feed publishing flow, which writes posts to databases and populates friends' feeds, and a feed retrieval flow, which aggregates friends' posts and displays them in reverse chronological order.

Compare the deep-dive focus for a URL shortener and a chat system.

A URL shortener's defining challenge is hash function design. A chat system's is latency reduction and handling online/offline status. The deep dive should target whichever component is most specific to the problem.

What belongs in the wrap-up?

Identifying remaining bottlenecks, summarizing the major design decisions and trade-offs, and proposing enhancements such as scaling from 1 million to 10 million users and handling server failures or network issues.

Introduction

System design interviews are a key part of the hiring process, simulating real-life problem-solving scenarios. These interviews evaluate not just technical skills but also collaboration, communication, and the ability to handle ambiguous requirements.

This chapter introduces a 4-step framework for navigating system design interviews effectively.

Step 1: Understand the Problem and Establish Design Scope

Key Objectives

  • Clarify requirements and assumptions.
  • Avoid jumping into solutions prematurely.
  • Showcase critical thinking by asking good questions.

Approach

  • Ask Clarifying Questions:
    • What are the most important features?
    • What scale does the system need to handle?
    • Are we building for web, mobile, or both?
    • Are there existing technologies or constraints?
  • Document Assumptions: Write assumptions on a whiteboard or paper for reference.

Example

Problem: Design a news feed system.
Questions:

  • Is it a mobile app, web app, or both?
  • How many friends can a user have?
  • Should the feed include images and videos?
  • Is the feed sorted by reverse chronological order?

Step 2: Propose High-Level Design and Get Buy-In

Key Objectives

  • Develop a high-level architecture.
  • Collaborate with the interviewer to refine the design.

Approach

  • Draft a Blueprint:
    • Use box diagrams for key components (e.g., clients, APIs, databases, caches, CDNs).
    • Treat the interviewer as a teammate to refine the design.
  • Perform Back-of-the-Envelope Calculations:
    • Ensure the design can handle the scale constraints.
  • Walk Through Use Cases: Identify edge cases and validate design assumptions.

Example

For a news feed system, divide the design into:

  1. Feed Publishing Flow: Writing posts into databases and populating friends' feeds.
  2. Feed Retrieval Flow: Aggregating and displaying friends' posts in reverse chronological order.

Step 3: Design Deep Dive

Key Objectives

  • Dive into critical components.
  • Showcase depth of understanding and adaptability.

Approach

  • Prioritize Key Components: Focus on areas most relevant to the problem.
  • Discuss Bottlenecks: Identify potential performance issues and propose solutions.
  • Balance Detail: Avoid over-engineering or unnecessary deep dives.

Example Topics

  • URL Shortener: Focus on hash function design.
  • Chat System: Explore latency reduction and online/offline status handling.
  • News Feed System: Examine feed publishing and retrieval processes.

Step 4: Wrap-Up

Key Objectives

  • Highlight areas for improvement.
  • Recap the design and discuss follow-ups.

Approach

  • Identify Bottlenecks: Discuss potential limitations and scaling strategies.
  • Summarize Design: Recap major design decisions and trade-offs.
  • Propose Enhancements:
    • How to scale from 1 million to 10 million users.
    • Error handling for server failures or network issues.

Best Practices

Dos

  • Ask Questions: Clarify ambiguities before diving into solutions.
  • Communicate: Share your thought process with the interviewer.
  • Iterate with the Interviewer: Treat them as a collaborator.
  • Show Flexibility: Suggest alternative approaches and refine your design.
  • Focus on Critical Components: Prioritize key parts of the system.

Don'ts

  • Avoid Premature Solutions: Don't design before understanding the requirements.
  • Don't Go Silent: Communicate regularly during the process.
  • Avoid Over-Engineering: Focus on practical, scalable solutions.

Time Management

Suggested Time Allocation (for 45-Minute Interviews):

  1. Understand Problem and Scope: 3–10 minutes
  2. High-Level Design and Buy-In: 10–15 minutes
  3. Deep Dive: 10–25 minutes
  4. Wrap-Up: 3–5 minutes
04

Rate Limiter

Picture this

A game studio announces a free in-game reward, one per account. Within minutes a bot farm is hammering the claim endpoint thousands of times a second, creating throwaway accounts and draining the reward pool, while real players stare at spinning loaders because the servers are drowning. Your cloud bill climbs by the minute. What you need is a bouncer at the door who counts, remembers, and politely says "not yet" with an HTTP 429 when someone is coming in too fast. That bouncer is a rate limiter, and the hard part is making it fast, accurate and consistent when it is running on many servers at once.

1 Macro Structure & Dependency Map

The design splits into four questions: what must it do, where does it sit, how does it count, and how does it stay correct at scale. The algorithm hub is the heart; the others are the body built around it.

  • Requirements & purpose — they decide which algorithm and placement are acceptable
    • Why: prevent DoS/resource starvation, reduce cost, prevent overload
      • Real uses: limiting posts, account creations, reward claims
    • Must: accurate throttling, minimal latency, low memory, distributed, clear exceptions, high fault tolerance
      • Server-side API limiter, multiple throttle rules, inform users when throttled
  • Placement — determines whether the limiter can be trusted and how it fits the stack
    • Client-side: unreliable (can be tampered with)
    • Server-side: preferred for control
    • Middleware / API gateway: flexible, natural with microservices
      • Guidelines: match current tech stack, pick algorithm by business needs, buy commercial if resources are limited
  • Counting algorithms — the core decision; each trades accuracy, memory and burst behavior differently
    • Token bucket: refill at fixed rate, each request spends a token
      • Parameters: bucket size, refill rate
    • Leaking bucket: FIFO queue drained at a fixed rate
      • Example implementation: uber-go/ratelimit
    • Fixed window counter: one counter per time slot
      • Edge-burst flaw
    • Sliding window log: store timestamps; sliding window counter: weighted blend of windows
  • Architecture & distributed correctness — one limiter is easy; many limiter instances sharing counters is the real problem
    • Counters in in-memory cache (Redis); middleware checks, then forwards or rejects
    • Race conditions and sync: locks, Lua scripts, Redis sorted sets, centralized store
      • Multi-data center for latency, eventual consistency, monitoring and rule tuning

Requirements come first because "low memory" and "accurate" pull in opposite directions and force the algorithm choice. Placement decides where the counting happens; the algorithm decides how; and the Redis-backed architecture decides whether that counting still holds when dozens of servers are counting at once. The algorithms hub is where interviewers spend the most time.

2 Black-Box Cause & Effect Flow

Every request passes the same short gauntlet: identify, count, compare, decide. Each box is small and fast, because the limiter sits on the hot path of every call.

Client

Input: A user action, e.g. "claim reward".

Output: An HTTP request sent toward the API.

A guest walking up to the club door. You cannot trust the guest to count their own entries, which is why client-side limiting is unreliable.

→ feeds into: rate limiter middleware

Rate limiter middleware (API gateway)

Input: The request plus an identity to limit on (such as a user or IP) and the matching throttle rule.

Output: A lookup of the relevant counter or bucket in Redis.

The bouncer checking the guest list before letting anyone near the bar.

→ feeds into: Redis counter store

Redis counter store

Input: A key for this client and window/bucket.

Output: The current count or token level, updated atomically.

A shared tally board in memory that every bouncer at every door reads and writes, fast because it never touches disk.

→ feeds into: algorithm decision

Algorithm decision

Input: Current count/tokens and the rule's limit.

Output: Allow or throttle.

The rulebook: "no more than N entries per minute" or "one token per entry".

→ feeds into: API servers (allowed) or a throttled response (rejected)

API servers

Input: Only the requests that passed.

Output: Normal responses, with servers kept below overload.

The bar inside the club, never more crowded than it can serve.

→ feeds into: the client's response

Throttled response + monitoring

Input: Rejected requests and analytics about them.

Output: A clear error telling the user they are throttled (commonly HTTP 429 Too Many Requests), plus data used to tune rules.

The bouncer saying "come back in a minute", and the manager later reviewing the door log to decide if the rules are too strict or too loose.

→ feeds into: rule and algorithm adjustments

Follow one request

  1. A player taps "Claim reward". The app sends a request to the API gateway, not directly to the reward service.
  2. The middleware identifies the caller and finds the matching throttle rule, say a token bucket of size 4 refilled with 4 tokens per minute.
  3. It reads the player's bucket from Redis: 1 token left. Because Redis is in memory, the lookup adds only minimal latency.
  4. The request consumes the token (bucket now 0) and is forwarded to the API servers, which process the claim.
  5. A bot using the same account fires a second request 2 seconds later. The bucket is empty, so the middleware rejects it immediately and the API servers never see it.
  6. The client receives a clear throttled error (commonly HTTP 429) and knows to back off, rather than silently failing.
  7. The refiller adds tokens at the next interval; the player's legitimate next claim goes through.
  8. Meanwhile monitoring shows how many requests were dropped, so the team can adjust the bucket size or refill rate if real players are being blocked.

3 Purpose & Concept Beacons

A rate limiter controls how fast clients or services may send traffic, protecting servers from abuse, cost blowouts and overload. The design is a choice of placement and counting algorithm, backed by a fast shared counter store that stays correct under concurrency.

Mental picture

Picture a nightclub. The bouncer at the door is the rate limiter middleware: it stands in front of the club (the API servers) so the crowd inside never exceeds capacity. The clicker counter in the bouncer's hand is the Redis counter; when a club has several doors, all bouncers share one tally board, which is why the store must be centralized and updated atomically. The house rules ("four guests a minute", "one wristband per entry") are the algorithm and its parameters. A guest turned away is told why and when to return, which is the throttled response. And the manager reviewing the door logs each night is monitoring, tuning the rules so real customers are not left outside.

Server-side / middleware placementThe limiter must sit where clients cannot tamper with it; API gateway is natural with microservices.
Token bucketTokens refill at a fixed rate; each request spends one. Allows bursts up to bucket size.
Bucket size + refill rateThe two knobs of token bucket; mis-tuning them is its main weakness.
Leaking bucketFIFO queue drained at a fixed rate; gives a stable outflow but bursts delay newer requests.
Fixed window counterOne counter per time slot; simple, but bursts at window edges can exceed the quota.
Sliding window logKeeps a timestamp per request; most accurate, but memory-hungry.
Sliding window counterBlends current and previous window counts; memory-efficient, smooths spikes, slightly approximate.
Redis (in-memory counters)Fast shared counter storage; signals that the limiter is centralized, not per-server.
Race conditionTwo servers read the same count and both allow; fixed with locks, Lua scripts or sorted sets.
Eventual consistencyAcross data centers, counters sync lazily, trading a little accuracy for low latency.
Throttled responseUsers must be clearly told they were limited (commonly HTTP 429), part of the "clear exception handling" requirement.

4 Opportunistic Drilling

Interviewers probe the algorithms hardest, especially token bucket and the fixed-window edge problem, then the distributed race condition. Placement is quick but must be justified.

Where the limiter lives

A client-side limiter is unreliable: a malicious client can simply remove or bypass it. Server-side limiting gives you control. A popular middle path is middleware, often an API gateway, sitting between clients and API servers so that throttled requests never reach your business logic.

  1. Evaluate your current tech stack and choose the option that fits it efficiently.
  2. Select the algorithm that matches business needs.
  3. If you already use microservices with an API gateway, put the limiter there.
  4. If engineering resources are limited, a commercial solution may be the better choice.

Token bucket: the default workhorse

Imagine a bucket that holds a fixed number of tokens. A refiller drops new tokens in at a steady rate; once the bucket is full, extra tokens overflow and are lost. Each incoming request must take one token. If a token is available, the request passes; if the bucket is empty, the request is dropped.

Because tokens accumulate while traffic is quiet, a short burst up to the bucket size can pass all at once. That makes it forgiving for real users, and it needs only a count and a timestamp per bucket, so it is memory-efficient.

Gains

Easy to implement, memory-efficient, and allows short bursts of traffic.

Costs

Two parameters, bucket size and refill rate, can be tricky to tune correctly.

Comparing the five algorithms

The leaking bucket is the token bucket's strict sibling: requests enter a FIFO queue and are processed at a fixed rate, like water dripping from a hole. The outflow is perfectly steady, but a burst fills the queue with old requests and newer ones wait or are dropped.

The window-based algorithms count requests in time. The fixed window counter uses one counter per interval and resets it at each boundary. The sliding window log stores every request's timestamp and counts only those inside the rolling window. The sliding window counter estimates the rolling count from the current window's count plus a weighted share of the previous window's.

AlgorithmMechanismProsCons
Token bucketFixed-rate refill; request spends a tokenEasy, memory-efficient, allows burstsParameter tuning
Leaking bucketFIFO queue processed at fixed rateMemory-efficient, stable outflowBursts delay recent requests
Fixed window counterCounter per fixed intervalSimple, efficientEdge bursts exceed quota
Sliding window logTimestamps in rolling windowAccurateHigh memory
Sliding window counterBlend of current and previous windowMemory-efficient, smooths spikesApproximate, not perfectly strict

The fixed-window edge problem

A fixed window counter looks airtight: "5 requests per minute, reset on the minute". But the counter only knows about its own slot. If a client sends 5 requests in the last seconds of one minute and 5 more in the first seconds of the next, both windows see a legal 5, yet 10 requests passed within a few seconds.

This is the classic weakness interviewers want you to spot, and it is exactly why the sliding window variants exist: they measure a rolling window, so a burst straddling the boundary is still counted together.

Common trap: saying the fixed window is "accurate" because each window respects its limit. Its failure is precisely at the edges, where a rolling view would reject the extra requests.

Distributed correctness with Redis

Counters live in Redis because in-memory operations are fast enough to sit on every request's path. The flow is simple: the client hits the middleware, the middleware checks and updates the counter in Redis, and the request is processed or rejected.

The danger appears with many limiter instances. If two instances read "count = 3" at the same moment, both increment to 4 and both allow, even though one should have been blocked. That is a race condition. Locks fix it but slow everything down; Lua scripts run the read-and-update as one atomic step inside Redis; sorted sets suit timestamp-based sliding windows. A centralized data store keeps every instance looking at the same numbers.

ChallengeRemedy in the notes
Race conditionsLocks, Lua scripts, Redis sorted sets
Synchronization across instancesCentralized data store
Latency for global usersMulti-data center setup
Syncing counters across data centersEventual consistency
Rules drifting from realityMonitoring and analytics to adjust rules

Test yourself

Sketch or write your answer in the margin with your stylus, then reveal.

Why is client-side rate limiting considered unreliable?

The client is under the user's control, so a malicious user can modify or bypass it. Server-side or middleware limiting keeps enforcement where you control it.

Compare token bucket and leaking bucket.

Token bucket refills tokens at a fixed rate and lets requests through as long as tokens remain, so it allows bursts up to the bucket size. Leaking bucket queues requests in FIFO order and processes them at a fixed rate, giving a stable outflow but delaying recent requests during bursts. Both are memory-efficient.

What happens with a fixed window counter if a burst lands at a window boundary?

Requests at the end of one window and the start of the next are counted separately, so each window stays under its limit while the combined burst exceeds the quota. Sliding window algorithms fix this by measuring a rolling window.

Why would you choose a sliding window counter over a sliding window log?

The log is accurate but stores a timestamp per request, which consumes a lot of memory. The counter approximates the rolling count from two window counters, so it is memory-efficient and still smooths spikes, at the cost of not being perfectly strict.

What race condition can occur in a distributed rate limiter, and how is it solved?

Two instances can read the same counter value simultaneously, both increment, and both allow a request that should have been blocked. Solutions include locks, Lua scripts that make the read-and-update atomic in Redis, and Redis sorted sets, with a centralized data store for synchronization.

Why store counters in Redis instead of a database on disk?

The limiter runs on every request, so it must add minimal latency. In-memory counters in Redis are fast to read and update, whereas disk access would slow down every call.

What are the two parameters of a token bucket and why do they matter?

Bucket size (how many tokens it can hold, which caps the burst) and refill rate (tokens added per unit time, which sets the sustained rate). Tuning them well is the main challenge of the algorithm.

Introduction

This chapter explores the design and implementation of a rate limiter—a system component used to control traffic rates sent by clients or services. Rate limiters are crucial for preventing abuse, reducing costs, and ensuring the stability of server resources. Examples of their use include limiting posts, account creations, and reward claims.

Benefits of Rate Limiting

  • Preventing DoS Attacks: Blocking excess calls to avoid resource starvation.
  • Cost Reduction: Limiting unnecessary requests to reduce server expenses.
  • Preventing Overloads: Filtering out excessive requests to stabilize server performance.

Step 1: Understanding the Problem

Key Features

  • Server-side API rate limiter.
  • Support for multiple throttle rules.
  • Handle large-scale systems in distributed environments.
  • Option for a standalone service or application-level code.
  • Inform users when throttled.

Requirements

  • Accurate request throttling.
  • Minimal latency.
  • Low memory usage.
  • Distributed capability.
  • Clear exception handling.
  • High fault tolerance.

Step 2: High-Level Design

Placement Options

  1. Client-Side Implementation: Unreliable due to potential misuse.
  2. Server-Side Implementation: Preferred for control and reliability.
  3. Middleware (API Gateway): A flexible option for integrated rate limiting.

Guidelines for Placement

  • Evaluate current tech stack and choose efficient options.
  • Select appropriate algorithms based on business needs.
  • Use an API gateway if microservices are employed.
  • Opt for commercial solutions if resources are limited.

Step 3: Rate Limiting Algorithms

1. Token Bucket

  • Description: Tokens are added to a bucket at a fixed rate; each request consumes a token.
  • Parameters: Bucket size and refill rate.
  • Pros: Easy to implement, memory-efficient, supports traffic bursts.
  • Cons: Requires careful parameter tuning.

2. Leaking Bucket

  • Description: Processes requests at a fixed rate using a FIFO queue.
  • Pros: Memory-efficient, stable outflow rate.
  • Cons: Traffic bursts may delay recent requests.

Example: https://github.com/uber-go/ratelimit

3. Fixed Window Counter

  • Description: Divides time into fixed intervals and uses counters to limit requests.
  • Pros: Simple, efficient for specific use cases.
  • Cons: Traffic spikes at window edges can exceed limits.

Sudden burst of traffic at the edges of time windows could cause more requests than allowed quota to go through.

4. Sliding Window Log

  • Description: Tracks timestamps to allow a rolling time window.
  • Pros: Accurate rate limiting.
  • Cons: High memory consumption.

5. Sliding Window Counter

  • Description: Combines fixed window and sliding log methods for smoothing spikes.
  • Pros: Memory-efficient, handles traffic bursts.
  • Cons: Approximation may not be perfectly strict.

High-Level Architecture

  • Data Storage: Use in-memory caching (e.g., Redis) for fast counter operations.
  • Steps:
    1. Client sends request to middleware.
    2. Middleware checks counters in Redis.
    3. Request is processed or rejected based on limits.

Advanced Considerations

Distributed Environments

  • Challenges: Race conditions, synchronization issues.
  • Solutions: Use locks, Lua scripts, or sorted sets in Redis. Employ centralized data stores for synchronization.

Performance Optimizations

  • Multi-data center setups for reduced latency.
  • Eventual consistency models for synchronization.

Monitoring

  • Regular analytics to ensure algorithm effectiveness and adjust rules as needed.
05

Consistent Hashing

Picture this

It is 9 p.m. on a Friday and your cache cluster of four servers is humming along, each one holding a quarter of your hottest keys. Then server 1 quietly dies. With the classic formula hash(key) % N, N drops from 4 to 3, and in one instant almost every key on every surviving server now "belongs" somewhere else. The caches are still full of data, but nobody is looking in the right place: a storm of cache misses slams straight into your database. Consistent hashing exists so that losing (or adding) one server disturbs only the keys that server actually touched.

1 Macro Structure & Dependency Map

From 10,000 feet this chapter is one problem, one shape, one lookup rule and one fix. Read the map top-down: each hub is a load-bearing idea; the grey peripheral items are details you can reconstruct once the hub is solid.

  • The rehashing problem — the pain that motivates everything else
    • serverIndex = hash(key) % N works while N is fixed
      • Example: 4 servers, keys spread by hash % 4
    • Change N and most keys remap
      • Server 1 goes offline → hash % 3 → most keys land on a new server → cache misses
  • The hash ring — the shape that makes change local instead of global
    • Hash space 0 to 2^160 − 1 (e.g. SHA-1), ends joined into a circle
      • Same hash function f places both servers (by IP or name) and keys
    • Clockwise lookup rule: a key belongs to the first server found walking clockwise
  • Adding & removing servers — the payoff: only one arc of keys moves
    • Added server: keys between it and its anticlockwise predecessor move to it
    • Removed server: keys between its predecessor and it move to the next server clockwise
      • Worked examples: s4 added between s3 and s0; s1 removed, its keys go to s2
  • Virtual nodes — the fix that makes the ring fair
    • Problems with the basic ring: uneven partition sizes, non-uniform key distribution
    • Each server appears many times on the ring
      • More virtual nodes → smaller standard deviation → more balanced load

The rehashing problem is the "why"; the ring is the "how"; the add/remove behaviour is the proof that the ring works; virtual nodes patch the one weakness the plain ring still has. Each hub leans on the previous one, so if you can draw the ring and trace a key clockwise, the rest follows.

2 Black-Box Cause & Effect Flow

Treat each step as a sealed box: something goes in, something comes out, and the output of one is the input of the next. This is the causal chain from "a key arrives" to "the cluster changed and barely noticed".

Hash function f (e.g. SHA-1)

Input: a key string, or a server's IP/name.

Output: a number in the range 0 to 2^160 − 1.

A blender that turns any name into a seemingly random position number. The same input always lands in the same place, which is what makes lookups repeatable.

→ feeds into: placement on the ring

Ring placement

Input: hash values for every server and every key.

Output: points dotted around a circle (s0, s1, s2... and k0, k1, k2...).

Bend the number line until 2^160 − 1 touches 0, and you get a clock face. Servers and keys now share one geography.

→ feeds into: clockwise lookup

Clockwise lookup

Input: a key's position on the ring.

Output: the owning server — the first server met walking clockwise.

Each server "owns" the arc of ring just behind it (anticlockwise). A key simply walks forward until it bumps into an owner.

→ feeds into: routing the read/write to that server

Membership change (add or remove)

Input: a server joining or leaving the ring.

Output: one arc of keys changes owner; every other key stays put.

Adding a house on a circular street only changes the postman's route for the stretch just before the new house.

→ feeds into: minimal redistribution (the whole point)

Virtual nodes

Input: each physical server, replicated as many labelled points (s0_0, s0_1, s0_2...).

Output: many small, interleaved arcs per server instead of one big lopsided arc.

Instead of one big slice of pie per guest, everyone gets many thin slices scattered around the dish, so nobody ends up with half the pie by accident.

→ feeds into: balanced load, no hotspots

Follow one key

  1. A request arrives for key0. The system runs it through the same hash function f used for the servers.
  2. The resulting hash lands key0 near the top of the ring, just anticlockwise of server s0.
  3. Walking clockwise, the first server met is s0, so s0 stores and serves key0.
  4. Traffic grows and you add s4. Its hash places it on the ring between key0 and s0.
