  5. Now the clockwise walk from key0 hits s4 first, so key0 moves to s4.
  6. Which keys moved? Only those between s4 and its anticlockwise predecessor s3. key1, key2 and key3 never notice.
  7. Later s1 fails. Only keys between s0 and s1 are affected, and they slide clockwise to s2. Everything else keeps hitting a warm cache.

3 Purpose & Concept Beacons

Consistent hashing lets you scale horizontally by guaranteeing that a change in server count remaps only a fraction of keys, while virtual nodes keep the data spread evenly enough to avoid hotspots.

Mental picture

Imagine a circular running track with lockers bolted at random spots around it — those lockers are your servers, placed by hashing their names. Every runner (a key) starts at a spot determined by their own hash and jogs clockwise until they reach the first locker, and that is where their bag lives. Bolt a new locker onto the track and only the runners who started in the short stretch just before it change lockers; everyone else jogs to the same place as before. Rip a locker out and only its runners jog a little further to the next one. Finally, to stop one locker from covering a huge empty stretch of track, each owner bolts many small lockers all around the loop — those are virtual nodes — so every owner covers a fair share of the distance.

hash(key) % NThe naive mapping; the instant you see N change, expect most keys to move.
Rehashing problemServer count changes → mass key reassignment → cache misses and overload.
Hash ringThe hash space with its ends joined; the shape that makes change local.
0 to 2^160 − 1The SHA-1 hash space; connect 0 to the maximum value and the line becomes the ring.
Clockwise lookupA key belongs to the first server found moving clockwise from its position.
Affected range (add)From the new server anticlockwise to its predecessor; those keys move to the new server.
Affected range (remove)From the removed server anticlockwise to its predecessor; those keys move to the next server clockwise.
Uneven partitionsWith few servers, arcs between them differ wildly in length.
Non-uniform key distributionKeys can cluster so that one server receives far more than the rest.
Virtual nodesMany ring positions per server; more of them means lower standard deviation and better balance.
HotspotA server overloaded with a disproportionate share of keys — what the ring plus virtual nodes mitigates.
Dynamo, Cassandra, Discord, Akamai, MaglevReal systems using the technique — drop these names to show it is industrial-strength.

4 Opportunistic Drilling

Three ideas carry nearly all the exam and interview weight: why modulo hashing breaks, exactly which keys move on the ring, and why virtual nodes are non-negotiable. Drill these; skim the rest.

Why modulo hashing collapses when N changes

With four servers, serverIndex = hash % 4 spreads keys neatly: key1 and key3 on server 0, key0 and key4 on server 1, and so on. The formula is perfectly fine as long as the pool never changes size.

Now server 1 goes offline. The formula becomes hash % 3, and because the divisor changed, the remainder changes for most keys — not just the ones that lived on server 1. Keys that were happily cached on servers 0, 2 and 3 are suddenly routed elsewhere. The data is still sitting in memory; clients are just knocking on the wrong door.

Common trap: saying "only the dead server's keys are lost". With modulo hashing the damage is global — most keys on healthy servers are remapped too, which is what causes the cache-miss storm.

Exactly which keys move on the ring

The rule to memorise: start at the server that changed and walk anticlockwise until you hit the next server. That arc is the affected range. Nothing outside it moves.

When a server is added, the keys in that arc used to walk past the gap and land on the next server clockwise; now the new server intercepts them. When a server is removed, the keys in its arc keep walking clockwise and land on its successor.

EventAffected rangeWhere the keys goExample from the notes
Server addedNew server → anticlockwise to predecessorTo the new servers4 added; keys between s3 and s4 move to s4
Server removedRemoved server → anticlockwise to predecessorTo the next server clockwises1 removed; keys between s0 and s1 move to s2
Common trap: mixing up directions. Lookup walks clockwise; finding the affected range walks anticlockwise. Say both out loud when you draw it.

Virtual nodes: turning a lumpy ring into a fair one

The plain ring has two flaws. Server positions are effectively random, so with only a handful of servers one might own a huge arc while another owns a sliver (uneven partition sizes). And keys themselves may bunch up, so one server receives far more than its share (non-uniform key distribution).

The fix is to place each server on the ring many times. Server 0 becomes s0_0, s0_1, s0_2; server 1 becomes s1_0, s1_1, s1_2. Each physical server now owns many short, interleaved arcs. Statistically, the more virtual nodes you add, the smaller the standard deviation of load, and the more balanced the data.

Gains

Much more even load; fewer hotspots; when a server leaves, its many small arcs are spread across many neighbours rather than dumped on one.

Costs

More positions to store and search on the ring — extra metadata in exchange for balance.

Why it matters: the three benefits

  1. Minimised redistribution — only a fraction of keys move when servers come and go.
  2. Horizontal scalability — you can add servers without a cluster-wide reshuffle.
  3. Hotspot mitigation — with virtual nodes, data is balanced so no single server is overloaded.

These are why Amazon DynamoDB, Apache Cassandra, Discord, Akamai's CDN and the Maglev load balancer all lean on consistent hashing. In the next chapter, the key-value store uses this exact ring for partitioning and replication.

Test yourself

Sketch a ring in the margin and answer with your stylus before tapping to reveal.

Why does hash(key) % N cause a cache-miss storm when one server dies?

Because N changes, the remainder changes for most keys, not just those on the dead server. Keys still cached on healthy servers are routed to different servers, so lookups miss even though the data exists.

How is the owning server of a key found on the hash ring?

Hash the key onto the ring with the same function used for servers, then walk clockwise from its position. The first server encountered owns the key.

What happens if server s1 is removed from the ring, with s0 before it and s2 after it?

Only keys between s0 and s1 are affected. They continue clockwise and are reassigned to s2. All other keys keep their servers.

You add s4 between s3 and s0. Which keys move and to where?

The keys in the arc from s3 up to s4 (walking anticlockwise from s4 until you hit s3). They used to go to s0; now they stop at s4.

What two problems does the basic ring have, and what fixes them?

Uneven partition sizes and non-uniform key distribution. Virtual nodes fix both by giving each server many ring positions, which shrinks the standard deviation of load.

Compare modulo hashing and consistent hashing when a server is added.

Modulo hashing reshuffles most keys across all servers because the divisor changes. Consistent hashing moves only the keys in one arc to the new server; everything else stays.

What would happen with too few virtual nodes per server?

Arc lengths would vary a lot, so load would be lopsided and some servers would become hotspots. More virtual nodes means lower standard deviation and more balanced data.

Introduction

This chapter explores consistent hashing, a technique essential for achieving horizontal scaling by efficiently distributing requests and data across servers. It minimizes data redistribution when servers are added or removed and ensures an even distribution of data to mitigate issues like server hotspots.

The Rehashing Problem

Explanation

In traditional hashing methods, such as serverIndex = hash(key) % N, data redistribution becomes problematic when the number of servers changes. For example:

  • Removing a server causes most keys to be reassigned, leading to cache misses.
  • Adding a server results in unnecessary key redistributions.

This approach works well when the size of the server pool is fixed. However, problems arise when new servers are added, or existing servers are removed.

Key Issue

Redistribution of most keys when server count changes causes inefficiency and overload.

Consistent Hashing

Definition

Consistent hashing ensures that only a fraction of keys are remapped when servers are added or removed. This minimizes disruptions and enhances scalability.

Key Concepts

  1. Hash Space and Ring: The hash space forms a continuous ring, with hash values distributed from 0 to 2^160-1 (e.g., using hash function like SHA-1). By connecting both ends we get a ring.

Using the same hash function f, we map servers based on server IP or name onto the ring.

  1. Server Lookup

A key's server is determined by traversing clockwise on the ring until a server is found.

  1. Adding and Removing Servers

Adding a server redistributes only nearby keys. Only a fraction of keys are redistributed to the new server.

Removing a server affects only the keys in its range. Only keys from the removed server are reassigned to the next server clockwise.

Challenges and Solutions

Two Issues in Basic Approach

  1. Uneven Partition Sizes: Servers may have unequal data partitions.
  2. Non-uniform Key Distribution: Some servers may receive significantly more keys than others.

Solution: Virtual Nodes

  • Each server is represented by multiple virtual nodes on the ring uniformly distrubuted on the ring.
  • Virtual nodes improve key distribution and balance load. As the number of virtual nodes increases, the distribution of keys becomes more balanced. This is because the standard deviation gets smaller with more virtual nodes, leading to balanced data distribution.

Affected Keys

When servers are added or removed:

  • Added Server: Affected keys are those between the new server and its predecessor. In the following example server 4 is added onto the ring. The affected range starts from s4 (newly added node) and moves anticlockwise around the ring until a server is found (s3). Thus, keys located between s3 and s4 need to be redistributed to s4.
  • Removed Server: Affected keys are those between the removed server and its predecessor. In the following example when a server (s1) is removed, the affected range starts from s1 (removed node) and moves anticlockwise around the ring until a server is found (s0). Thus, keys located between s0 and s1 must be redistributed to s2.

Benefits of Consistent Hashing

  • Minimized Redistribution: Only a fraction of keys are reassigned.
  • Scalability: Enables horizontal scaling.
  • Mitigates Hotspots: Balances data distribution to avoid server overload.

Real-World Applications

  • Amazon Dynamo DB
  • Apache Cassandra
  • Discord
  • Akamai CDN
  • Maglev Load Balancer
06

Key-Value Store

Picture this

A shopper in Mumbai adds sneakers to a cart at the exact moment a fibre cable between two of your data centres is cut. One replica heard about the sneakers; two did not. Should the next get(cart) refuse to answer until the network heals, or answer now with possibly stale data? A single-server hash table never faces this question, but the moment you spread put and get across many machines, you are negotiating with the CAP theorem on every request. This chapter builds a store that stays up, scales out, and lets you tune how strict "consistent" needs to be.

1 Macro Structure & Dependency Map

The whole design is a stack of answers to one question: how do you keep small key-value pairs (under 10 KB) available and correct when they live on many fallible machines? Read the hubs in order — each exists because the previous one created a new problem.

  • CAP trade-off — sets the rules of the game before any component is chosen
    • Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance: pick two
      • CA cannot exist in practice because network partitions are unavoidable
    • So the real choice during a partition: CP (block writes) or AP (serve possibly stale data)
      • CP example: banking systems
  • Partitioning & replication on the ring — where data lives and how many copies exist
    • Consistent hashing spreads keys; virtual nodes proportional to server capacity
      • Automatic scaling as servers join or leave
    • Replicate to the first N servers clockwise
      • Place replicas in distinct data centres
  • Quorum consistency & conflict resolution — the dial between speed and correctness
    • N, W, R and the rule W + R > N
      • Typical: N = 3, W = R = 2
    • Consistency models: strong, weak, eventual
    • Vector clocks detect concurrent (sibling) versions
      • Clients reconcile; clocks may need trimming
  • Failure handling — detect, survive, and heal
    • Detection: gossip protocol with heartbeat counters
    • Temporary failures: sloppy quorum + hinted handoff
    • Permanent failures: Merkle trees for anti-entropy sync
      • Data-centre outages: replicate across data centres
  • Storage engine: write & read paths — what one node does with a single request
    • Write: commit log → memory cache → flush to SSTable
    • Read: memory cache → Bloom filter → SSTable
      • Based on Cassandra's architecture

CAP decides the philosophy; the ring decides placement; quorums and vector clocks decide what "correct" means; failure handling keeps the promises when machines die; the storage engine is the local plumbing on each node. If you remember the order “choose, place, agree, heal, store”, you can rebuild the chapter.

2 Black-Box Cause & Effect Flow

Follow the machinery from the client's API call down to the disk and back out. Each box consumes what the previous box produced.

Client API + coordinator

Input: put(key, value) or get(key).

Output: the request forwarded to the right replicas, and a single response back to the client.

The coordinator is a concierge: any node can play it, it knows who holds what, and it hides the crowd of replicas behind one simple desk.

→ feeds into: ring lookup

Consistent-hash ring (partitioning + replication)

Input: the key.

Output: an ordered list of N replica nodes — the first N servers clockwise from the key.

Same ring as the previous chapter, but the walk does not stop at the first server; it collects N of them, ideally in different data centres.

→ feeds into: quorum

Quorum (N, W, R)

Input: the request fanned out to N replicas, plus the chosen W and R.

Output: success once W write-ACKs or R read replies arrive.

A vote: the coordinator does not wait for everyone, only for enough voters. W + R > N guarantees the read voters and write voters overlap on at least one up-to-date node.

→ feeds into: versioning (on reads) and the storage engine (on each replica)

Versioning with vector clocks

Input: multiple versions of the same key, each tagged with [server, counter] pairs.

Output: either "one version is the ancestor, keep the newer" or "siblings in conflict, let the client reconcile".

Each version carries a family tree. If one tree contains the other, there is no fight; if they branched, someone has to merge them.

→ feeds into: the value returned to the client

Failure machinery (gossip, sloppy quorum, hinted handoff, Merkle trees)

Input: heartbeat counters, down nodes, divergent replicas.

Output: an accurate membership view, uninterrupted writes, and replicas re-synchronised.

The immune system: gossip notices illness, sloppy quorum routes around it, hinted handoff returns borrowed data, and Merkle trees find exactly which cells need repair.

→ feeds into: the quorum having enough healthy voters

Node storage engine

Input: a write or read arriving at one replica.

Output: durable storage (commit log + SSTables) and fast reads (memory cache + Bloom filter).

Scribble the order in a ledger first so nothing is lost, keep a hot copy on the desk, and file it in sorted drawers when the desk fills up.

→ feeds into: the ACK or value returned to the coordinator

Follow one key

  1. The client calls put(key1, val1). It reaches node n6, which acts as coordinator.
  2. n6 hashes key1 onto the ring and walks clockwise, collecting N = 3 replicas: n0, n1 and n2.
  3. The coordinator sends put(key1, val1) to all three in parallel.
  4. On each replica the write is first appended to the commit log on disk, then stored in the memory cache.
  5. With W = 2, the coordinator replies "success" as soon as two ACKs arrive, without waiting for the slowest node.
  6. Suppose n2 is down. Gossip has already marked it offline, so a sloppy quorum uses the next healthy node on the ring instead; when n2 recovers, hinted handoff pushes the write back to it.
  7. Later, get(key1) arrives. With R = 2 the coordinator waits for two replies. Since W + R = 4 > 3, at least one reply carries the latest value.
  8. On the replica, the read checks the memory cache first; if the value was flushed, a Bloom filter points to the SSTables that might hold key1.
  9. If two replies carry sibling vector clocks, both versions go back to the client to reconcile.

3 Purpose & Concept Beacons

Build a decentralised, highly available key-value store where every node has the same responsibilities, data is partitioned and replicated on a hash ring, and the latency-versus-consistency trade-off is a dial (N, W, R) rather than a fixed decision.

Mental picture

Think of a chain of village libraries arranged around a lake (the hash ring). Every book (key) is shelved at the first three libraries you pass walking clockwise from its spot on the shore (N = 3 replicas). Any librarian can take your request and act as your concierge (the coordinator), and they only need two colleagues to confirm a new edition is shelved (W = 2) or two to report what they hold (R = 2). Librarians constantly pass notes about who is still open (gossip); if one library is closed, the next one keeps your book in a labelled box until it reopens (sloppy quorum and hinted handoff). Once in a while two libraries compare a one-line fingerprint of their whole catalogue, and only drill into shelves whose fingerprints differ (Merkle trees).

CAP theoremOnly two of consistency, availability, partition tolerance; since partitions happen, it is really CP vs AP.
CP vs APCP blocks writes to stay correct (banking); AP keeps serving and syncs later (eventual consistency).
N / W / RReplicas, write ACKs needed, read replies needed — the tuning knobs for latency vs consistency.
W + R > NRead and write sets overlap, so strong consistency is guaranteed; typical N = 3, W = R = 2.
R = 1, W = NOptimised for fast reads. Flip it (W = 1, R = N) for fast writes.
Eventual consistencyGiven enough time, all updates propagate and replicas converge.
Vector clock D([S1, v1] ... [Sn, vn])Per-server version counters that reveal whether versions are ancestor/descendant or conflicting siblings.
Gossip protocolNodes share heartbeat counters with random peers; a stale counter means the node is offline.
Sloppy quorumUse the first W/R healthy servers on the ring instead of insisting on the designated ones.
Hinted handoffThe stand-in server pushes changes back once the downed server recovers.
Merkle treeHash tree over key buckets; compare roots, descend only into mismatches, sync only what differs.
Commit log / memory cache / SSTable / Bloom filterDurable append, hot in-memory copy, sorted on-disk files, and a quick "which file might have it" check.

4 Opportunistic Drilling

Quorums, vector clocks and the failure toolkit are where interviewers probe and where the numbers live. The storage paths are a short, reliable win. Go deep here and treat the rest as recall.

CAP in one scenario: what happens when n3 is cut off

Three replicas, n1, n2 and n3. n3 drops off the network. Writes accepted by n1 and n2 cannot reach n3; anything written to n3 just before the cut has not reached n1 and n2 either. Somebody is now holding stale data.

A CP system responds by blocking writes to n1 and n2 so replicas cannot diverge — correct, but unavailable. An AP system keeps accepting reads (possibly stale) and writes on n1 and n2, and syncs to n3 when the partition heals — always up, but only eventually consistent.

Common trap: proposing a "CA" design. In a distributed system network failure is unavoidable, so partition tolerance is mandatory; CA cannot exist in real-world applications.

Quorum consensus: the latency vs consistency dial

The coordinator sends every write to all N replicas but declares success after W acknowledgements. Every read is sent to replicas and returns after R replies. Waiting for fewer nodes is faster; waiting for more is safer.

The magic inequality is W + R > N. If the write set and read set must be larger together than the total, they must share at least one node — and that node has the newest value. With N = 3, W = R = 2, any two readers overlap any two writers.

SettingOptimised forStrong consistency?
R = 1, W = NFast readsYes (1 + N > N)
W = 1, R = NFast writesYes (N + 1 > N)
N = 3, W = R = 2Balanced, the usual choiceYes (4 > 3)
W + R ≤ NLowest latencyNot guaranteed

Vector clocks: spotting a real conflict

Each data item carries a list of [server, version] pairs. When a server writes the item, it bumps its own counter if it is already in the list, or adds itself with counter 1 if not.

To compare two versions X and Y: if every counter in X is less than or equal to its counterpart in Y, X is simply an ancestor and Y wins. If some counter in Y is smaller than in X (and vice versa), they are siblings — concurrent edits — and the system hands both to application logic or the client to reconcile.

Gains

Detects conflicts precisely instead of silently losing one of two concurrent writes.

Costs

Pushes merge logic onto clients, and the clock grows with every server that writes, so it may need trimming.

The failure toolkit: detect, bridge, repair

Detect. One node's accusation is not enough; you want at least two independent sources. In gossip, each node keeps a member list with heartbeat counters, increments its own counter, and periodically sends heartbeats to random nodes. If a member's counter has not increased for a predefined period, it is considered offline.

Bridge temporary failures. A strict quorum would stall if a designated replica is down. A sloppy quorum instead picks the first W healthy servers (for writes) and first R healthy servers (for reads) on the ring. The stand-in holds the data, and hinted handoff pushes it back when the original returns.

Repair permanent failures. Merkle trees make replica comparison cheap. Divide the key space into buckets, hash each key, hash each bucket, then hash pairs upward until one root hash remains. Two replicas compare roots: equal means in sync; different means descend into child hashes until the mismatched bucket is found, and sync only that data.

  1. Divide the key space into buckets.
  2. Hash each key in a bucket with a uniform hash.
  3. Create one hash per bucket.
  4. Combine bucket hashes upward to a single root; compare roots, then children, to find the divergent bucket.

For whole data-centre outages, the answer is simply replication across multiple data centres.

Inside one node: the write and read paths

Borrowed from Cassandra. A write is first persisted to the commit log on disk (so a crash cannot lose it), then saved in the memory cache. When the cache fills, it is flushed to an SSTable — a sorted string table on disk.

A read checks the memory cache first. If the key is not there, a Bloom filter quickly tells which SSTables might contain it, so the node reads only those, then returns the value.

Test yourself

Write your answer in the margin first, then tap to check yourself.

Why can't a real distributed key-value store be a CA system?

Network failure is unavoidable, so the system must tolerate partitions. That leaves a choice between consistency and availability only when a partition occurs.

With N = 3, why does W = R = 2 guarantee strong consistency but W = R = 1 does not?

2 + 2 = 4 > 3, so any read set overlaps any write set on at least one node holding the latest value. 1 + 1 = 2 ≤ 3, so a read might hit only replicas that missed the latest write.

What happens during a partition in a CP system versus an AP system?

CP blocks writes to the reachable nodes to avoid inconsistency, sacrificing availability. AP keeps accepting reads and writes, possibly returning stale data, and syncs when the partition heals.

Given D3([Sx,2],[Sy,1]) and D4([Sx,2],[Sz,1]), is there a conflict? Why?

Yes. D3 has Sy = 1 where D4 has 0, and D4 has Sz = 1 where D3 has 0, so neither dominates. They are siblings and must be reconciled by the client or application logic.

Compare sloppy quorum with hinted handoff.

Sloppy quorum keeps the system available by using the first W or R healthy servers on the ring instead of down ones. Hinted handoff is the follow-up: when the down server recovers, the stand-in pushes the changes back to restore consistency.

Why are Merkle trees efficient for syncing replicas after a permanent failure?

Replicas compare root hashes first and only descend into subtrees whose hashes differ, so they locate inconsistent buckets without scanning everything. Only the differing data is transferred.

Why does the write path append to a commit log before updating the memory cache?

The commit log on disk makes the write durable; if the node crashes, data only held in the memory cache would otherwise be lost. The cache is later flushed to SSTables when full.

Introduction

A key-value store is a type of non-relational database where data is stored as key-value pairs. Each key is unique, and values are accessed using these keys. This chapter details how to design a scalable, high-availability distributed key-value store that supports operations like:

  • put(key, value) for inserting data.
  • get(key) for retrieving data.

Characteristics of the Design

  • Small key-value pairs (<10 KB).
  • Supports big data with high availability and scalability.
  • Automatic scaling and tunable consistency.
  • Low latency.

Single Server Key-Value Store

Implementation

  • Use a hash table to store key-value pairs in memory.
  • Optimizations:
    • Data compression.
    • Storing less frequently accessed data on disk.

Limitation

A single server's memory is limited, requiring a distributed approach for scalability.

Distributed Key-Value Store

A distributed key-value store partitions data across multiple servers and must address trade-offs outlined by the CAP theorem.

CAP Theorem

  1. Consistency: All clients see the same data simultaneously.
  2. Availability: The system responds to every request, even if some nodes are down.
  3. Partition Tolerance: The system continues to operate despite network partitions.

Trade-off: According to CAP theorem only two of the three guarantees can be achieved.

System Types:

  • CP Systems: Consistency and partition tolerance while sacrificing availability (e.g., banking systems).
  • AP Systems: Availability and partition tolerance while sacrificing consistency (e.g., eventual consistency).
  • CA Systems: Consistency and Availability while sacrificing partition tolerance.

Since network failure is unavoidable, a distributed system must tolerate network partition. Thus, a CA system cannot exist in real-world applications.

In a distributed system, partitions are inevitable. When a partition occurs, we must choose between consistency and availability. For example, if node n3 goes down, any data written to nodes n1 or n2 cannot be propagated to n3. Conversely, if data is written to n3 but not yet propagated to n1 and n2, nodes n1 and n2 will have stale data.

  • If we choose CP system, we must block all write operations to n1 and n2 to avoid data inconsistency.
  • If we choose AP system, the system keeps accepting reads, even though it might return stale data. For writes, n1 and n2 keep accepting writes, and data will be synced to n3 when the network partition is resolved.

System Components

1. Data Partitioning

  • Technique: Consistent Hashing is used to distribute data across multiple servers evenly.
  • Advantages:
    • Automatic scaling with server addition/removal.
    • Heterogeneity through virtual nodes. The number of virtual nodes for a server is proportional to the server capacity.

2. Data Replication

  • Replicate data across N servers for high availability.
  • The N servers are chosen by walking clockwise from the server position and choose the first N servers on the ring to store data copies. Place replicas in distinct data centers to improve reliability in case of virtual nodes.

3. Consistency

Since data is replicated at multiple nodes, it must be synchronized across replicas.

  • Quorum Consensus:
    • N: Total replicas.
    • W: Write quorum size. For a write to be considered successful, write must be acknowledged from W replicas.
    • R: Read quorum size. For a read to be considered as successful, read must wait for responses from at least R replicas.
    • Rule: W + R > N ensures strong consistency.
    • The configuration of W, R and N is a typical tradeoff between latency and consistency.
  • If R = 1 and W = N, the system is optimized for a fast read.
  • If W = 1 and R = N, the system is optimized for fast write.
  • If W + R > N, strong consistency is guaranteed (Usually N = 3, W = R = 2).
  • If W + R <= N, strong consistency is not guaranteed.
  • Models:
    • Strong Consistency: A read operation returns a value corresponding to the result of the most updated write data item.
    • Weak Consistency: Subsequent read operations may not see the most updated value.
    • Eventual Consistency: Given enough time, all updates are propagated, and all replicas are consisten

4. Inconsistency Resolution

Replication gives high availability but causes inconsistencies among replicas. Versioning and vector locks are used to solve inconsistency problems.

  • Versioning:
    • Use vector clocks to track data versions and resolve conflicts.
    • Versioning means treating each data modification as a new immutable version of data.

    Server 1 changes the name, and server 2 also changes the name. These two changes are performed simultaneously. Now, we have conflicting values, called versions v1 and v2.

  • Vector Clock
    1. Setup: A vector clock is a [server, version] pair associated with a data item. It can be used to check if one version precedes, succeeds, or in conflict with others.
      • Assume a vector clock represented by D([S1, v1], [S2, v2], …, [Sn, vn]), If data item D is written to server Si, the system must perform one of the following tasks.
      • Where: D is the data item. Si is the server identifier. vi is the version counter for the data at server Si.
    2. Updating the Vector Clock: When a data item is modified at a server:
      • If the server exists in the vector clock, its version counter is incremented.
      • Otherwise, a new entry is added to the vector clock.
    3. Conflict Detection:
      • No Conflict: A version X is an ancestor of version Y if all counters in X are less than or equal to those in Y.
      • Conflict Exists: Two versions are siblings if there is at least one counter in Y that is less than its counterpart in X.
    4. Conflict Resolution: When conflicts are detected (sibling versions), the system relies on application-specific logic or client intervention to reconcile the data.
  • Challenges:
    • Increased complexity for clients.
    • Vector clock size may grow with many updates, requiring trimming strategies to limit its size.

5. Handling Failures

a. Failure Detection

It is insufficient to believe that a server is down because another server says so. Usually, it requires at least two independent sources of information to mark a server down.

  • Gossip Protocol:
    • Each node maintains member IDs and heartbeat counters.
    • Each node periodically increments its heartbeat counter.
    • Each node periodically sends heartbeats to a set of random nodes.
    • If the heartbeat has not increased for more than predefined periods, the member is considered as offline

b. Temporary Failures

  • Sloppy Quorum: Use healthy nodes to maintain operations temporarily.
    • After detecting failures, the system needs to deploy certain mechanisms to ensure availability
    • Instead of enforcing the quorum requirement, the system chooses the first W healthy servers for writes and first R healthy servers for reads on the hash ring.
    • Offline servers are ignored. If a server is unavailable, another server will process requests temporarily
  • Hinted Handoff: Offline servers catch up with changes upon recovery.
    • When the down server is up, changes will be pushed back to achieve data consistency

c. Permanent Failures

  • Use Merkle Trees for efficient synchronization between replicas. A Merkle Tree (or hash tree) is a data structure to efficiently detect and resolve inconsistencies between replicas during permanent failures.
  • Working
    1. Structure:
      • Leaf Nodes store the hash of individual data blocks.
      • Non-Leaf Nodes store the hash of their child nodes.
      • The root hash represents the combined state of all data in the tree.
    2. Building a Merkle Tree:
      • Step 1: Divide the key space into buckets.
      • Step 2: Hash each key in a bucket using uniform hashing.
      • Step 3: Create a single hash for each bucket.
      • Step 4: Combine hashes of buckets to compute higher-level hashes, culminating in the root hash.
    3. Synchronization:
      • To synchronize two replicas:
        • Compare their root hashes.
        • If the root hashes match, the replicas are consistent.
        • If the root hashes differ, compare child hashes recursively to identify inconsistent buckets.
      • Only the inconsistent data is synchronized.
  • Advantages
    • Efficiency: Only inconsistent data is synchronized, reducing data transfer.
    • Scalability: Effective for large datasets with minimal synchronization overhead.
    • Reliability: Ensures data consistency across replicas.

6. Handling Data Center Outages

  • Replicate data across multiple data centers to ensure availability during outages.

Write and Read Paths

1. Write Path (Based on Cassandra architecture)

  • Persist the write in a commit log.
  • Save data to a memory cache.
  • Flush data to SSTable (Sorted String Table) on disk when cache is full.

2. Read Path

  • Check memory cache for the data.
  • If absent, use a Bloom Filter to locate the data in SSTables.
  • Retrieve and return the data.

Final Architecture

  • Clients communicate with the key-value store through simple APIs: get(key) and put(key, value).
  • A coordinator is a node that acts as a proxy between the client and the key-value store.
  • Nodes are distributed on a ring using consistent hashing.
  • The system is completely decentralized so adding and moving nodes can be automatic.
  • Data is replicated at multiple nodes.
  • There is no single point of failure as every node has the same set of responsibilities.
07

Unique-Id Generator

Picture this

On a single database, giving every new row an ID is trivial: auto_increment hands out 1, 2, 3 like a deli-counter ticket roll. Now picture that deli with dozens of counters in several cities, all serving customers at once, and a rule that no two tickets may ever share a number — and that the numbers must roughly tell you who arrived first. Passing one ticket roll around is far too slow; letting each counter print its own risks duplicates. This chapter designs a generator that produces over 10,000 unique, time-sortable, 64-bit numeric IDs per second, with no central ticket roll to become a bottleneck.

1 Macro Structure & Dependency Map

The chapter is a requirements checklist followed by four candidate designs, each tested against that checklist. Snowflake is the winner, so it is the biggest hub; the other three are useful mainly as foils that show why each requirement matters.

  • Requirements — the scorecard every design is judged against
    • Unique and numeric, fits in 64 bits
    • Ordered by date (increasing with time, but not strictly +1)
    • Over 10,000 IDs per second
      • Why plain auto_increment fails: scalability and synchronisation in distributed setups
  • Rejected designs — each fails at least one requirement, which teaches you the requirement
    • Multi-master replication: auto_increment by +k for k servers
      • Hard across data centres; not time-ordered; painful when servers change
    • UUID: 128-bit, generated independently
      • No coordination, scales easily — but too long, not time-sortable, may be non-numeric
    • Ticket server: one central DB hands out numbers
      • Simple, numeric — but a single point of failure
  • Twitter Snowflake bit layout — the chosen design: split 64 bits into meaningful sections
    • 1 sign bit + 41 timestamp + 5 datacenter + 5 machine + 12 sequence
    • Timestamp: milliseconds since a custom epoch (Twitter default 1288834974657)
      • Epoch = Nov 04, 2010, 01:42:54 UTC
    • Sequence: up to 4096 IDs per millisecond per machine, reset every millisecond
  • Operational concerns — what can still go wrong after the design is chosen
    • Clock synchronisation via NTP
    • Section-length tuning for the use case
    • High availability: redundancy and failover

Requirements are the root: without them you cannot say why UUID or a ticket server loses. The rejected designs each expose one tension (coordination vs uniqueness, size vs independence, simplicity vs single point of failure). Snowflake resolves all three by baking time, location and a per-millisecond counter into the bits, and the operational concerns are the fine print on that bargain.

2 Black-Box Cause & Effect Flow

Inside a Snowflake generator, an ID is assembled field by field. Treat each field as a box that contributes a slice of the final 64-bit number.

Requirement filter

Input: candidate designs (multi-master, UUID, ticket server, Snowflake).

Output: Snowflake, the only one that is 64-bit, numeric, time-ordered, decentralised and fast.

A sieve: each requirement shakes out one contender until only one is left in the pan.

→ feeds into: the bit layout

Timestamp section (41 bits)

Input: the machine clock in milliseconds, minus the custom epoch.

Output: the high-order bits of the ID.

Because time sits in the most significant bits, a later ID is numerically bigger — sorting by ID is sorting by time.

→ feeds into: the assembled ID

Datacenter ID + machine ID (5 + 5 bits)

Input: fixed identifiers chosen when the machine starts.

Output: the middle bits, unique per generator (up to 32 × 32 generators).

A return address stamped on every ticket. Two machines printing in the same millisecond still cannot collide, because their addresses differ.

→ feeds into: the assembled ID

Sequence number (12 bits)

Input: how many IDs this machine already issued in the current millisecond.

Output: the low-order bits, 0 to 4095, reset to 0 each new millisecond.

A tally counter clicked for every ticket within the same tick of the clock, wiped clean when the clock ticks over.

→ feeds into: the assembled ID

Clock sync (NTP) and HA

Input: drift between machine clocks; generator failures.

Output: clocks kept close together; generators backed by redundancy and failover.

The whole scheme trusts the clocks, so NTP is the metronome keeping every counter in rhythm.

→ feeds into: IDs that stay correctly ordered across machines

Follow one ID

  1. A web server needs a new ID for a freshly created record. It asks its local Snowflake generator — no network round-trip to a central server.
  2. The generator reads the current time and subtracts Twitter's epoch 1288834974657. In the notes' example the result is 297616116568 milliseconds.
  3. That number fills the 41 timestamp bits, right after the sign bit, which is always 0.
  4. Next come the datacenter bits 01010 (datacenter 10) and the machine bits 01100 (machine 12), configured when the generator started.
  5. This is the first ID this machine has issued in that millisecond, so the 12 sequence bits are all zeros.
  6. The fields are concatenated into one 64-bit number and returned.
  7. Reading it back: take the timestamp bits, convert to decimal (297616116568), add the epoch to get 1586451091225, and convert milliseconds to UTC — Apr 09 2020 16:51:31 UTC. The ID literally carries its birth time.

3 Purpose & Concept Beacons

Generate unique, date-sortable, 64-bit numeric IDs at over 10,000 per second across many machines without any central coordinator, by encoding time, location and a per-millisecond counter directly into the bits.

Mental picture

Imagine every ID as a postmarked envelope. The big date-and-time stamp across the front is the 41-bit timestamp, so stacking envelopes by postmark sorts them by when they were sent. Below it is the post office's region code and branch number — the 5-bit datacenter ID and 5-bit machine ID — so two branches stamping at the same instant still produce different envelopes. In the corner is a little counter the clerk clicks for each envelope within the same millisecond — the 12-bit sequence — reset at every tick. No branch ever phones head office for permission, which is why there is no single point of failure; the only shared thing is the clock on the wall, kept in step by NTP.

64 bitsThe hard size limit; instantly rules out 128-bit UUIDs.
Sortable by dateRules out UUID and multi-master; forces time into the high bits.
10,000+ IDs/secThe throughput bar; a single ticket server becomes the bottleneck and SPOF.
Multi-master (+k)Each DB increments by k (e.g. 1,3,5 and 2,4,6); unique but not time-ordered and awkward to resize.
UUID (128-bit)Coordination-free and easy to scale, but too long, not time-sortable, may be non-numeric.
Ticket serverCentralised auto_increment; simple and numeric, but a single point of failure.
1 | 41 | 5 | 5 | 12Sign, timestamp, datacenter, machine, sequence — the Snowflake layout to draw from memory.
Custom epoch 1288834974657Twitter's zero point (Nov 04, 2010, 01:42:54 UTC); timestamps count from here, not from 1970.
2^5 = 32Maximum datacenters, and maximum machines per datacenter.
2^12 = 4096IDs per machine per millisecond; the sequence resets to 0 each millisecond.
NTPNetwork Time Protocol keeps clocks close, since ordering depends on synchronised time.
Section-length tuningTrade sequence bits for timestamp bits (or vice versa) to fit the workload.

4 Opportunistic Drilling

Interviewers almost always ask you to draw the Snowflake layout and defend it against the alternatives. Nail the bit budget, the comparison table, and the clock caveat, and you have covered most of the chapter's yield.

The Snowflake bit budget, field by field

Sixty-four bits, five sections. The leading sign bit is always 0, keeping the number positive. The next 41 bits are milliseconds since the custom epoch — placing time in the most significant bits is what makes larger IDs later IDs. For scale, 2^41 milliseconds works out to roughly 69 years of headroom from the epoch.

Then 5 bits of datacenter ID and 5 bits of machine ID: 32 datacenters, each with up to 32 machines. Finally 12 bits of sequence: up to 4096 IDs per machine within one millisecond. That is far beyond the 10,000 per second requirement even on a single machine.

SectionBitsCapacitySet when
Sign1Always 0Fixed
Timestamp41ms since custom epochEvery ID
Datacenter ID532 datacentersStartup
Machine ID532 machines per datacenterStartup
Sequence124096 per ms, resets each msEvery ID

Decoding an ID back into a timestamp

Because the timestamp is embedded, any Snowflake ID can be read back into its creation time. Slice out the 41 timestamp bits, convert them to decimal, add the epoch, and convert the resulting milliseconds to UTC.

  1. Take the 41 bits after the sign bit.
  2. Convert binary to decimal: 297616116568.
  3. Add Twitter's epoch 1288834974657: 1586451091225.
  4. Interpret as milliseconds since the Unix epoch and convert to UTC: Apr 09 2020 16:51:31.

Why the other three designs lose

Multi-master replication uses each database's auto_increment but steps by k, where k is the number of servers — with two MySQL servers, one yields 1, 3, 5 and the other 2, 4, 6. Unique, yes, but IDs from different servers do not increase with time, it is hard to stretch across data centres, and changing k when servers join or leave is painful.

UUIDs are the opposite extreme: every server mints 128-bit IDs with no coordination at all. Superb for scaling, but they blow the 64-bit budget and do not sort by time. A ticket server centralises one auto_increment counter: simple and numeric, but every ID depends on one box, which is a single point of failure.

DesignFits 64-bit numericTime-sortableNo central SPOFMain weakness
Multi-masterYesNoYesHard to scale across DCs and resize
UUIDNo (128-bit)NoYesToo long, may be non-numeric
Ticket serverYesIncreasingNoSingle point of failure
SnowflakeYesYesYesDepends on synchronised clocks

The fine print: clocks, tuning, availability

Snowflake quietly assumes every machine agrees on the time. If one clock drifts, its IDs can sort out of order relative to other machines. The notes' remedy is Network Time Protocol (NTP) to minimise drift.

The 41/5/5/12 split is a default, not a law. A workload with low concurrency but a need for a longer lifespan could shrink the sequence and grow the timestamp. And because every insert in the system needs an ID, the generator is mission-critical: build in redundancy and failover.

Gains

Decentralised, 64-bit, time-ordered, 4096 IDs per ms per machine, no coordination per ID.

Costs

Relies on clock sync; datacenter and machine IDs must be assigned uniquely; bit sizes lock in capacity limits.

Common trap: claiming IDs increase by exactly 1. The requirement is only that IDs increase with time; Snowflake IDs jump in large, uneven steps.

Test yourself

Draw the bit layout in the margin from memory, then answer each question before revealing.

Why is UUID rejected even though it needs no coordination?

UUIDs are 128 bits, exceeding the 64-bit requirement, and they are not sortable by time and may be non-numeric. Easy scaling does not compensate for failing the size and ordering requirements.

What are the five Snowflake sections and their bit sizes?

Sign bit (1, always 0), timestamp (41), datacenter ID (5), machine ID (5), sequence number (12). Total 64 bits.

What happens to the sequence number when the millisecond changes?

It resets to 0. Within a single millisecond it counts up to 4095, allowing 4096 IDs per machine per millisecond.

Why does putting the timestamp in the high-order bits make IDs sortable by time?

The most significant bits dominate numeric comparison. An ID created later has a larger timestamp, so it is numerically larger regardless of the lower datacenter, machine and sequence bits.

What goes wrong if machine clocks drift apart, and what is the fix?

IDs from different machines may no longer reflect true creation order, since ordering depends on synchronised clocks. Use Network Time Protocol (NTP) to minimise drift.

Compare a ticket server and multi-master replication.

A ticket server is one central auto_increment: simple and numeric but a single point of failure. Multi-master spreads the load with +k steps, avoiding one SPOF, but IDs are not time-ordered and resizing is hard.

How many distinct generators can the default Snowflake layout support?

32 datacenters times 32 machines per datacenter, from 5 bits each (2^5 = 32).

Introduction

This chapter addresses the challenge of designing a unique ID generator for distributed systems. Traditional auto-increment keys are unsuitable in distributed environments due to scalability and synchronization challenges. The focus is on creating unique, sortable, 64-bit numerical IDs that meet the following requirements:

  • IDs must be unique and ordered by date.
  • IDs must fit within 64 bits.
  • The system should generate over 10,000 IDs per second.

Step 1: Understanding the Problem

Basic Requirements

  • IDs must be unique and numerical and should fit in 64 bits.
  • IDs increment with time but not strictly by +1.
  • IDs should be sortable by date.
  • System must handle high throughput (10,000 IDs/sec).

Step 2: High-Level Design Options

1. Multi-Master Replication

  • Approach: Use database auto_increment with step increments (e.g., +k for k servers).
  • Drawbacks:
    • Hard to scale across data centers.
    • IDs do not always increase with time.
    • Scaling issues when servers are added/removed.

2. UUID (Universally Unique Identifier)

  • Approach:
    • Generate 128-bit unique identifiers independently on each server using UUID.
    • UUIDs can be generated independently without coordination between servers
  • Advantages:
    • No coordination needed between servers.
    • Scales easily with web servers.
  • Drawbacks:
    • Exceeds 64-bit requirement.
    • IDs are not sortable by time and may be non-numeric.

3. Ticket Server

  • Approach: Use a centralized database server to increment and assign IDs.
  • Advantages:
    • Simple to implement for small-scale systems.
    • Generates numeric IDs.
  • Drawbacks:
    • Single point of failure.
    • Synchronization challenges in multi-server setups.

4. Twitter Snowflake Approach

Approach:

  • Divide IDs into sections to ensure uniqueness and scalability.
  • Sign Bit (1 bit): Always 0, potentially distinguishing signed and unsigned numbers.
  • Timestamp (41 bits): Milliseconds since a custom epoch (Twitter's default is 1288834974657, equivalent to Nov 04, 2010, 01:42:54 UTC). Ensures IDs are time-ordered.
  • Datacenter ID (5 bits): Identifies up to 2^5 = 32 datacenters.
  • Machine ID (5 bits): Identifies up to 2^5 = 32 machines within each datacenter.
  • Sequence Number (12 bits): Tracks IDs generated on a machine within the same millisecond, supporting up to 2^12 = 4096 IDs per millisecond. The sequence resets to 0 every millisecond.
  • Advantages:
    • Scalability: Handles 10,000+ IDs per second across multiple servers.
    • Time-Order: Ensures IDs are sortable by time.
    • Decentralization: No single point of failure.

Step 4: Additional Considerations

1. Clock Synchronization

  • Challenge: ID generation assumes synchronized clocks across servers.
  • Solution: Use Network Time Protocol (NTP) to minimize drift.

2. Section Length Tuning

  • Adjust section sizes (e.g., fewer sequence bits, more timestamp bits) based on use case.

3. High Availability

  • ID generators are mission-critical and must be fault-tolerant.
  • Consider redundancy and failover mechanisms.
08

URL Shortener

Picture this

Someone pastes a monstrous Amazon product link — a tangle of /dp/, tracking parameters and referral codes — and gets back tinyurl.com/qtj5opu. Minutes later that tiny link is in a million tweets, and every tap has to bounce instantly to the right page. Now multiply: 100 million new short links every day, kept alive for 10 years, with ten clicks for every link created. The job looks like a toy, but it is really a high-volume dictionary that must mint unique seven-character keys forever and answer lookups at lightning speed.

1 Macro Structure & Dependency Map

Two verbs drive the whole system: shorten (write) and redirect (read). Everything else either creates the short key, stores the mapping, or serves it fast. Read the hubs as layers from the outside in.

  • Requirements & scale — the numbers that size every other decision
    • 100 million URLs generated per day, supported for 10 years
      • 365 billion records, about 365 TB
    • 10:1 read-to-write ratio: reads dominate
    • Short URLs unique and as short as possible
  • API & redirect semantics — the contract with the outside world
    • POST api/v1/data/shorten with {longUrl} → shortURL
    • GET api/v1/shortUrl → longURL for redirection
    • 301 (permanent, browser caches) vs 302 (temporary, good for analytics)
  • Short-key generation — the heart of the design: turning a long URL into 7 characters
    • Base 62 conversion of a unique ID
      • Characters [0-9, a-z, A-Z]; 7 chars ≈ 3.5 trillion URLs
    • Hash (CRC32, MD5, SHA-1) + collision resolution
      • Take first 7 characters; append a predefined string on collision; Bloom filter to check existence
  • Storage & serving — keeping 365 billion mappings and returning them quickly
    • Relational table: id, shortURL, longURL
    • Cache in front of the database on the redirect path
    • Scaling: stateless web tier; DB replication and sharding
      • Rate limiter per IP; analytics on clicks, source, timestamps

The requirements tell you the key must be about seven characters and the read path must be heavily optimised. Key generation is the central decision because it determines whether you need a unique ID generator (from the previous chapter) and whether collisions exist at all. Storage and caching then follow directly from the 10:1 read ratio.

2 Black-Box Cause & Effect Flow

Two pipelines share one table. The shortening pipeline writes a mapping once; the redirecting pipeline reads it many times. Trace the boxes in order.

Shorten API (POST)

Input: {longUrl: longURLString}.

Output: a request to find or create a short key.

The front counter where you hand over your unwieldy address and wait for a claim ticket.

→ feeds into: duplicate check

Duplicate check

Input: the longURL.

Output: the existing shortURL if found; otherwise a signal to create a new one.

Before printing a new ticket, the clerk checks whether this exact address already has one, so the same long URL is not stored twice.

→ feeds into: ID generator (if new)

Distributed unique ID generator

Input: a request for a fresh ID.

Output: a globally unique number, e.g. 2009215674938.

The ticket roll. Because every number is unique, everything derived from it is unique too — no collisions to resolve.

→ feeds into: Base 62 encoder

Base 62 encoder

Input: the numeric ID.

Output: a compact string such as zn9edcu.

Rewrites a long decimal number using 62 symbols instead of 10, so it shrinks to a handful of characters — like writing a big number in a denser alphabet.

→ feeds into: database write

Relational database

Input: the row <id, shortURL, longURL>.

Output: a durable mapping, replicated and sharded for scale.

The master ledger of every claim ticket ever issued: 365 billion lines over 10 years.

→ feeds into: the cache and the redirect path

Redirect path (cache → DB → 301/302)

Input: GET on a shortURL.

Output: an HTTP redirect whose location header is the longURL.

The valet: hand over the ticket, the valet checks the nearby rack (cache) first, walks to the back lot (database) only if needed, then points you to your car.

→ feeds into: the user's browser landing on the long URL

Follow one click

  1. Earlier, someone POSTed https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Systems_design to api/v1/data/shorten. It was not in the database, so the ID generator issued 2009215674938.
  2. Base 62 turned that ID into zn9edcu, and the row <2009215674938, zn9edcu, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Systems_design> was saved.
  3. Now a reader taps https://tinyurl.com/zn9edcu. The browser sends a GET to the load balancer.
  4. The load balancer forwards it to one of many stateless web servers.
  5. The web server looks up zn9edcu in the cache. On a hit, it has the long URL immediately.
  6. On a miss, it queries the database for the <shortURL, longURL> mapping (and can populate the cache for next time).
  7. The server responds with a redirect whose location is the Wikipedia URL — 301 if you want browsers to cache it, 302 if you want every click to come back for analytics.
  8. The browser follows the redirect and the reader lands on the article.

3 Purpose & Concept Beacons

Map each long URL to a unique, as-short-as-possible key and serve a flood of redirects quickly, sized for 100 million new URLs a day over 10 years with reads outnumbering writes ten to one.

Mental picture

Picture a giant coat check at a stadium. When you hand over a bulky coat (the long URL), the attendant takes the next number off a never-repeating ticket roll (the unique ID generator) and writes it in a compact code (Base 62), then records coat and code in the master ledger (the relational database). When you return with your ticket (the short URL click), the attendant first glances at the rack right behind the counter where popular coats hang (the cache) before trekking to the back rooms (the database). Hand over a "permanent" slip (301) and you will never need to visit the counter again for that coat; hand over a "temporary" slip (302) and you come back every time, which lets the manager count visits (analytics).

100M/day × 10 years365 billion records, about 365 TB — the capacity every design choice must hold.
10:1 read-to-writeRedirects dominate, so cache the read path aggressively.
POST api/v1/data/shortenTakes a longUrl, returns a shortURL — the write API.
GET api/v1/shortUrlReturns the longURL to redirect to — the read API.
301 redirectPermanent; the browser caches it, so repeat clicks skip your service (less load).
302 redirectTemporary; every click reaches your service, which is useful for tracking clicks.
Base 62 [0-9, a-z, A-Z]Encode a unique ID in 62 symbols; no collisions, length grows with the ID.
62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillionSeven characters cover far more than the 365 billion URLs needed.
2009215674938 → zn9edcuThe notes' worked Base 62 example; a 13-digit ID collapses to 7 characters.
Hash + collision resolutionCRC32/MD5/SHA-1, keep first 7 chars; collisions need a retry loop or Bloom filter.
Bloom filterFast existence check that avoids hitting the database on every collision test.
Stateless web tier + sharded DBScale web servers by adding boxes; scale data with replication and sharding.

4 Opportunistic Drilling

The key-generation decision, the 301-vs-302 choice, and the two flows are where almost every interview question on this topic lands. The rest (rate limiting, analytics) is worth a sentence each.

Base 62 vs hash + collision resolution

Both approaches aim for a seven-character key. Base 62 starts from a unique numeric ID and simply rewrites it with 62 symbols. Because the input ID is unique, the output string is unique — collisions are impossible by construction. The price is that you need a distributed unique ID generator, and the length is not fixed: it grows as IDs grow.

Hashing starts from the long URL itself. Run it through CRC32, MD5 or SHA-1 and keep the first seven characters. That gives a fixed length and no dependency on an ID generator, but truncating a hash invites collisions: two different URLs can share the same first seven characters.

AspectHash + collision resolutionBase 62 conversion
Short URL lengthFixedNot fixed; grows with the ID
Needs unique ID generatorNoYes
CollisionsPossible; must be resolvedNot possible
Next short URL guessableNo; not based on an IDYes if IDs increment by 1 (security concern)
Common trap: forgetting that Base 62's sequential IDs make short URLs enumerable. If the ID goes up by 1, anyone can guess the next link — mention this as a security concern.

301 vs 302: load versus insight

A 301 says the short URL has permanently moved to the long URL. The browser caches that answer, so the next time the same user clicks, the browser goes straight to the destination without asking your service. Great for reducing load.

A 302 says the move is temporary, so the browser checks back every time. More traffic hits your servers, but you see every click — exactly what you want for analytics like click rates, sources and timestamps.

301 gains

Browser caching cuts repeat requests to your service, lowering load.

301 costs

Repeat clicks bypass you, so you cannot track them; choose 302 when analytics matter.

The shortening flow, step by step

The write path is a short decision tree. The first branch prevents duplicates; the second creates a new, collision-free key using the previous chapter's ID generator.

  1. Receive the longURL.
  2. Check whether it already exists in the database.
  3. If it does, return the existing shortURL.
  4. If not, generate a new unique ID with the distributed ID generator.
  5. Convert the ID to a shortURL with Base 62.
  6. Save <id, shortURL, longURL> in the database.

The redirect flow and scaling it

Because reads outnumber writes ten to one, the redirect path is where performance is won. The request passes through a load balancer to a stateless web server, which checks the cache first and falls back to the database only on a miss, then returns the long URL.

Scaling follows the usual pattern. Web servers hold no state, so you add or remove them freely. The database tier uses replication for availability and sharding to split 365 TB across machines. A rate limiter caps requests per IP to stop abuse, and click analytics (rates, sources, timestamps) feed business insight.

Test yourself

Scribble your answer beside each question before tapping to reveal.

Why are seven Base 62 characters enough for this system?

62^7 is about 3.5 trillion possible keys, while the system needs about 365 billion URLs over 10 years (100 million a day). Seven characters leave plenty of headroom.

When would you choose a 302 redirect instead of a 301?

When you need analytics such as click tracking. A 302 is temporary, so every click comes back to your service; a 301 is cached by the browser, so repeat clicks bypass you.

Compare Base 62 conversion with hash + collision resolution on collisions and dependencies.

Base 62 cannot collide because it encodes a unique ID, but it requires a unique ID generator and its length grows with the ID. Hashing needs no ID generator and has a fixed length, but truncating to seven characters causes collisions that must be resolved.

What happens if the same long URL is submitted twice?

The shortening flow first checks whether the longURL exists in the database. If it does, the existing shortURL is returned and no new ID is generated.

Why is resolving hash collisions by appending a predefined string expensive, and what helps?

Each retry requires checking whether the new short URL already exists, potentially a database query per attempt, and it may loop several times. A Bloom filter makes these existence checks fast.

What security concern does Base 62 introduce, and why?

If IDs increment by 1, the next short URL is easy to predict, so links can be enumerated. Hash-based keys do not have this property because they do not depend on a sequential ID.

Why does the redirect path check the cache before the database?

Reads outnumber writes 10:1, so most traffic is redirects. Serving popular mappings from the cache is faster and shields the database from the bulk of the load.

Introduction

This chapter discusses the design of a URL shortening service like TinyURL. The system's main goals include URL shortening, redirecting, and high scalability to handle large traffic volumes.

Requirements

  • Shortened URLs must be unique and as short as possible.
  • Handle 100 million URL generations per day with a 10-year support capacity.
  • Support efficient read operations with a 10:1 read-to-write ratio.
  • Store 365 billion records, requiring approximately 365 TB of storage over 10 years.

Step 1: High-Level Design

API Endpoints

  1. URL Shortening:
    • Endpoint: POST api/v1/data/shorten
    • Parameters: {longUrl: longURLString}
    • Returns: shortURL
  2. URL Redirecting:
    • Endpoint: GET api/v1/shortUrl
    • Returns: longURL for redirection.

URL Redirection

  • 301 Redirect: A 301 redirect shows that the requested URL is "permanently" moved to the long URL. The browser caches the response, and subsequent requests for the same URL will not be sent to the URL shortening service.
  • 302 Redirect: Temporary; useful for analytics like tracking clicks.

URL Shortening

  • Use a hash function to generate a short URL, mapping long URLs to unique shortened versions.
  • The hash function must satisfy the following requirements:
    • Each longURL must be hashed to one hashValue.
    • Each hashValue can be mapped back to the longURL.

Step 2: Deep Dive into Design

Data Model

Store <shortURL, longURL> mappings in a relational database to optimize memory usage. The table schema includes:

  • id (primary key),
  • shortURL,
  • longURL.

Hash Function

1. Base 62 Conversion:

  • Encodes numbers using characters [0-9, a-z, A-Z], providing 62 possible characters.
  • Base conversion is another approach commonly used for URL shorteners.
  • A unique id can be assigned to the short url and ID can be base 62 converted to get the short URL.
  • A 7-character hash supports up to 3.5 trillion unique URLs, enough for 365 billion URLs.

Example:
Convert ID 2009215674938 to Base 62:

  • 2009215674938 → zn9edcu.

2. Hash + Collision Resolution:

  • Use hash functions like CRC32, MD5, or SHA-1.
  • One approach is to collect the first 7 characters of a hash value; however, this method can lead to hash collisions.
  • To resolve collisions, recursively append a new predefined string until no more collision but this can be expensive.
  • Resolve collisions with Bloom Filters for efficient lookup.

Comparison

  • Hash + Collision Resolution:
    • Fixed short URL length
    • Does not need a unique ID generator
    • Collision is possible and needs resolution
    • Not possible to find the next available short URL because it does not depend on ID
  • Base 62 Conversion
    • The length is not fixed and goes up with ID
    • It needs a unique ID generator
    • Collision is not possible
    • Easy to find the next short URL if ID increments by 1 (Can be a security concern)

URL Shortening Flow

  1. Check if longURL exists in the database.
  2. If found, return the existing shortURL.
  3. Otherwise:
    • Generate a unique ID using a distributed ID generator.
    • Convert the ID to shortURL using Base 62.
    • Store the <id, shortURL, longURL> mapping in the database.

URL Redirecting Flow

  1. User clicks a shortURL.
  2. Query <shortURL, longURL> mapping:
    • Check the cache first for faster access.
    • If not in the cache, query the database.
  3. Redirect the user to longURL.

Additional Considerations

Rate Limiter

  • Prevent abuse by setting limits on requests per IP.

Scalability

  1. Web Tier: Stateless, scalable by adding/removing web servers.
  2. Database Tier: Use replication and sharding.

Analytics

  • Collect data like click rates, source, and timestamps for business insights.

High Availability and Reliability

  • Ensure consistent and reliable services using database replication and fault-tolerant design.
09

Web Crawler

Picture this

You are handed a short list of famous websites and told: "Starting from these, find the rest of the internet. Every page. Every month." Each page you open is a doorway to dozens more, many of them copies of pages you have already seen, some of them endless mazes built by accident or on purpose. Meanwhile, every website owner is watching their server logs, and if your robot hammers their small blog with hundreds of requests a second, you are the villain. The web crawler has to be greedy enough to swallow 1 billion pages a month, yet polite, careful and tireless enough never to trip, loop, or knock anyone over.

1 Macro Structure & Dependency Map

From 10,000 feet, a crawler is a loop: take a URL, download it, pull out new URLs, feed them back in. Read the map below as four hubs; everything else is a guard rail or tuning knob attached to one of them.

  • The crawl loop (BFS over the web graph) — the engine; every other component is a station on this circular conveyor belt
    • Seed URLs start the loop
      • chosen by locality or topic (sports, healthcare)
    • HTML Downloader + DNS Resolver fetch pages
      • DNS cache, short timeouts, geo-distributed servers, robots.txt
    • Content Parser validates pages
      • malformed pages are discarded
    • URL Extractor harvests new links
  • URL Frontier — the "to-do list" that decides what is fetched next, in what order, and how gently
    • Front queues = priority
      • Prioritizer scores by PageRank or update frequency
    • Back queues = politeness
      • one host per queue, one worker per queue, delay between downloads
    • Freshness
      • recrawl based on update history or importance
  • Deduplication ("Seen?" checks) — without it the loop drowns in repeats and never finishes
    • Content Seen? compares page hashes
    • URL Filter drops blacklisted or erroneous links
    • URL Seen? + URL Storage remember visited URLs
      • spider traps handled with URL length limits
  • Scale & robustness envelope — what lets the loop survive 1 billion pages a month and 30 PB of data
    • Distributed crawl servers + consistent hashing
    • Error handling and data validation
    • Extensibility via plug-in modules
      • PNG downloader, web monitor for copyright
    • Content Storage: disk, with popular content in memory

The crawl loop is the heartbeat; nothing exists without it. The URL Frontier sits at the top of the loop and controls its rhythm (priority and politeness). Deduplication sits at the bottom of the loop, deciding what is allowed back in. The scale envelope wraps the whole thing so it can run on many machines without falling over.

2 Black-Box Cause & Effect Flow

Treat each station as a sealed box: something goes in, something comes out. Follow the arrows and you have walked the whole architecture.

Seed URLs

Input: A hand-picked list of starting pages, grouped by locality or topic.

Output: The first entries in the URL Frontier.

The kindling for the fire. Good seeds are well-connected pages, so following their links reaches as much of the web as possible.

→ feeds into: URL Frontier

URL Frontier

Input: New, unseen URLs (from seeds and from the extractor).

Output: The next URL to download, chosen by priority and paced by politeness.

An air-traffic controller. It holds every URL waiting for takeoff and releases them in an order that favours important pages and never crowds one host's runway.

→ feeds into: HTML Downloader

HTML Downloader + DNS Resolver

Input: A URL.

Output: Raw HTML of the page (after resolving the hostname to an IP and checking robots.txt).

The courier. It looks up the street address (DNS), checks the "no entry" signs (robots.txt), then fetches the parcel, giving up quickly on slow servers.

→ feeds into: Content Parser

Content Parser + Content Seen?

Input: Raw HTML.

Output: A valid, never-before-seen page, stored in Content Storage; malformed or duplicate pages are dropped.

The quality inspector and the "haven't we seen this already?" clerk. The page is hashed and the hash compared with stored hashes, so duplicates are caught without comparing text character by character.

→ feeds into: Content Storage and URL Extractor

URL Extractor + URL Filter

Input: A parsed, new page.

Output: A clean list of candidate links, minus blacklisted or erroneous ones.

A prospector panning the page for links, then tossing out the fool's gold.

→ feeds into: URL Seen?

URL Seen? + URL Storage

Input: Candidate URLs.

Output: Only URLs never visited or queued before, which are added to the Frontier and recorded.

The bouncer with a guest list. If your name is on the "already been here" list, you do not get back in, which is what stops the loop from circling forever.

→ feeds into: URL Frontier (loop closes)

Follow one URL

  1. A sports-news homepage is placed in the Frontier as a seed URL (topic strategy: sports).
  2. The Prioritizer scores it highly (high PageRank, frequently updated), so it lands in a high-priority front queue.
  3. The biased queue selector picks that front queue; the queue router drops the URL into the back queue mapped to that host.
  4. The worker thread owning that back queue takes it. The DNS Resolver finds the IP (cached, since the host was hit before), robots.txt allows the path, and the page downloads within the short timeout.
  5. The Content Parser confirms the HTML is well-formed. Its hash does not match any stored hash, so the page is written to Content Storage.
  6. The URL Extractor finds, say, 120 links. The URL Filter removes blacklisted ad-tracker URLs and broken links.
  7. URL Seen? discovers most of the remaining links were already visited; only the handful of brand-new article URLs pass.
  8. Those new URLs enter the Frontier and are recorded in URL Storage. The loop begins again, roughly 400 times a second on average, up to 800 at peak.

3 Purpose & Concept Beacons

A web crawler is a breadth-first traversal of the web graph, disciplined by a Frontier that enforces priority and politeness, and by "Seen?" filters that stop it from repeating itself.

Mental picture

Imagine a vast library expedition. The seed URLs are the first few shelves you are told to start from. The URL Frontier is the expedition's master to-do board, sorted so rare manuscripts (high-priority pages) are fetched first, and split into one lane per library building (host) so no single librarian is overwhelmed. The downloader couriers carry the books back; the Content Parser is the conservator who rejects crumbling volumes; Content Seen? is the archivist who stamps each book's fingerprint (hash) and refuses a second copy. The URL Extractor reads each book's bibliography for new titles, and URL Seen? is the catalogue that says "we already have that one."

1B pages/month = 400 QPS (peak 800)The volume demands many parallel downloaders on distributed servers.
30 PB over 5 yearsStorage is disk-first; only popular content stays in memory.
BFS, not DFSThe web is too deep for depth-first; BFS explores level by level.
Plain BFS ignores importanceSignals that a prioritizer is needed on top of the FIFO queue.
URL FrontierThe scheduling brain: priority, politeness and freshness all live here.
Front queues (f1..fn)Priority lanes; the selector picks high-priority lanes more often.
Back queues (b1..bn)Politeness lanes; one host per queue, one worker per queue.
Hash comparisonDuplicate content is caught by comparing page fingerprints, not full text.
URL Seen?Visited-URL memory; prevents re-downloading and infinite loops.
robots.txtThe site owner's rules; the downloader must obey them.
Spider trapAn infinite URL maze; defended with limits such as maximum URL length.
Consistent hashingSpreads crawl load across servers so they can be added or removed smoothly.

4 Opportunistic Drilling

If you only have time for a few deep dives, spend them here: the Frontier's two queue layers are the signature idea of this chapter, and deduplication plus robustness are what interviewers probe next.

Politeness: the back queues

A naive crawler pulls URLs off one big FIFO queue. Because pages link heavily to their own site, that queue fills with long runs of URLs from the same host, and a fleet of workers would fire them all at once. To the website, that looks like a denial-of-service attack.

The fix is to guarantee one request per host at a time, with a delay between downloads. The trick is structural: give each host its own FIFO queue, and give each queue exactly one worker thread. A single worker is naturally sequential, so the host can never receive two parallel requests from you.

  1. Queue router looks at the URL's hostname.
  2. Mapping table answers "which queue owns this host?"
  3. The URL is appended to that host's back queue, so each queue holds one host only.
  4. Queue selector hands each queue to its assigned worker thread.
  5. The worker downloads sequentially, pausing between tasks.
Common trap: Saying "add a rate limiter" without structure. The point is that politeness comes for free from the host-to-queue-to-single-worker mapping; you do not need global coordination to stop two workers hitting the same host.

Priority: the front queues

Not every page is equal. A forum post with no inbound links is far less valuable than a major news homepage. Plain BFS treats them the same, so the crawler would waste its 400 pages a second on junk.

The Prioritizer takes each URL and computes a priority (for example from PageRank or how often the page changes). URLs are then dropped into front queues f1..fn, each with an assigned priority. A queue selector randomly chooses a front queue, but with a bias towards high-priority ones, so important pages move faster while low-priority pages still trickle through.

LayerJobOrganised bySelector behaviour
Front queuesPrioritizationImportance scoreRandom, biased towards high priority
Back queuesPolitenessHostnameEach queue bound to one worker

Layered together, URLs flow front (what matters most) then back (who can safely be asked). A third concern, freshness, feeds URLs back in for recrawl based on update history or importance, which covers the "track new and updated pages" requirement.

Common trap: Mixing up the two layers. Front = priority, back = politeness. A memorable hook: you decide what first (front), then where it can be sent (back).

Deduplication and problematic content

The web repeats itself constantly: mirrored pages, the same article under several URLs, and links pointing back to pages you already have. There are two separate guards, and they catch different things.

GuardQuestion it answersHow
Content Seen?Have I already stored this exact content, maybe under a different URL?Hash the page and compare with stored hashes
URL Seen?Have I already visited or queued this URL?Look it up in URL Storage

A hash turns a whole page into a short fingerprint. Comparing fingerprints is fast, whereas comparing two full HTML documents character by character across billions of pages would be hopeless.

Beyond duplicates, watch for spider traps (infinitely deep URL structures, defended with URL length limits) and data noise such as ads or spam, which is filtered out as irrelevant.

Common trap: Assuming URL Seen? makes Content Seen? redundant. Two different URLs can serve identical content; only the content hash catches that.

Downloader performance, robustness and extensibility

At 800 QPS peak, small inefficiencies multiply. The downloader relies on four optimizations: distribute crawling across many servers; keep a DNS cache so every URL on a known host does not trigger a fresh lookup; place crawl servers close to the sites they crawl; and use a short timeout so one slow server cannot stall a worker.

Robustness comes from consistent hashing to spread load across downloaders, careful error handling so one bad page cannot crash the system, and data validation to protect content integrity.

Gains

DNS caching and short timeouts keep workers busy; geo-distribution cuts download latency; plug-in modules add new content types cheaply.

Costs

A short timeout may abandon slow but legitimate pages; many distributed servers mean more coordination and more places for failures to hide.

Test yourself

Cover the answer, write your own in the margin with your stylus, then tap to check.

Why does the crawler use BFS rather than DFS, and what is BFS still missing?

The web graph can be extremely deep, so DFS could disappear down one site for a very long time. BFS explores level by level. But plain BFS treats every URL as equally important, which is why the Frontier adds a prioritizer.

How does the back-queue design guarantee only one request per host at a time?
