The mapping table assigns each host to a single back queue, and each queue is served by exactly one worker thread. Because one worker downloads sequentially, and can pause between tasks, a host never receives parallel requests from the crawler.

Compare front queues and back queues.

Front queues handle priority: URLs are sorted by importance and a biased random selector favours higher-priority lanes. Back queues handle politeness: URLs are sorted by host and each lane is bound to one worker.

What happens if you remove the Content Seen? check but keep URL Seen?

The crawler would still avoid revisiting the same URL, but it would store identical pages reached through different URLs. That wastes storage in a system already budgeting about 30 PB over five years, and pollutes the index with duplicates.

What is a spider trap and how do you defend against it?

A spider trap is a URL structure that generates effectively infinite new links, keeping the crawler looping forever. One defence from the notes is a maximum URL length, cutting off absurdly long, auto-generated paths.

Name the four downloader performance optimizations and what each protects.

Distributed crawling (throughput), a DNS cache (avoids repeated slow lookups), geographically distributed crawl servers (lower latency to target sites), and short timeouts (stops unresponsive servers from tying up workers).

Introduction

A web crawler, also known as a spider or robot, is used to discover and collect web content, such as web pages, images, and videos. This chapter focuses on designing a scalable web crawler for search engine indexing.

Applications of Web Crawlers

  1. Search Engine Indexing: Collect web pages to create searchable indexes (e.g., Googlebot).
  2. Web Archiving: Preserve web data for future use (e.g., US Library of Congress).
  3. Web Mining: Extract knowledge from web data (e.g., financial analysis of shareholder reports).
  4. Web Monitoring: Detect copyright or trademark infringements.

Design Challenges

A good web crawler must address:

  • Scalability: Handle billions of pages using parallelization.
  • Robustness: Manage bad HTML, crashes, and malicious links.
  • Politeness: Avoid overwhelming servers with too many requests.
  • Extensibility: Support new content types with minimal changes.

Step 1: Understanding the Problem

Requirements

  1. Crawl 1 billion web pages per month (400 pages/second, peak 800 QPS).
  2. Collect HTML-only content.
  3. Track new and updated pages.
  4. Ignore duplicate content.
  5. Store crawled data for 5 years, requiring ~30 PB of storage.

Step 2: High-Level Design

Components

  1. Seed URLs: Starting points for the crawler.
    • Need to selective as a good starting point that a crawler can utilize to traverse as many links as possible.
    • Can be based on locality based on different popular website or based on topics.
    • Strategies: Categorize by locality or topic (e.g., sports, healthcare).
  2. URL Frontier: Stores URLs to be downloaded.
    • Implemented as a FIFO queue.
  3. HTML Downloader: Downloads web pages from URLs provided by the URL Frontier.
  4. DNS Resolver: Converts URLs to IP addresses.
  5. Content Parser: Validates and parses web pages.
    • Discards malformed pages.
  6. Content Seen?: Checks for duplicate content using hash comparisons (compare the hash values of the two web pages).
  7. Content Storage: Stores HTML pages on disk (popular content in memory to reduce latency).
  8. URL Extractor: Extracts new links from parsed pages.
  9. URL Filter: Excludes blacklisted or erroneous URLs.
  10. URL Seen? Tracks visited URLs to avoid duplication.
  11. URL Storage: Stores already visited URLs.

Workflow

  1. Add Seed URLs to the URL Frontier.
  2. HTML Downloader fetches URLs and resolves their IPs via the DNS Resolver.
  3. Content Parser validates and passes content to the "Content Seen?" component.
  4. If the content is new, extract links via the URL Extractor.
  5. Filter and add unique links to the URL Frontier.

Step 3: Deep Dive into Key Components

DFS/BFS

  • The web can be though of as a directed graph where web pages are nodes and hyperlinks (URLs) as edges.
  • BFS is usually used for graph traversal as the depth can be be very deep thus DFS is not ideal.
  • Standard BFS does not take the priority of a URL into consideration, not every page has the same level of quality and importance.

URL Frontier

  • Politeness:
    • Ensure only one request per host at a time. Add a dealy b/w two download tasks.
    • Use a mapping from hostnames to queues and worker (download) threads.
    • Each downloader thread has a separate FIFO queue and only downloads URLs from that queue.
    • Queue router: Ensures that each queue (b1, b2, … bn) only contains URLs from the same host.
    • Mapping table: It maps each host to a queue.
    • Queue selector: Each worker thread is mapped to a FIFO queue, and it only downloads URLs from that queue. The queue selection logic is done by the Queue selector.
    • Worker thread 1 to N. A worker thread downloads web pages sequentially from the same host. A delay can be added between two download tasks.
  • Priority:
    • Assign higher priority to important pages (e.g., by PageRank or update frequency).
    • Prioritizer: It takes URLs as input and computes the priorities.
    • Queue f1 to fn: Each queue has an assigned priority. Queues with high priority are selected with higher probability.
    • Queue selector: Randomly choose a queue with a bias towards queues with higher priority.
    • Front queues: manage prioritization
    • Back queues: manage politeness
  • Freshness: Recrawl based on update history or importance.

HTML Downloader

  • Robots.txt Compliance: Respect rules in robots.txt files.
  • Performance Optimizations:
    1. Distributed crawling using multiple servers.
    2. Use a DNS cache to avoid repeated lookups.
    3. Geographically distribute crawl servers for faster downloads.
    4. Use a short timeout to avoid slow or unresponsive servers.

Robustness

  1. Consistent Hashing: Distribute load among servers effectively.
  2. Error Handling: Prevent system crashes from exceptions.
  3. Data Validation: Ensure content integrity.

Extensibility

  • Add modules for new content types (e.g., PNG downloader, web monitor).
  • Example: Plug in a module to monitor web content for copyright violations.

Avoiding Problematic Content

  1. Duplicate Content: Detect using hash comparisons.
  2. Spider Traps: Avoid infinite loops with techniques like URL length limits.
  3. Data Noise: Filter irrelevant content like ads or spam.

Step 4: Wrap Up

Key Takeaways

  1. Web crawlers must balance scalability, robustness, politeness, and extensibility.
  2. Politeness prevents overloading servers, while priority ensures important pages are crawled first.
  3. Efficient storage and error handling are crucial for handling large-scale crawling.

Additional Considerations

  • Server-Side Rendering: Handle dynamic content generated by JavaScript or AJAX.
  • Anti-Spam Measures: Exclude low-quality or irrelevant pages.
  • Database Sharding: Scale the data layer using replication and sharding.
  • Horizontal Scaling: Use stateless servers to scale crawl jobs efficiently.
  • Analytics: Collect and analyze data for insights.

Notification System

Picture this

It is 9 a.m. and a dozen services all want to talk to your users at once: billing wants to send payment reminders, shipping wants to say "your parcel is out for delivery," marketing wants to announce a sale. Some messages must reach an iPhone, some an Android phone, some an inbox, some a plain old SMS. Every day that adds up to 10 million push notifications, 1 million texts and 5 million emails. If one server hiccups, a reminder vanishes; if a retry fires twice, a customer gets the same text two times and rolls their eyes. The notification system is the post office that sits between all those eager senders and the user's pocket, and it has to be fast, reliable, and never annoying.

1 Macro Structure & Dependency Map

At the highest level there are senders on the left, delivery providers on the right, and a pipeline in the middle. Read the map as four hubs: the channels you deliver through, the pipeline that carries events, the reliability guarantees, and the user-facing controls.

  • Delivery channels & third-party providers — you never talk to a phone directly; everything is handed to a provider
    • iOS push via APNS; Android push via FCM
    • SMS via Twilio or Nexmo; email via SendGrid or Mailchimp
    • Contact info gathering
      • device tokens table for push; user table for email and phone
  • Decoupled sending pipeline — the backbone that turns "please notify" into delivered messages at scale
    • Trigger services (micro-service, cron job, distributed system)
    • Notification servers (APIs, validation, fetch render data)
      • horizontally scaled; DB and cache moved out
    • Message queues as buffers
      • monitor queue depth to scale workers
    • Workers pull events and call providers
  • Reliability — a notification must not be lost, and must not be sent twice
    • Notification log database for persistence
    • Retry mechanism when providers fail
    • Deduplication by event ID
  • User-facing controls & polish — what keeps the system respectful and measurable
    • Notification settings (opt-in / opt-out per channel)
    • Rate limiting per user
    • Templates for consistent formatting
    • event tracking: open rate, click rate, engagement
    • security: AppKey and AppSecret on push APIs

The channels define the destination and the pipeline defines the route. Reliability is layered onto the pipeline, since queues and workers are exactly where messages can be lost or duplicated. The user controls sit at the front of the pipeline, deciding whether a message should be sent at all.

2 Black-Box Cause & Effect Flow

Each box below receives something and hands something on. Chain them together and you have the final design from the notes.

Trigger service

Input: A business event (a bill is due, a parcel shipped) or a scheduled job.

Output: An API call to the notification servers saying "notify user X about Y."

The customer walking into the post office with a letter. It knows what to say, but not how to deliver it.

→ feeds into: Notification servers

Notification server

Input: The API request.

Output: A validated, fully rendered notification event, placed on the right queue.

The counter clerk. It authenticates the sender, applies rate limits, checks the email or phone number is valid, and looks up the device token, settings and user info from cache or database.

→ feeds into: Message queue for that channel

Message queue

Input: Notification events.

Output: The same events, released at the pace workers can handle.

A holding bay. During a flood of notifications it absorbs the surge, so a busy SMS provider cannot slow down iOS pushes.

→ feeds into: Workers

Worker

Input: One event from the queue.

Output: A request to the third-party provider, a record in the notification log, and a retry if the provider fails.

The courier who actually takes the parcel to the delivery company, writes it in the logbook, and tries again if the depot is closed.

→ feeds into: APNS / FCM / SMS / email provider

Third-party provider

Input: A formatted notification plus the device token, phone number or address.

Output: The message on the user's device or inbox.

The national postal network. You do not own it, so you must plan for it being slow or unavailable.

→ feeds into: User device, and back to analytics via click tracking

Follow one notification

  1. The shipping service (a trigger service) sees an order leave the warehouse and calls the notification API: "tell this user their parcel is on its way."
  2. A notification server authenticates the caller and checks the rate limit for that user.
  3. It reads the user's notification settings from cache: push is opted in. It fetches the user's iOS device token (gathered when the app was installed).
  4. The server builds the event, with a unique event ID, and puts it on the iOS push queue. Analytics records "send pending."
  5. A worker pulls the event, checks the event ID has not been seen before, fills in the "Your order has shipped" template, and writes it to the notification log.
  6. The worker calls APNS. APNS returns an error; the worker puts the event back for retry.
  7. On the second attempt APNS accepts it and delivers the push to the phone. Analytics records "sent."
  8. The user taps the notification. Click tracking reports back to analytics, feeding the open and click-rate metrics.

3 Purpose & Concept Beacons

A notification system is a decoupled, queue-buffered pipeline that turns internal events into messages delivered by third-party providers, without losing them, duplicating them, or spamming the user.

Mental picture

Think of a busy regional post office. Customers at the front counter are the trigger services; the counter clerks are the notification servers, checking the address book (cache and database) and refusing anyone who sends too much (rate limiting). Behind them are four sorting bins, one per channel: these are the message queues. Couriers (workers) take letters from their bin, log each one in a ledger (the notification log), and hand them to outside carriers like APNS or an SMS company. If a carrier's depot is shut, the courier puts the letter back in the bin and tries later, and a stamp with a unique serial number (the event ID) makes sure nobody delivers the same letter twice.

10M push / 1M SMS / 5M email per dayVolume varies per channel, so each channel gets its own queue and workers.
Soft real-timeA small delay is acceptable, which is what makes queueing a good fit.
APNS / FCMApple and Google own the last mile for push; you must go through them.
Device tokenThe address for a push notification, collected at app install.
Single point of failureThe flaw of the first design: one notification server does everything.
Message queue as bufferDecouples producers from senders and absorbs traffic spikes.
Notification logPersistence layer that stops data loss and enables retries.
Event ID dedup"Seen this ID before? Discard it." Prevents double sends.
Opt-in / opt-out settingsChecked before sending; users control each channel.
Rate limitingCaps how often a user is notified, so they do not switch you off.
Queue monitoringA growing queue means you need more workers.
AppKey + AppSecretOnly authenticated clients may call the push APIs.

4 Opportunistic Drilling

The heart of this chapter is the evolution from a fragile single server to a queue-based design, plus the reliability tricks that make it trustworthy. Drill those first.

From the naive design to the decoupled design

The first sketch is simple: trigger services call one notification server, which reads the database and calls the providers directly. It works on a whiteboard, but it has three cracks. It is a single point of failure: if that server crashes, nothing is sent. It is hard to scale, because database, cache and sending logic are bundled together. And it is a performance bottleneck, because rendering and sending notifications is resource-hungry.

The improved design attacks each crack. Databases and caches move out of the notification server. Several notification servers run side by side (horizontal scaling). Message queues sit between the servers and the sending logic, and workers pull from those queues and call the providers.

Problem in first designFix in improved design
Single point of failureMultiple notification servers
Hard to scale parts independentlyDB and cache moved out; servers, queues and workers scale separately
Performance bottleneckQueues buffer load; workers do the heavy sending
Common trap: Putting one shared queue for all channels. The diagram gives each channel its own queue, so an outage at one provider only backs up its own queue and leaves the others flowing.

Reliability: no loss, no duplicates

Two opposite failures haunt a notification system. The first is loss: a worker crashes or a provider errors, and the notification simply disappears. The second is duplication: a retry succeeds but the original also went through, and the user gets the same message twice.

To prevent loss, workers persist notification data in a notification log database and use a retry mechanism. If a provider fails, the event is retried rather than dropped.

To prevent duplicates, every event carries an event ID. When an event arrives, the system checks whether that ID has been seen before. Seen: discard. New: send.

  1. Event arrives at worker.
  2. Look up event ID. Already seen? Drop it.
  3. Otherwise, record it in the notification log and send to the provider.
  4. Provider error? Put it back for retry.
Common trap: Treating retries and dedup as separate features. They are a pair: retries make duplicates more likely, and event-ID dedup is what makes retrying safe.

The final flow and the supporting cast

The updated design adds the components that make the system respectful and measurable. Notification servers now perform authentication and rate limiting at the door. Workers use notification templates so messages are consistent and quick to build. An analytics service records "send pending", "sent" and click tracking, producing open rate, click rate and engagement metrics.

Notification settings live in a dedicated table, and are checked before anything is sent: a user who opted out of SMS should never receive one. Queue monitoring watches how many notifications are waiting; a growing backlog is the signal to add workers.

Gains

Queues let each tier scale on its own and absorb bursts; the log and retries give durability; settings and rate limits protect the user experience.

Costs

More moving parts to operate; delivery is soft real-time rather than instant; you still depend on third parties you cannot control.

Contact info gathering

You cannot notify someone without an address. Contact details are collected when the user installs the app or signs up. Device tokens, needed for push, go into a device tokens table; email addresses and phone numbers live in the user table.

A single user can have several device tokens, one per device, which is why push tokens get their own table rather than a single column on the user record.

Common trap: Forgetting that iOS and Android need different providers. The device token is only useful when sent to the right one: APNS for iOS, FCM for Android.

Test yourself

Jot your answer in the margin with your stylus first, then tap to reveal.

What were the three problems with the initial single-server design?

It was a single point of failure, it was hard to scale the database, cache and processing independently, and it was a performance bottleneck because sending notifications is resource-intensive.

Why put message queues between notification servers and workers?

Queues decouple the parts of the system and act as buffers when a large volume of notifications must go out. Servers can accept requests quickly while workers drain the queues at their own pace, and each tier can scale separately.

What happens if APNS is down for a few minutes?

Workers get errors and use the retry mechanism, returning events to the queue to try again. The notification log keeps the data safe. Because each channel has its own queue, Android, SMS and email keep flowing.

How does the system avoid sending the same notification twice?

Each notification event has an event ID. When an event arrives, the system checks whether that ID has been seen before; if so it is discarded, otherwise the notification is sent.

Compare notification settings and rate limiting.

Settings are the user's choice: opt in or out of each channel, stored in a notification settings table. Rate limiting is the system's choice: a cap on how often any user is notified, to avoid overwhelming them.

What signal tells you to add more workers?

The number of queued notifications. Monitoring queues shows when the backlog is growing, meaning workers cannot keep up.

Introduction

A notification system is essential for modern applications, providing timely updates like product notifications, events, offers, and alerts. Notifications can be sent through:

  1. Push notifications (mobile or desktop),
  2. SMS messages, and
  3. Emails.

The chapter focuses on designing a scalable system capable of sending millions of notifications daily.

Step 1: Understanding the Problem

Requirements

  • Notification Types: Push notifications, SMS, and Emails.
  • Delivery: Soft real-time system with minimal delays.
  • Platforms: iOS, Android, and desktop.
  • Triggers: Notifications can be triggered by client applications or scheduled on servers.
  • Scale:
    • Push Notifications: 10 million/day,
    • SMS: 1 million/day,
    • Emails: 5 million/day.
  • Opt-out Support: Users can disable specific notification types.

Step 2: High-Level Design

Components

  1. Notification Types:
    • iOS Push Notifications: Use Apple Push Notification Service (APNS).
    • Android Push Notifications: Use Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM).
    • SMS Messages: Third-party services like Twilio or Nexmo.
    • Emails: Commercial email services like SendGrid or Mailchimp.
  2. Contact Info Gathering:
    • Collect device tokens, phone numbers, or email addresses during app installation or signup.
    • Store contact info in the database:
      • Device Tokens Table: For push notifications.
      • User Table: For emails and phone numbers.
  3. Notification Sending Flow:
    • Trigger Services:
      • Generate events to initiate notifications (e.g., billing reminders, shipping updates).
      • A service can be a micro-service, a cron job, or a distributed system that triggers notification sending events.
    • Notification Server:
      • Provide APIs for services to send notifications.
      • Carry out basic validations to verify emails, phone numbers.
      • Query the database or cache to fetch data needed to render a notification.
    • Third-Party Services: Deliver notifications to users.

Challenges in Initial Design

  • Single Point of Failure (SPOF): One notification server can crash the entire system.
  • Scalability Issues: Hard to scale databases, caches, and processing components independently.
  • Performance Bottlenecks: High resource demands for sending notifications.

Improved Design

  • Move databases and caches out of the notification server.
  • Introduce horizontal scaling with multiple notification servers.
  • Use message queues to decouple system components.
    • Message queues serve as buffers when high volumes of notifications are to be sent out.
  • Add workers that pull notification events from message queues and send them to corresponding third party services.

Step 3: Design Deep Dive

Reliability

  1. Prevent Data Loss:
    • Persist notification data in a database and implement a retry mechanism.
    • The Notification log database is included for data persistence.
  2. Deduplication:
    • Check event IDs to avoid sending duplicate notifications.
    • When a notification event first arrives, check if it is seen before by checking the event ID. If seen before discard it, otherwise send out the notification.

Additional Components

  1. Notification Templates: Preformatted templates for consistent and efficient notifications.
  2. Notification Settings:
    • Users can opt-in or opt-out for specific channels (push, SMS, or email).
    • Stored in a dedicated notification settings table.
  3. Rate Limiting: Cap the frequency of notifications sent to users.
  4. Retry Mechanism: Retry sending notifications if third-party services fail.
  5. Monitoring Queues: Track queued notifications to scale workers dynamically.
  6. Event Tracking: Collect metrics like open rate, click rate, and engagement.

Security

  • Use AppKey and AppSecret to authenticate and secure APIs for push notifications.

Notification Flow

  1. Trigger services call APIs to send notifications.
  2. Notification servers validate requests and fetch metadata from caches or databases.
  3. Notification events are sent to message queues.
  4. Workers process events and interact with third-party services.
  5. Third-party services deliver notifications to users.

Key Optimizations

  1. Horizontal Scaling: Add more notification servers for load distribution.
  2. Message Queues: Decouple processing to handle high volumes.
  3. Caching: Reduce latency by caching frequently accessed data.
  4. Distributed Crawling: Optimize message delivery geographically for better performance.

News Feed System

Picture this

You post a beach photo and, within seconds, it appears near the top of the feed of each of your friends: hundreds of people, scattered across the world, each opening the app at a different moment. Now multiply that by 10 million daily active users, some with up to 5,000 friends, all posting and scrolling at the same time. Every scroll must feel instant, yet every new post must somehow find its way into thousands of personal timelines. The news feed system is a giant sorting machine that decides, for every user, "what are the latest things from the people I care about?", and it has to answer before your thumb stops moving.

1 Macro Structure & Dependency Map

The whole design splits into two flows, a write path (publishing) and a read path (building the feed), joined in the middle by a cache of post IDs. Read the map as four hubs.

  • Feed publishing (write path) — where a post is born and stored
    • POST /v1/me/feed with content and auth_token
    • Web servers: authentication and rate limiting
      • rate limits prevent spam
    • Post Service writes to post DB and post cache
    • Notification Service tells friends
  • Fanout service — the bridge that copies one post into many feeds; the chapter's central design decision
    • Fanout on write (push) vs fanout on read (pull)
      • hybrid: push for most users, pull for celebrities
    • Graph DB for friend IDs; user cache for settings (muted friends)
    • Message queue and fanout workers
  • News feed building (read path) — what the reader actually experiences
    • GET /v1/me/feed with auth_token
    • News Feed Service reads post IDs from the news feed cache
      • then hydrates full post details from cache or DB
    • Reverse chronological order
  • Cache architecture & scaling — memory is what makes both paths fast
    • Five cache layers: news feed, content, social graph, action, counters
      • hot cache for popular posts
    • DB sharding and read replicas; stateless web tier
    • consistent hashing, monitoring QPS, latency and cache hit rate

Publishing produces posts; building consumes them. The fanout service is the hinge between them, and its choice of push or pull decides how much work lands on each side. The cache layers underneath are what let either path run at 10 million users without crushing the database.

2 Black-Box Cause & Effect Flow

Follow the causal chain from a user pressing "Post" to a friend seeing it. Each box hides its internals; focus on what goes in and what comes out.

Load balancer + web servers

Input: An API call: POST /v1/me/feed (content, auth_token) or GET /v1/me/feed (auth_token).

Output: An authenticated, rate-checked request routed to the right service.

The front gate. It checks your ticket (auth_token), stops anyone posting too much, and points you down the right corridor.

→ feeds into: Post Service and Fanout Service (write), or News Feed Service (read)

Post Service

Input: The new post.

Output: The post saved in the post database and post cache, with a post ID.

The archive clerk. The full content is stored exactly once here; everyone else will only pass around its ID.

→ feeds into: Content cache used by the read path

Fanout Service

Input: The new post ID and the author's user ID.

Output: A filtered friend list plus the post ID, placed on a message queue.

The mail-merge engine. It asks the graph database "who are this person's friends?", removes anyone who muted them, and queues up the delivery job.

→ feeds into: Fanout workers

Fanout workers

Input: Jobs from the queue (post ID plus friend IDs).

Output: The post ID appended to each friend's list in the news feed cache.

A team of postal workers slipping the same small index card (the post ID, not the whole post) into each friend's pigeonhole.

→ feeds into: News feed cache

News Feed Service

Input: A user's GET feed request.

Output: A list of full posts in reverse chronological order.

The reader's assistant. It grabs the stack of index cards from your pigeonhole, then fetches the actual posts, author details and like counts from the other caches.

→ feeds into: The user's screen

Follow one post

  1. Maya, who has 300 friends, posts "Hello" through POST /v1/me/feed with her auth_token.
  2. The load balancer routes her to a web server, which authenticates the token and checks she is within her rate limit.
  3. The Post Service stores the post in the post DB and post cache and assigns it a post ID.
  4. The Fanout Service fetches Maya's 300 friend IDs from the graph DB, then checks the user cache: 2 friends have muted her, so 298 remain.
  5. The post ID and the 298 friend IDs go onto the message queue. The Notification Service separately alerts her friends.
  6. Fanout workers pick up the job and append Maya's post ID to each of the 298 friends' lists in the news feed cache. Old IDs beyond the configured limit fall off the end.
  7. Her friend Raj opens the app: GET /v1/me/feed. The News Feed Service reads his list of post IDs from the news feed cache.
  8. It hydrates each ID into a full post from the content cache, plus Maya's profile and the like counter, and returns them newest first. Maya's "Hello" is at the top.

3 Purpose & Concept Beacons

A news feed system precomputes each user's timeline as a list of post IDs in cache, so reading is fast, and uses a hybrid fanout so that writing stays affordable even for users with huge audiences.

Mental picture

Picture an office building where every employee has a pigeonhole. When someone writes a memo, the original goes into the central filing room (Post Service and post DB). The mailroom (Fanout Service) looks up who should get it in the company directory (graph DB), crosses out anyone who asked not to receive that person's memos (user cache settings), and hands the list to a team of runners (fanout workers). The runners drop a small slip with the memo number into each pigeonhole (the news feed cache), not a full copy. When you check your pigeonhole (GET feed), your assistant (News Feed Service) reads the slips and fetches the actual memos from the filing room, newest first. For the CEO, whose memos would need thousands of slips, the runners skip the slips and readers go and fetch the CEO's latest memo themselves (pull for celebrities).

10M DAU, up to 5,000 friendsA single post can fan out to thousands of feeds, so writes are expensive.
POST /v1/me/feedPublishing API; params are content and auth_token.
GET /v1/me/feedRetrieval API; only the auth_token is needed.
Reverse chronologicalNewest first; a simplifying choice that avoids ranking.
Fanout on write (push)Precompute feeds at post time: fast reads, heavy writes.
Fanout on read (pull)Build feeds at read time: cheap for inactive users, slow reads.
Hybrid fanoutPush for most, pull for celebrities; the standard answer.
Graph DBStores friendships; the source of "who should receive this?"
<post_id, user_id> in cacheStore IDs, not objects, to keep feed cache memory small.
Configurable feed limitOnly recent IDs are cached, because users mostly read the latest.
Five cache layersNews feed, content, social graph, action, counters; each tuned for its data.
Stateless web tierAny server can handle any request, so you scale by adding servers.

4 Opportunistic Drilling

Fanout strategy is the question every interviewer asks about this system, and the fanout pipeline and cache layers are how you back up your answer. Drill these three and you own the chapter.

Push vs pull: choosing a fanout model

There are two moments when you could assemble a feed. Fanout on write does the work at post time: the moment Maya posts, her post ID is pushed into every friend's feed. When a friend opens the app, their feed is already waiting, fully assembled. It feels real-time and reads are fast.

The catch appears with big audiences. If a user has thousands of friends, a single post triggers thousands of cache writes, which is resource-intensive. And much of that work is wasted on friends who will not log in for weeks.

Fanout on read flips it: nothing is precomputed, and the feed is assembled when the reader asks for it. Inactive users cost nothing, but every read has to gather posts on the spot, so retrieval is slower.

Fanout on write (push)Fanout on read (pull)
When the work happensWhen the post is publishedWhen the feed is requested
Feed retrievalFast, precomputedSlower, built on demand
FreshnessReal-time updatesBuilt fresh at each read
Weak spotUsers with many friendsEvery read pays the cost
Good forMost normal usersInactive users, celebrities

The hybrid approach takes the best of both: push for the vast majority of users, so their friends get fast feeds, and pull for high-connection accounts such as celebrities, whose posts are fetched at read time instead of being copied into millions of caches.

Common trap: Picking one model and defending it absolutely. The expected answer names the trade-off and lands on the hybrid, with celebrities as the reason.

Inside the fanout service

The fanout service is a five-step pipeline. It pulls two kinds of data (who the friends are, and whether they want this post), then hands the heavy lifting to a queue and a pool of workers so the user's post request returns quickly.

  1. Fetch friend IDs from the graph database.
  2. Filter friends using settings in the user cache, removing muted friends or those excluded by selective sharing.
  3. Send to message queue: the filtered friend list plus the new post ID.
  4. Fanout workers pull from the queue.
  5. Store in news feed cache: append the post ID to each friend's list, respecting the configurable limit on how many recent IDs are kept.

The memory trick is crucial: the cache stores <post_id, user_id> pairs, not full post and user objects. A post ID is tiny compared with a post containing text, image links and metadata, so thousands of feeds can reference the same post without thousands of copies.

Gains

The queue decouples publishing from delivery, so posting stays fast; storing IDs keeps cache memory manageable; the size limit caps growth.

Costs

Reads need a second step to hydrate IDs into full posts; very old posts fall out of the cache and must come from the database.

The five-layer cache

A feed is not one piece of data. To draw a single card on screen you need the list of posts, the post itself, the author, whether you already liked it, and how many likes it has. Each of these has a different size, lifespan and access pattern, so the cache is split into five layers.

LayerHoldsUsed for
News FeedPost IDs per userWhich posts are in your feed
ContentPost details; hot cache for popular postsHydrating IDs into posts
Social GraphFollowers and followingFanout and author info
ActionLiked, replied, other actionsShowing "you liked this"
CountersLike, reply, follower and other countsThe numbers under each post
Common trap: Describing "a cache" as one blob. Naming the layers shows you understand that a feed read is really several small lookups stitched together.

Scaling and keeping it healthy

Around the core, the notes list the standard scaling toolkit. The database is scaled horizontally with sharding, and read replicas absorb high-traffic queries. The web tier is kept stateless so more servers can be added freely. Consistent hashing spreads requests evenly across servers, and message queues decouple components and buffer bursts of traffic.

Finally, you watch the system: QPS and latency tell you if users are waiting, and cache hit rate tells you whether the caches are doing their job. A falling hit rate is the cue to adjust cache configuration.

Test yourself

Write your answer beside each question with your stylus, then tap to compare.

Compare fanout on write and fanout on read.

Fanout on write pushes the post into friends' feeds when it is published, giving real-time updates and fast retrieval but costing a lot for users with many friends. Fanout on read assembles feeds at request time, which is efficient for inactive users but makes retrieval slower.

Why does the hybrid model use pull for celebrities?

A celebrity has an enormous number of connections, so pushing each post into every follower's cache would be extremely resource-intensive. Pulling their posts at read time avoids that write storm, while normal users keep the fast push model.

Why does the news feed cache store post IDs instead of full posts?

To save memory. Storing <post_id, user_id> pairs means the full post lives once in the content cache and database, while each feed holds only small references. A configurable limit on recent IDs keeps memory usage bounded further.

What happens if a friend has muted the author?

In step 2 of the fanout, the service checks user settings in the cache and filters that friend out. The post ID is never written to their news feed cache.

Walk through what the News Feed Service does on GET /v1/me/feed.

It fetches the user's list of post IDs from the news feed cache, then retrieves the complete post details (and related user and counter data) from the caches or database, returning them in reverse chronological order.

Why put a message queue between the fanout service and the workers?

It decouples publishing from delivery and buffers traffic. The user's post request does not have to wait for thousands of cache writes; workers process the jobs at their own pace and can be scaled independently.

Introduction

A news feed system displays a constantly updating list of posts (status updates, photos, videos, and links) from a user's connections. Examples include Facebook's news feed, Instagram's feed, and Twitter's timeline. This chapter explores the design of a scalable news feed system.

Step 1: Understanding the Problem

Requirements

  1. Platform: The system supports both web and mobile apps.
  2. Features:
    • Users can publish posts.
    • Users can view posts from friends in their news feed.
  3. Sorting: Feeds are sorted in reverse chronological order for simplicity.
  4. Scale:
    • Users can have up to 5,000 friends.
    • 10 million daily active users (DAU).
    • Feeds may include text, images, and videos.

Step 2: High-Level Design

Overview

The design includes two main flows:

  1. Feed Publishing: A user publishes a post, which is written to the database and propagated to their friends' feeds.
  2. News Feed Building: A user retrieves their news feed by aggregating posts from friends in reverse chronological order.

News Feed APIs

  1. Feed Publishing API:
    • Endpoint: POST /v1/me/feed
    • Params: content (post text) and auth_token (authentication).
  2. News Feed Retrieval API:
    • Endpoint: GET /v1/me/feed
    • Params: auth_token (authentication).

Feed Publishing

  1. User Interaction: The user publishes a post via the feed publishing API.
  2. Load Balancer: Distributes traffic to web servers.
  3. Web Servers: Authenticate requests and redirect to services.
  4. Post Service: Stores the post in the database and cache.
  5. Fanout Service: Propagates the post to friends' news feeds in the cache.
  6. Notification Service: Sends notifications to friends.

News Feed Building

  1. User Interaction: The user requests their news feed via the retrieval API.
  2. Load Balancer: Distributes traffic to web servers.
  3. Web Servers: Forward requests to the news feed service.
  4. News Feed Service: Fetches post IDs from the news feed cache and retrieves complete post details from the database or cache.

Step 3: Design Deep Dive

Feed Publishing Deep Dive

  1. Web Servers:
    • Authenticate users using auth_token.
    • Enforce rate limits to prevent spam.
  2. Fanout Service:
    • Fanout on Write: Push posts to friends' feeds at write time.
      • Pros: Real-time updates, fast feed retrieval.
      • Cons: Resource-intensive for users with many friends.
    • Fanout on Read: Pull posts at read time.
      • Pros: Efficient for inactive users.
      • Cons: Slower feed retrieval.
    • Hybrid Approach: Use a push model for most users and a pull model for high-connection users (e.g., celebrities).

The fanout service works as following:

  1. Fetch Friend IDs: Retrieve the friend list from a graph database.
  2. Filter Friends from Cache: Access user settings in the cache to exclude certain friends (e.g., muted friends or selective sharing preferences).
  3. Send to Message Queue: Send the filtered friend list along with the new post ID to a message queue for processing.
  4. Fanout Workers: Workers retrieve data from the message queue and update the news feed cache. The cache stores <post_id, user_id> mappings instead of full user and post objects to save memory.
  5. Store in News Feed Cache: Append new post IDs to the friends' news feed cache. A configurable limit ensures that only recent posts are stored, as most users focus on the latest content, keeping cache memory consumption manageable.

News Feed Retrieval Deep Dive

Cache Architecture

The cache is divided into five layers:

  1. News Feed Cache: Stores post IDs for quick retrieval.
  2. Content Cache: Stores post details (popular posts in hot cache).
  3. Social Graph Cache: Stores user relationship data.
  4. Action Cache: Tracks user actions (likes, replies, shares).
  5. Counter Cache: Maintains counts for likes, replies, followers, etc.

Key Optimizations

Scaling

  1. Database Scaling:
    • Horizontal scaling and sharding.
    • Use of read replicas for high-traffic queries.
  2. Stateless Web Tier: Keep web servers stateless to enable horizontal scaling.

Caching

  1. Store frequently accessed data in memory.
  2. Use cache layers to reduce latency and database load.

Reliability

  1. Consistent Hashing: Distribute requests evenly across servers.
  2. Message Queues: Decouple system components and buffer traffic.

Monitoring

  1. Track key metrics like QPS (queries per second) and latency.
  2. Monitor cache hit rates and adjust configurations accordingly.
