Chat System

Picture this

You type "running 5 min late" and hit send on your phone. Before you have locked the screen, your friend's phone buzzes across the city, the little green dot next to your name tells them you are online, and when you open your laptop that evening the same message is waiting there too. It feels effortless, but behind it 50 million daily users are holding open live connections, messages must arrive in the right order, and history must be kept forever. The chat system is a switchboard that never hangs up: it has to know where everyone is plugged in, route each message to the right socket in milliseconds, and remember everything that was ever said.

1 Macro Structure & Dependency Map

The system hangs on four hubs: the live connection, the servers split by whether they hold state, the message store with its ID scheme, and the presence machinery. Read the tree top-down; peripheral items are nice-to-know.

  • Real-time connection (WebSocket) — without a live, two-way pipe, the server cannot push messages to the receiver
    • Receiver-side options compared: polling, long polling, WebSocket
      • polling wastes requests; long polling wastes held connections for inactive users
    • WebSocket chosen for both sending and receiving
    • Service discovery (Apache Zookeeper) picks the chat server
      • based on geography and server capacity
  • Stateless vs stateful services — the architectural split that decides how each part scales
    • Stateless: API servers for signup, login, profile, behind a load balancer
    • Stateful: chat servers holding persistent WebSocket connections
    • Presence servers (online/offline) and notification servers (push)
      • notifications reuse the Notification System design
  • Message storage & ordering — chat history is permanent and must stay in sequence
    • Key-value store for chat history
      • easy horizontal scaling, low latency, used by Facebook Messenger and Discord
    • Message ID decides order; group key is (channel_id, message_id)
      • Snowflake global IDs vs local per-channel sequence numbers
    • Multi-device sync with cur_max_message_id
  • Message flows & presence — how messages and green dots actually move
    • One-on-one: store, then forward or push-notify
    • Group chat: copy to each member's inbox (message sync queue)
      • max 100 members keeps copying affordable
    • Heartbeats for online status; pub-sub channels per friend pair

The WebSocket is the precondition for everything real-time, and it is what makes chat servers stateful. That stateful/stateless split then shapes scaling and discovery. The KV store and its ID scheme guarantee order and history, and the message and presence flows are the traffic running over this foundation.

2 Black-Box Cause & Effect Flow

Here is the chain of boxes a message passes through, from login to delivery. For each, notice what goes in and what comes out.

API servers (stateless, over HTTP)

Input: Login, signup, profile requests via the load balancer.

Output: An authenticated user, and a recommended chat server to connect to.

The reception desk. Interchangeable clerks check you in and hand you a room number.

→ feeds into: Service discovery

Service discovery (Zookeeper)

Input: The user's location plus the load on each chat server.

Output: The best chat server for this client.

The seating host at a busy restaurant, sending you to a nearby table that is not already overcrowded.

→ feeds into: WebSocket connection to that chat server

Chat server (stateful)

Input: Messages arriving over the sender's WebSocket.

Output: A message with a unique ID, stored in the KV store and routed toward the recipient.

A switchboard operator with your line plugged in. It stamps each message with a sequence number and patches it through.

→ feeds into: KV store, then the recipient's chat server or the notification servers

Key-value store

Input: Messages keyed by message ID, or by (channel_id, message_id) for groups.

Output: Permanent, ordered history that any device can query.

The ever-growing ledger. Every message is written once, in order, and kept forever.

→ feeds into: Message sync on each device

Presence servers

Input: Periodic heartbeats from clients.

Output: Online/offline status, published to friends' channels.

The lobby attendant who marks you "in the building" while you keep waving, and "gone" once you have not waved for a while.

→ feeds into: Friends' presence indicators

Notification servers

Input: Messages for users who are offline.

Output: A push notification to the user's device.

The note slipped under the door when nobody answers the phone.

→ feeds into: The offline user's device

Follow one message

  1. Asha logs in on her phone over HTTP. The API servers authenticate her, and service discovery (Zookeeper) recommends Chat Server 1, which is nearby and lightly loaded.
  2. Her phone opens a persistent WebSocket to Chat Server 1 and starts sending heartbeats to the presence servers. Her friends see her go online.
  3. She sends "running 5 min late" to Ben. The message travels over her open WebSocket to Chat Server 1.
  4. Chat Server 1 assigns it the next message ID for their one-on-one channel and stores it in the key-value store.
  5. Ben is online, connected to Chat Server 2. The message is forwarded there, and Chat Server 2 pushes it down Ben's WebSocket instantly.
  6. Ben's phone updates its cur_max_message_id to the new message's ID.
  7. That evening Ben opens his laptop, whose cur_max_message_id is older. It asks for messages where the recipient is Ben and the message ID is larger than its value, and "running 5 min late" appears there too.
  8. Had Ben been offline, step 5 would instead send a push notification via the notification servers.

3 Purpose & Concept Beacons

A chat system keeps a persistent WebSocket between each client and a stateful chat server, stores every message permanently in a key-value store ordered by per-channel IDs, and layers presence and push notifications on top.

Mental picture

Imagine an old-fashioned telephone exchange for a whole city. The front office where you register and update your details is the stateless API tier: any clerk can help you. When you are ready to talk, a dispatcher (Zookeeper service discovery) assigns you to an operator near you, and that operator keeps your line physically plugged in (the WebSocket on a stateful chat server). Every call is transcribed into a permanent ledger with numbered lines (the KV store and message IDs), so any of your extensions at home or at work can catch up by asking "give me everything after line 653" (cur_max_message_id). A light on the switchboard stays lit while you keep tapping the line (heartbeats), and if you are not home, a note goes in your letterbox (push notification).

50M DAU, permanent historyStorage grows forever; it needs a store that scales horizontally.
Group max 100 membersSmall enough that copying each message to every inbox is acceptable.
PollingClient keeps asking "anything new?"; mostly wasted requests.
Long pollingServer holds the request open until data arrives; wasteful for inactive users.
WebSocketBi-directional, persistent; the server can push at any time.
Stateful chat serversThey hold live connections, so clients must be routed to a specific one.
Zookeeper service discoveryChooses the best chat server by geography and capacity.
Key-value storeLow latency, easy horizontal scaling, handles the long tail of old data.
(channel_id, message_id)Composite key for group messages; ordering is per channel.
Local sequence IDsUnique only within a channel, which is all ordering needs.
cur_max_message_idEach device's bookmark; fetch anything newer to sync.
Heartbeat, x = 30sNo heartbeat within the threshold means the user is marked offline.

4 Opportunistic Drilling

The connection protocol, the storage and ID scheme, multi-device sync and presence are where the real reasoning lives. Master these four and the rest of the chapter follows.

Choosing the connection: polling, long polling, WebSocket

Sending is easy: the client just makes a request to the server. Receiving is the hard part, because the server has something to say and the client did not ask for it. HTTP is client-initiated, so the question becomes: how does the server reach the receiver?

Polling has the client ask at intervals, "any new messages?" Most answers are "no," so it burns requests. Long polling improves on this: the client asks, and the server holds the connection open until a message arrives. But for inactive users, those held connections sit idle and still cost resources.

WebSocket opens a single, persistent, two-way connection. Either side can send whenever it likes. The design uses it for both sending and receiving, which is why the chat servers become stateful.

TechniqueHow it worksWeakness
PollingClient asks periodicallyFrequent, redundant requests
Long pollingConnection held open until a message arrivesInefficient for inactive users
WebSocketPersistent bi-directional connectionChosen; makes servers stateful
Common trap: Putting chat servers behind the same load balancer as API servers and treating them as interchangeable. They hold live connections, so a client must stay with its assigned chat server; that is why service discovery exists.

Storage and message IDs

Chat history is permanent, so the data only ever grows, and most reads hit recent messages while a vast "long tail" of old messages sits mostly untouched. The notes choose a key-value store because it scales horizontally, gives very low latency, and avoids a weakness of relational databases: when indexes grow large, random access becomes expensive. Facebook Messenger and Discord both use KV stores.

Order matters: messages must show up in the sequence they were sent. The message ID is the primary key and decides that sequence. For group chat the key is the composite (channel_id, message_id).

Where do IDs come from? One option is a global 64-bit generator like Snowflake. The better option in the notes is a local sequence number generator: IDs are unique only within one channel. That is enough, because you only ever need order within a one-on-one conversation or a single group, never across the whole system.

Gains

Local IDs are simpler to generate than a global sequence; the KV store scales out cheaply and serves recent messages fast.

Costs

IDs are not comparable across channels; a KV store gives up the rich querying of a relational database.

Common trap: Insisting on globally unique, globally ordered IDs. Ordering only needs to hold within a channel, so local sequences are sufficient.

Group chat and multi-device sync

In group chat, when User A sends a message, the chat server copies it into a separate inbox (message sync queue) for each recipient. Each recipient's inbox collects messages from every sender they talk to, so a client only has to check one place.

Multi-device sync solves a different problem: the same user on a phone and a laptop. Each device keeps a bookmark, cur_max_message_id, the latest message ID it has seen. A message is new for that device when both conditions hold:

  1. The recipient ID equals the logged-in user's ID.
  2. The message ID in the KV store is larger than that device's cur_max_message_id.
Common trap: Thinking inbox copying scales to huge groups. The notes flag it as expensive for larger groups; it works here because of the 100-member cap.

Online presence: heartbeats and fanout

How do you know someone is online? You could mark them offline the instant their connection drops, but mobile connections flicker constantly, and the green dot would blink on and off. Instead, clients send a heartbeat to the presence servers at regular intervals. As long as heartbeats keep arriving, the user is online. If none arrives within a threshold (x = 30 seconds in the diagram), they are marked offline.

Once status changes, friends must hear about it. The notes use publish-subscribe with one channel per friend pair. When User A's status changes, it is published to channels A-B, A-C and A-D, which Users B, C and D subscribe to. This works well for small groups; the cost grows with the number of friends.

MechanismAnswersKey parameter
HeartbeatIs this user online?Threshold x = 30s
Pub-sub fanoutWho needs to know?One channel per friend pair

Test yourself

Answer each one in the margin with your stylus before you tap to check.

Why was WebSocket chosen over polling and long polling?

Polling floods the server with redundant requests, and long polling wastes held connections on inactive users. WebSocket is a persistent, bi-directional connection, so the server can push messages the instant they arrive, and it is used for both sending and receiving.

Compare stateless and stateful services in this design.

Stateless API servers handle signup, login and profiles; any server can serve any request behind a load balancer. Stateful chat servers hold persistent WebSocket connections, so each client is tied to one server, chosen by service discovery.

Why use a key-value store for chat history instead of a relational database?

KV stores scale horizontally easily and provide very low latency. Relational databases do not handle the long tail of data well: when indexes grow large, random access becomes expensive. Facebook Messenger and Discord both use KV stores.

Why are local, per-channel message IDs good enough?

Message order only needs to be maintained within a one-on-one channel or a group channel. IDs unique within the channel, combined with channel_id as a composite key, give that ordering without a global sequence generator.

A user's phone has cur_max_message_id = 653. Which messages does it fetch when it reconnects?

Every message in the KV store whose recipient ID is the logged-in user and whose message ID is greater than 653. After fetching, the phone updates its bookmark to the newest ID.

What happens if a client stops sending heartbeats?

If no heartbeat arrives within the threshold (30 seconds in the example), the presence server marks the user offline and publishes the change to each friend-pair channel, so subscribed friends see the update.

What happens when User A messages User B, who is offline?

Chat Server 1 still assigns a message ID and stores the message in the KV store. Because B is offline, a push notification is sent instead of forwarding over a WebSocket. When B reconnects, sync fetches the message using cur_max_message_id.

Introduction

A chat system supports real-time messaging between users. This chapter focuses on designing a chat app that includes:

  • One-on-One Chat
  • Group Chat (max 100 users)
  • Online Presence Indicators
  • Multiple Device Support
  • Push Notifications

The system targets 50 million daily active users (DAU) and stores chat history permanently.

Step 1: Understanding the Problem

Requirements

  1. Features:
    • One-on-one and group chat (max 100 members).
    • Text-based messages (up to 100,000 characters).
    • Online/offline indicators.
    • Support for multiple devices.
    • Push notifications.
  2. Scale: Design for 50 million DAU.
  3. Storage: Permanent chat history.

Step 2: High-Level Design

Communication Protocols

  1. Sender Side: HTTP for sending messages, leveraging persistent connections for efficiency.
  2. Receiver Side:
    • Polling:
      • Client periodically asks the server if there are messages available.
      • Inefficient due to frequent, redundant requests.
    • Long Polling:
      • Keeps the connection open until messages arrive.
      • Inefficient for inactive users.
    • WebSocket:
      • A bi-directional, persistent connection for real-time communication, chosen for both sending and receiving messages.
      • Uses WebSockets (ws) protocol for sending and recieving messages.

Components

  1. Stateless Services:
    • Handle signup, login, and user profile management.
    • Integrated with service discovery to recommend the best chat server.
  2. Stateful Services:
    • Chat servers maintain persistent WebSocket connections.
    • Responsible for message delivery and synchronization.
  3. Third-Party Integration:
    • Push notification services notify users about new messages.
    • Refer Notification System chapter for notifications implementation.

Design

The client maintains a persistent WebSocket connection to a chat server for real-time messaging.

  • Chat servers facilitate message sending/receiving.
  • Presence servers manage online/offline status.
  • API servers handle everything including user login, signup, change profile, etc.
  • Notification servers send push notifications.
  • Finally, the key-value store is used to store chat history. Key-value stores for the database of the chat history data for following reasons:
    • It allows easy horizontal scaling.
    • KV stores provide very low latency to access data.
    • Relational databases do not handle long tail of data well. When the indexes grow large, random access is expensive.
    • KV stores are adopted by other proven reliable chat applications. For example, both Facebook messenger and Discord.

Following are the data models for one-to-one chat and group chat.

  • The primary key is message id, which helps to decide message sequence.
  • For the group chat the composite primary key is (channel_id, message_id).
    • IDs can be generated using a global 64-bit sequence number generator like Snowflake.
    • A better approach is to use local sequence number generator. Local means IDs are only unique within a group.
    • The reason why local IDs work is that maintaining message sequence within one-on-one channel or a group channel is sufficient.

Step 3: Design Deep Dive

Service Discovery

  • The primary role of service discovery is to recommend the best chat server for a client based on the criteria like geographical location, server capacity.
  • Uses Apache Zookeeper to allocate chat servers based on criteria like geographic location and server capacity.
  • Ensures efficient load distribution and minimizes latency.

Messaging Flows

One-on-One Chat

  1. User A sends a message to Chat Server 1.
  2. Chat Server 1 assigns a unique message ID and stores the message in a key-value store.
  3. If User B is online, the message is forwarded to Chat Server 2, maintaining a persistent WebSocket connection.
  4. If User B is offline, a push notification is sent.

Group Chat

  • Messages are copied to individual inboxes for each recipient in the group.
  • Simplifies synchronization but becomes expensive for larger groups.
  • On the recipient side, a recipient can receive messages from multiple users. Each recipient has an inbox (message sync queue) which contains messages from different senders.

Message Synchronization

Many users have multiple devices. We need to synchronize the message across the devices. Each device maintains a variable called cur_max_message_id, which keeps track of the latest message ID on the device. Messages that satisfy the following two conditions are considered as news messages:

  • The recipient ID is equal to the currently logged-in user ID.
  • Message ID in the key-value store is larger than cur_max_message_id

Online Presence

  1. Heartbeat Mechanism:
    • Clients send periodic heartbeats to presence servers to indicate they are online.
    • If no heartbeat is received within a threshold (for eg x = 30), the user is marked offline.
  2. Fanout Model:
    • Presence updates are pushed to friends using a publish-subscribe model in which each friend pair maintains a channel.
    • When User A's online status changes, it publishes the event to three channels, channel A-B, A-C, and A-D.
    • Those three channels are subscribed by User B, C, and D, respectively which get the online status updates.
    • The above design is effective for a small user groups.

Additional Considerations

Scalability

  • Horizontal Scaling: Add servers as user count increases.
  • Load Balancing: Distribute traffic evenly across servers.
  • Caching: Reduce database load and improve latency.

Error Handling

  • Retry Mechanisms: Handle message delivery failures with retries and queuing.
  • Server Failures: Use service discovery to allocate new servers in case of failures.

Future Extensions

  1. Media Support: Add handling for photos and videos, including compression and cloud storage.
  2. End-to-End Encryption: Ensure message privacy.
  3. Client-Side Caching: Reduce data transfer for better performance.
  4. Improved Load Times: Use geographically distributed caching networks.
13

Search Autocomplete

Picture this

You type two letters, t and w, and before your finger has even left the glass a neat list slides down: twitter, twitch, twilight, twin peak, twitch prime. It feels like the search box read your mind. Behind that list is a promise to answer in under 100 ms, for 10 million people a day, at peaks of 48,000 requests every second, where every single keystroke is a fresh request. The hard part is not finding matching words; it is finding the five most popular ones, instantly, while the world keeps searching and the popularity scores keep shifting underneath you.

1 Macro Structure & Dependency Map

At 10,000 feet the system is two rivers that never cross in real time: a slow river that learns what people search (data gathering) and a fast river that answers keystrokes (query service). A trie sits in the middle as the shared artifact they both depend on.

  • The Trie (prefix tree) — the single data structure the whole design is built to create, store, shard and read
    • Nodes = prefixes, each storing query popularity
      • Compact storage: shared prefixes stored once
    • Top-k cached at every node
      • Cap prefix length (e.g. 50 chars)
  • Query Service — the hot path; every keystroke lands here and must return 5 results in <100 ms
    • Prefix lookup → read cached top-k → respond
    • Client-side speedups
      • AJAX (lightweight async requests)
      • Browser caching of results
    • Filter layer
      • Strips hate speech etc.; physical delete happens later, asynchronously
  • Data Gathering Pipeline — the offline factory that turns raw searches into a fresh trie
    • Analytics logs (append-only, unindexed)
    • Aggregators → frequency table
      • Weekly for most apps; shorter windows for Twitter-like real-time needs
    • Workers rebuild the trie asynchronously
  • Trie Storage & Scaling — where the built trie lives and how it is split when one machine is not enough
    • Trie Cache (distributed, in memory) in front of Trie DB
    • Trie DB options
      • Document store (MongoDB snapshot of serialized trie)
      • Key-value store: prefix → node data
    • Sharding by prefix range + shard map manager
      • Unicode and country-specific tries; trending-query weighting

The trie is the hub because every other box either produces it (gathering pipeline), stores it (cache, DB, shards) or reads it (query service). The key architectural insight is the split: writes are batched and slow, reads are cached and instant. If you remember only one thing, remember that the trie is rebuilt offline, not edited live.

2 Black-Box Cause & Effect Flow

Treat each component as a sealed box: what goes in, what comes out. Read the first four boxes as the weekly factory line, and the last three as the per-keystroke fast lane.

Analytics Logs

Input: Every raw query users submit, with a timestamp.

Output: An append-only, unindexed stream of query records.

A giant receipt roll: it only ever gets longer, nobody sorts it, and it is cheap to write because nothing is looked up.

→ feeds into: Aggregators

Aggregators

Input: A window of raw log records (usually a week; shorter for real-time products like Twitter).

Output: A frequency table: query → how many times it was searched.

The tally clerk who reads the receipt roll and writes "best: 35, bet: 29, bee: 20" on a clean ledger.

→ feeds into: Workers

Workers

Input: The aggregated frequency table.

Output: A freshly built trie, with top-k lists cached at every node, written to Trie DB.

Asynchronous builders who construct next week's trie in the back room while the old one keeps serving customers.

→ feeds into: Trie DB and Trie Cache

Trie DB + Trie Cache

Input: The built trie (as a MongoDB snapshot, or as prefix → node key-value pairs).

Output: Fast in-memory reads from the distributed cache, backed by durable storage.

The DB is the warehouse; the cache is the shop shelf holding everything customers reach for.

→ feeds into: Query Service

Shard Map Manager

Input: A prefix, e.g. "tw".

Output: The identity of the server that owns that prefix range.

A receptionist with a floor plan: "Words starting with t? Third floor, room n-z."

→ feeds into: the correct Query Service shard

Query Service

Input: The prefix the user has typed so far.

Output: Up to 5 suggestions sorted by popularity, after the filter layer removes unwanted ones.

Walks to the prefix node and simply reads the pre-written top-5 list pinned to it; no searching, no sorting.

→ feeds into: the browser dropdown (and browser cache)

Follow one keystroke

  1. You have already typed "b" and now add "e". The browser fires a lightweight AJAX request for prefix "be" without reloading anything.
  2. The browser first checks its own cache. If you searched "be" earlier today, the answer is already on your device and no network trip happens at all.
  3. Cache miss: the request reaches the backend, where the shard map manager sees the prefix begins with "b" and routes it to the server owning the a-m range.
  4. That server looks up prefix "be" in the Trie Cache (in memory). In a key-value layout this is a single hash lookup: key "be" → node data.
  5. The node for "be" already carries its cached top-k list: best: 35, bet: 29, bee: 20, be: 15, beer: 10. No subtree walk, no sort.
  6. The filter layer scans the five results against its rules and drops anything harmful before it leaves the building.
  7. The list returns to your browser, is rendered in the dropdown, and is saved in the browser cache for next time. Total budget: under 100 ms.
  8. Meanwhile your finished search is appended to the analytics log. It will not change any suggestion until the next aggregation and trie rebuild.

3 Purpose & Concept Beacons

Autocomplete trades freshness for speed: it precomputes the answer for every possible prefix once a week so that each keystroke becomes a lookup rather than a search.

Mental picture

Imagine a library of signposts arranged as a branching road. Each fork in the road is a letter, so walking t → w puts you at the "tw" fork: that is a trie node. Nailed to every fork is a small board listing the five most-visited destinations beyond it: that board is the cached top-k list. Once a week a survey crew counts foot traffic from the visitor logbook (analytics logs and aggregators) and repaints every board overnight (workers rebuilding the trie). Travellers never wait for a survey; they just read the board where they stand (query service reading the cache).

Trie (prefix tree)Tree where each node is a prefix; tells you lookups cost O(prefix length), not O(number of queries).
Top-k = 5Only five suggestions are ever returned, so caching them per node is small and cheap.
<100 msThe latency budget that forces precomputation and in-memory caching.
48,000 peak QPSEvery keystroke is a request; reads dwarf writes, so optimise the read path.
Cache top-k at each nodeTrades memory for time: no subtree traversal or sorting at query time.
Prefix cap (~50 chars)Users rarely type long queries; bounding depth bounds the cost of finding a node.
Append-only analytics logCheap, unindexed writes; the raw material for batch aggregation.
Weekly rebuildThe trie is replaced, not patched; suggestions are slightly stale by design.
Prefix → node KV storeFlattens the tree into a hash table, so any prefix is one key lookup away.
Shard by prefix rangea-m / n-z, then finer (aa-ag, ah-an) to even out skewed letters; a shard map manager routes.
Filter layerRemoves harmful suggestions instantly at read time; physical deletion happens asynchronously.
0.4 GB/dayNew query data per day: modest growth, well suited to periodic batch processing.

4 Opportunistic Drilling

Three ideas carry most of the marks: how the trie answers in constant-ish time, why data gathering is batched instead of live, and how storage and sharding keep it all in memory. Drill these; skim the rest.

The trie and the cached top-k trick

A plain trie answers "what are the top 5 for prefix be?" in three steps: find the prefix node, traverse its entire subtree collecting every complete query, then sort those by frequency and keep the top k. The first step is fast. The second and third are the problem: a popular prefix like "b" may have millions of descendants, and you would be walking and sorting them on every keystroke.

The fix is to do that work once, at build time, and pin the answer to the node. Every node stores its own top-k list. Now a query is: find the node, read its list, done. Combined with a cap on prefix length (around 50 characters), finding the node is bounded too, so the whole query is effectively constant time.

Gains

Query time no longer depends on how many queries share the prefix. No sorting on the hot path. Easily meets the 100 ms budget.

Costs

Extra memory at every node (the same popular query is copied into many ancestors' lists). Updating one frequency means touching every ancestor, which is why updates are batched.

Common trap: saying "we sort the children at query time". That is the naive version. The interview answer is "we precompute and cache top-k at each node, so the query is a lookup".

Why data gathering is batched, not real time

The first high-level sketch updates frequencies the moment someone searches. It looks tidy but collapses at scale: users can enter billions of queries a day, and each update would ripple through every ancestor's cached top-k list. Worse, the payoff is tiny, because top suggestions barely move once the trie is built.

So the design turns a firehose into a weekly delivery. Raw queries go to append-only analytics logs. Aggregators condense a window of logs into a frequency table. Workers rebuild a brand new trie asynchronously and write it to storage. The old trie keeps serving until the new one is ready.

AspectReal-time updatesBatched pipeline
Write costUpdate trie on every queryAppend to log; rebuild weekly
FreshnessInstantUp to a week stale (shorter window for Twitter-like apps)
Read path impactConstant locking/rewriting of hot nodesRead-only trie, easy to cache
FitImpractical at billions/dayChosen design
Common trap: forgetting that the aggregation window is a dial. For trending, real-time products you shorten it or weight recent queries more heavily; for most products, once a week is enough.

Storing, deleting and sharding the trie

Where does the finished trie live? Reads go to the Trie Cache, a distributed in-memory cache. Behind it sits the Trie DB, with two options. A document store such as MongoDB can hold a serialized snapshot of the whole weekly trie. A key-value store flattens the tree: every prefix becomes a key and that node's data (including its top-k list) becomes the value, so any prefix is a single hash lookup.

Deletion is handled in two speeds. A filter layer sits in front of the cache and removes unwanted results (such as hate speech) on the way out, immediately and by flexible rules. The physical removal from the database happens later, asynchronously.

When the trie outgrows one machine, shard by prefix range: a-m on one server, n-z on another. Letters are not evenly popular, so split further inside busy ranges (aa-ag, ah-an). A shard map manager holds the routing table and tells the web tier which server owns which range.

  1. Coarse split by first letter range (a-m, n-z).
  2. Measure load; split hot ranges more finely (aa-ag, ah-an).
  3. Record the mapping in the shard map manager.
  4. Route every request through the map to the owning shard.
Common trap: sharding naively by 26 letters. Far more words start with "s" or "c" than with "x", so fixed letter shards end up badly unbalanced.

Squeezing the last milliseconds and going global

Two client-side tricks shave latency before the server is even involved. AJAX requests send just the prefix and receive just the list, with no page refresh. Browser caching keeps recent results locally, so retyping a common prefix costs zero network time.

Scaling beyond English means storing Unicode characters in the trie and building separate tries per country or region, since what is popular in one market is noise in another. Trending events are handled by dynamically updating trie nodes or weighting recent queries more heavily.

Test yourself

Write your answer in the margin with your stylus first, then tap to reveal.

Why is the top-k list cached at every trie node instead of computed on demand?

Computing on demand means traversing the whole subtree below the prefix and sorting all matches, which is huge for short prefixes like "b". Caching turns the query into "find node, read list", keeping it within the 100 ms budget at 48,000 peak QPS. The cost is extra memory and harder updates.

What would happen if the trie were updated on every search query?

With billions of queries a day, each update would ripple through the cached top-k lists of every ancestor node, creating constant write contention on the hottest nodes. The benefit would be negligible because top suggestions rarely change. That is why queries go to logs and the trie is rebuilt in batches.

Compare storing the trie in a document store versus a key-value store.

A document store like MongoDB holds a serialized snapshot of the weekly trie, which is simple to write and restore. A key-value store maps every prefix to its node data, so any prefix is a single hash lookup, which suits fast serving and fine-grained access.

A harmful suggestion is discovered on Tuesday; the next rebuild is Sunday. What happens?

The filter layer in front of the trie cache blocks it immediately at read time using its filter rules. The physical removal from the database happens asynchronously, and the next rebuild will not include it.

Why shard by prefix range with a shard map manager rather than one shard per letter?

Letter popularity is very uneven, so fixed letter shards would be imbalanced. Prefix ranges can be split further where traffic is heavy (aa-ag, ah-an), and the shard map manager records the mapping so requests are routed correctly as ranges change.

How would you adapt this design for a Twitter-like product where trends matter within hours?

Shorten the aggregation window so the trie is rebuilt more often, and weight recent queries more heavily or update trending nodes dynamically. The weekly cadence is a default for products where popularity is stable.

Introduction

Autocomplete, also known as typeahead or incremental search, provides real-time suggestions to users as they type in search boxes. The system must efficiently deliver top-k relevant and popular suggestions based on historical query data.

Key Features

  • Suggest up to 5 autocomplete results.
  • Based on query popularity (frequency).
  • Support only lowercase English characters.
  • Fast response time (<100 ms) and scalable.

Step 1: Understanding the Problem

Requirements

  1. Real-Time Suggestions: Display relevant matches as the user types.
  2. Top-k Results: Return up to 5 results sorted by popularity.
  3. Scalability: Handle 10 million DAU with a peak QPS of 48,000.
  4. High Availability: Handle failures without system downtime.
  5. Data Growth: Support daily storage growth of 0.4 GB for new query data.

Step 2: High-Level Design

At the high-level, the system is broken down into two services:

  1. Data Gathering Service:
    • Collects user queries and aggregates them for frequency analysis in real-time.
    • Real-time processing is not practical for large data sets; however, it is a good starting point
  2. Query Service: Provides the top-k suggestions based on the user's input.

Data Gathering Service

  • Aggregates query data from analytics logs and updates the frequency table.
  • Processes historical data weekly to build a trie (prefix tree).

Query Service

  • Uses the frequency table from data gathering service.
  • Processes user input and retrieves top-k suggestions from the frequency table using a Trie.
  • Optimized for fast lookups using caching and efficient data structures.
  • For example when a user types "tw" in the search box, the following top 5 searched queries are displayed.

Step 3: Design Deep Dive

Trie Data Structure

The trie is a tree-like data structure used to store and retrieve query strings efficiently.

Key Features

  1. Compact Storage: Represents prefixes hierarchically to minimize redundancy.
  2. Frequency Information: Stores the popularity of queries at each node.

Steps to get top k most searched queries

  • Find the prefix
  • Traverse the subtree from prefix node to get all valid children
  • Sort the children and get top k

Optimizations:

  • Cache top-k queries at each node to speed up retrieval and avoid traversing the whole trie.
  • Limit prefix length to reduce search space as users rarely type a long search query (say 50).

Trie Operations

  1. Create:
    • Built weekly using aggregated query data.
    • The source of data is from Analytics Log/DB.
  2. Update: Rarely updated in real-time; weekly updates replace old data.
  3. Delete:
    • Filters remove unwanted or harmful suggestions (e.g., hate speech).
    • Having a filter layer gives us the flexibility of removing results based on different filter rules.
    • Unwanted suggestions are removed physically from the database asynchronically.

Query Processing Flow

  1. Prefix Search:
    • Identify the prefix node corresponding to the user's input.
    • Traverse the subtree to collect valid suggestions.
  2. Top-k Sorting:
    • Cache top-k suggestions at each node to minimize sorting overhead.
  3. Response Construction:
    • Construct results using cached data for fast response times.

Optimizations

  1. Cache at Each Node: Store the top-k queries to avoid redundant traversals.
  2. Limit Prefix Length: Cap prefix length to a small value (e.g., 50 characters) for faster lookups.
  3. AJAX Requests: Use lightweight asynchronous requests for real-time responses.
  4. Browser Caching: Save autocomplete results in the browser cache for frequently searched terms.

Data Gathering Pipeline

In the high-level design, whenever a user types a search query, data is updated in real-time. This approach is not practical.

  • Users may enter billions of queries per day. Updating the trie on every query is not feasible.
  • Top suggestions may not change much once the trie is built.

Updated Design

  1. Analytics Logs:
    • Stores raw query data as logs for weekly aggregation.
    • Logs are append-only and are not indexed
  2. Aggregators:
    • Process logs into frequency tables, suitable for trie construction.
    • For real-time applications such as Twitter, aggregate data in a shorter time interval.
    • For other cases, aggregating data less frequently, say once per week is good enough.
  3. Workers: Asynchronous servers rebuild the trie and store it in persistent storage.
  4. Storage Options:
    • Trie Cache: Trie Cache is a distributed cache system that keeps trie in memory for fast read.
    • Trie DB
      1. Document Store (e.g., MongoDB): Since a new trie is built weekly, we can periodically take a snapshot of it, serialize it, and store the serialized data in the database like MongoDB
      2. Key-Value Store:
        • Maps prefixes to node data for fast access.
        • Every prefix in the trie is mapped to a key in a hash table.
        • Data on each trie node is mapped to a value in a hash table.

Scalability

  1. Sharding:
    • Distribute trie nodes across servers based on prefix ranges (e.g., a-m, n-z).
    • Further shard within prefixes to balance uneven distributions (e.g., aa-ag, ah-an).
  2. Load Balancing:
    • Use a shard map manager to route requests to the appropriate server.

Step 4: Advanced Features

Multi-Language Support

  1. Unicode Characters: Use Unicode to support non-English languages.
  2. Country-Specific Tries: Build separate tries for different countries or regions.

Trending Queries

  • Handle real-time events by dynamically updating trie nodes or weighting recent queries more heavily.
14

YouTube

Picture this

A creator finishes editing a 300 MB clip on a train and taps "Upload" on a patchy mobile connection. Minutes later someone on a smart TV across the world presses play and it starts instantly, crisp in HD, then quietly drops to a lower resolution when their Wi-Fi stutters, without buffering. Between those two moments the raw file was chopped up, inspected, re-encoded into many resolutions and formats, thumbnailed, watermarked and pushed to edge servers near every viewer. Do that for millions of daily users, adding 150 TB of new video a day, while CDN bills alone run around $150,000 a day, and you see why the hard problems here are heavy processing and heavy bandwidth.

1 Macro Structure & Dependency Map

YouTube is two pipelines joined by storage: an upload pipeline that turns one raw file into many streamable versions, and a streaming pipeline that serves those versions from the CDN. Read the map top-down: flows first, the transcoding engine second, the optimisations last.

  • Video Upload Flow — everything starts with getting the raw file and its metadata in safely
    • Two parallel paths: file → original storage, metadata → API servers → metadata DB
    • Completion queue + completion handler update metadata and inform the user
    • Upload hardening
      • Pre-signed URLs for authorised uploads
      • Chunked, resumable parallel uploads; CDNs as upload centres
  • Video Transcoding (DAG engine) — the expensive heart that makes one upload playable everywhere
    • Why: smaller storage, device compatibility, quality that adapts to network
      • Container (MP4, AVI) vs codec (H.264, VP9)
    • Preprocessor → DAG scheduler → resource manager → task workers
    • Temporary storage for retries
      • GOP (Group of Pictures) splitting
  • Video Streaming Flow — the part viewers actually feel; must be fast and cheap
    • CDN edge servers stream directly to clients
    • Streaming protocols
      • MPEG-DASH, Apple HLS, Adobe HDS
  • Optimisations & Error Handling — the levers for speed, safety and the huge CDN bill
    • Speed: parallel uploads, message queues between modules
    • Safety: pre-signed URLs, DRM, AES encryption, watermarking
    • Cost: CDN only for popular videos, on-demand encoding, regional distribution
      • Custom CDNs and ISP partnerships
    • Recoverable errors retry; non-recoverable errors stop with an error code

Upload feeds transcoding; transcoding feeds transcoded storage and the CDN; the CDN feeds streaming. The optimisations are not a separate system but dials on each of those three hubs. The transcoding engine is the deepest hub because it decides how fast a video becomes watchable and how much compute it burns.

2 Black-Box Cause & Effect Flow

Follow the file as it moves from the creator's phone to the viewer's screen. Each box transforms it in one specific way.

API Servers (upload gatekeeper)

Input: A POST /upload request plus video metadata (file name, size, format).

Output: A pre-signed URL for the client, and a metadata record saved in the metadata DB.

A front desk that checks your ID and hands you a one-time key to the storage room, instead of carrying your luggage itself.

→ feeds into: client uploads directly to Original Storage

Original Storage (blob)

Input: The raw video, often in parallel chunks.

Output: A durable raw copy ready for processing.

The loading dock where unprocessed crates are stacked before the factory opens them.

→ feeds into: Transcoding servers

Preprocessor + DAG Scheduler

Input: Raw video and configuration files written by client programmers.

Output: GOP-aligned chunks cached in temporary storage, and a DAG split into stages of tasks.

The planner who cuts the job into pieces and writes the recipe: split into video, audio, metadata first, then encode and thumbnail.

→ feeds into: Resource Manager's task queue

Resource Manager + Task Workers

Input: Prioritised tasks and worker-utilisation info.

Output: Each task executed on the best available worker; encoded video assembled.

A dispatcher matching jobs to free, capable hands, then tracking who is doing what.

→ feeds into: Transcoded Storage and the Completion Queue (in parallel)

Transcoded Storage → CDN

Input: Encoded versions of the video in multiple resolutions and formats.

Output: Copies distributed to CDN edge servers close to viewers.

The finished goods warehouse ships stock to corner shops in every neighbourhood.

→ feeds into: streaming to clients

Completion Queue + Completion Handler

Input: Transcoding-complete events.

Output: Updated metadata (video is ready) and a notification to the creator.

The bell that rings when the order is done, so the front desk can update the ticket and call the customer.

→ feeds into: Metadata DB / cache; user sees "ready"

CDN Edge Streaming

Input: A viewer's play request.

Output: A stream in a protocol such as MPEG-DASH or Apple HLS, at a quality suited to their device and network.

The corner shop hands you the video immediately; nobody drives to the central warehouse.

→ feeds into: the viewer's player

Follow one upload

  1. The creator's app sends POST /upload to the API servers. In parallel it sends metadata: file name, size (300 MB), format.
  2. API servers authorise the user, store the metadata, and return a pre-signed URL granting temporary permission to write to original storage.
  3. The client splits the 300 MB file into smaller chunks and uploads them in parallel to the nearest upload centre (a CDN edge acting as an upload hub). If the train enters a tunnel, only the missing chunks are resent.
  4. Once the raw video lands in original storage, the preprocessor splits it by GOP alignment, builds the DAG from configuration files, and caches the GOPs and metadata in temporary storage.
  5. The DAG scheduler emits stage 1 (split into video, audio, metadata) and then stage 2 (video encoding and thumbnail, alongside audio encoding) into the task queue.
  6. The resource manager's task scheduler pops the highest-priority task, picks the best worker from the worker queue, records the pair in the running queue, and dispatches. An encoding worker fails halfway? The task is retried from the data in temporary storage.
  7. Encoded outputs are assembled. In parallel, they go to transcoded storage (then out to the CDN) and a completion event goes to the completion queue.
  8. The completion handler marks the video ready in the metadata DB and notifies the creator.
  9. A viewer on a smart TV presses play; the nearest CDN edge streams it, switching resolution if the network weakens.

3 Purpose & Concept Beacons

The design turns one raw upload into many device-ready versions through a parallel, retryable DAG pipeline, then serves them from the edge while aggressively controlling bandwidth cost.

Mental picture

Think of a film-processing factory with a network of corner kiosks. The front desk (API servers) issues you a stamped pass (pre-signed URL) so you can drop your reels straight at the loading dock (original storage). Inside, a planner (preprocessor and DAG scheduler) cuts the reel into short segments (GOPs) and writes a recipe of steps that can run side by side. A dispatcher (resource manager) assigns each step to the best free technician (task workers), keeping spare copies in a back room (temporary storage) in case someone spills chemicals. Finished prints go to a warehouse (transcoded storage) and then out to kiosks on every street (CDN edges), while a bell (completion queue) tells the front desk the order is ready.

5M DAU, 300 MB avg, 1 GB maxUploads are large; they must be chunked and resumable, not single requests.
150 TB/day storageStorage grows relentlessly; blob storage, not databases, holds video.
5M × 5 × 0.3 GB × $0.02 = $150,000/dayCDN is the dominant cost, which is why cost optimisations target serving, not compute.
TranscodingRe-encoding into many resolutions and formats: saves storage, fits every device, adapts to bandwidth.
Container vs codecContainer (MP4, AVI) is the box holding video, audio and metadata; codec (H.264, VP9) is the compression algorithm.
DAG modelTasks as a directed acyclic graph: dependencies are explicit, independent tasks run in parallel.
GOP (Group of Pictures)A self-contained chunk of frames; the natural unit to split video for parallel work.
Task / worker / running queueThe resource manager's three queues: what to run, who is free, what is in flight.
Temporary storagePersisted intermediate data so a failed encode retries instead of restarting from scratch.
Pre-signed URLA time-limited upload permission; clients write straight to blob storage but only if authorised.
Completion queueDecouples "encoding finished" from "update metadata and notify user".
MPEG-DASH / HLS / HDSStreaming protocols; different ones support different encodings and players.

4 Opportunistic Drilling

Interviewers probe three things: the upload flow's parallel paths, the DAG transcoding architecture, and how you tame the CDN bill. Master those and the rest is vocabulary.

The upload flow: two parallel paths and a completion bell

Uploading is really two things happening at once. The heavy path pushes the video bytes into original storage. The light path sends metadata (file name, size, format) to the API servers, which write it to the metadata database. Separating them means the metadata record exists even while hundreds of megabytes are still in flight.

After the file lands, transcoding servers produce the encoded versions. Then two things happen in parallel again: the encoded files go to transcoded storage and on to the CDN (3a, 3a.1), and a completion event is placed on the completion queue so completion handlers can update metadata and tell the user (3b, 3b.1). The queue means a slow metadata update never holds up distribution, and vice versa.

Common trap: routing video bytes through the API servers. The API servers only hand out pre-signed URLs and handle metadata; bytes go straight to blob storage.

Transcoding as a DAG: split, parallelise, assemble

Transcoding is computationally expensive and slow if done as one long job. The DAG model breaks it into tasks with explicit dependencies. First the original video is split into video, audio and metadata. The video branch fans out into tasks such as inspection, video transcoding (resolutions, codecs, bitrates), thumbnail generation (user-supplied or automatic) and watermarking (an identifying overlay). The audio branch goes through audio encoding. Finally everything is assembled.

Because the graph is acyclic and the branches are independent, many tasks run simultaneously. Different creators can also get different DAGs, because the preprocessor builds the graph from configuration files that client programmers write.

Gains

High parallelism, flexible per-video pipelines, and each task can fail and retry independently.

Costs

Needs orchestration: a scheduler to stage tasks, a resource manager to place them, and temporary storage to hold intermediate results.

Inside the transcoding architecture

Five components turn the DAG into running work. Think of them as planner, foreman, dispatcher, crew and safety locker.

  1. Preprocessor: splits video into GOP-aligned chunks (also for old clients), generates the DAG from config files, and caches GOPs and metadata in temporary storage for retries.
  2. DAG scheduler: splits the graph into stages (stage 1: video, audio, metadata; stage 2: video encoding and thumbnail) and pushes tasks into the resource manager's task queue.
  3. Resource manager: holds a task queue (priority queue of tasks), a worker queue (priority queue of worker utilisation), and a running queue (current task/worker pairs). Its task scheduler picks the optimal task and worker and instructs the worker.
  4. Task workers: execute the work; different workers may specialise in different tasks.
  5. Temporary storage: holds intermediate data; the store type depends on data type, size, access frequency and lifespan.
Common trap: describing the resource manager as "a queue". It is three queues plus a scheduler; the worker queue is what lets it pick the least-loaded capable worker.

Speed, safety and the $150,000-a-day bill

Speed comes from parallelism everywhere. Uploads are split into chunks by GOP so they are faster and resumable; CDNs serve as distributed upload centres near users; and message queues sit between modules so, for example, encoding does not wait for downloading to finish before it can take the next job.

Safety uses pre-signed URLs so only authorised users can upload, and protects content with DRM (Apple FairPlay, Google Widevine), AES encryption and visual watermarking.

Cost leverIdea
Popularity-based servingOnly popular videos go through the CDN; the long tail is served from high-capacity video servers.
On-demand encodingRarely watched videos are encoded only when needed, not into every format up front.
Regional distributionVideos popular in one region are not pushed to every other region.
Own CDN and ISP partnersBuilding a custom CDN and partnering with ISPs cuts bandwidth costs.

Errors split into two families: recoverable ones (a failed upload chunk, transcoding task or resource allocation) are retried; non-recoverable ones (a malformed video) stop processing and return an error code.

Test yourself

Sketch or jot your answer in the margin first, then tap to check.

Why is transcoding necessary at all?

Raw video is huge, so encoding reduces storage. Different devices and browsers support different formats, so multiple encodings ensure compatibility. And multiple resolutions and bitrates let playback adapt to the viewer's network.

What does a pre-signed URL solve, and who issues it?

The API servers issue it after a POST /upload. It gives the client time-limited permission to upload straight to original storage, so only authorised users can write, and the video bytes never pass through the API servers.

What happens if a task worker crashes midway through encoding?

It is a recoverable error, so the task is retried. The preprocessor and workers persisted GOPs and intermediate data in temporary storage, so the retry resumes from that data instead of reprocessing the whole upload.

Compare the task queue, worker queue and running queue.

The task queue is a priority queue of work waiting to run. The worker queue is a priority queue of worker utilisation, used to pick the best worker. The running queue records which tasks are currently executing on which workers.

Why put a completion queue between transcoding and metadata updates?

It decouples the two: transcoded files can flow to storage and the CDN in parallel while completion handlers update metadata and notify users at their own pace. A slow or failed handler does not block distribution.

The CDN bill is too high. Name three changes from the notes.

Serve only popular videos via the CDN and the rest from high-capacity servers; encode rarely watched videos on demand; distribute regionally by popularity. Longer term, build a custom CDN and partner with ISPs.

How does chunked upload help the creator on a patchy connection?

The video is split (by GOP) into smaller chunks uploaded in parallel, which is faster, and if the connection drops only the unfinished chunks need resending, making the upload resumable.

Introduction

YouTube is a massive video streaming platform supporting video uploads, playback, and various interactions. This chapter focuses on designing a scalable video streaming system with the following core features:

  • Fast video uploads
  • Smooth video streaming
  • Ability to change video quality
  • Low infrastructure cost
  • High availability and reliability

Key Statistics (2020)

  • 2 billion monthly active users
  • 5 billion videos watched per day
  • 37% of mobile internet traffic comes from YouTube
  • Available in 80 languages
  • $15.1 billion ad revenue in 2019

Step 1: Understand the Problem and Scope

Core Functionalities

  1. Upload videos
  2. Watch videos

Supported Platforms

  • Mobile apps, web browsers, and smart TVs

Assumptions

  • Daily Active Users (DAU): 5 million
  • Average Video Size: 300 MB
  • Upload Limits: Max 1 GB per video
  • Daily Storage Need: 150 TB
  • CDN Costs: 5 million * 5 videos * 0.3GB * $0.02 = $150,000/day (using Amazon CloudFront)

Step 2: High-Level Design

Components

  1. Client: Devices like smartphones, computers, and TVs.
  2. CDN (Content Delivery Network): Stores and streams videos.
  3. API Servers: Handles all user interactions except video streaming (e.g., uploads, metadata updates).
  4. Metadata Database: Stores video metadata (e.g., title, description, size).
  5. Original Storage: Blob storage for uploaded videos.
  6. Transcoding Servers: Convert videos into multiple resolutions and formats.
  7. Transcoded Storage: Blob storage for transcoded videos.

Core Workflows

1. Video Uploading Flow

Parallel Processes:

  1. Upload video to original storage.
  2. Update video metadata in the database.

Video Upload (Steps):

  • [1] Videos are uploaded to blob storage.
  • [2] Transcoding servers convert videos to multiple formats.
  • [3] One transcoding is complete, following two steps are executed in parallel.
    • [3a] Transcoded videos are sent to transcoded storage.
    • [3b] Transcoding completion events are queued in the completion queue.
  • [3a.1] Videos are distributed to the CDN.
  • [3b.1] Completion handlers update metadata and inform users.

Metadata Upload (Steps):

  • The client in parallel sends a request to update the video metadata
  • The request contains video metadata, including file name, size, format, etc.

2. Video Streaming Flow

  • Videos are streamed directly from the CDN using edge servers to minimize latency.
  • Some of the popular streaming protocols are MPEG_DASH, Apple HLS, Adobe HDS.
  • Different streaming protocols support different video encodings and playback players.

Step 3: Design Deep Dive

Video Transcoding

Importance

  1. Raw video consumes large amounts of storage space. It reduces storage space.
  2. Ensures compatibility across devices and browsers.
  3. Adapts video quality to network conditions.

Components

  • Container: Encapsulates video, audio, and metadata (e.g., MP4, AVI).
  • Codecs: Compression and Decompression algorithms (e.g., H.264, VP9).

Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) Model

  • Transcoding a video is computationally expensive and time-consuming.
  • DAG Model defines tasks like encoding, thumbnail generation, and watermarking.
  • Allows high parallelism in video processing.
  • The original video is split into video, audio, and metadata.
    • Video encodings: Videos are converted to support different resolutions, codec, bitrates.
    • Thumbnail: It can either be uploaded by a user or automatically generated by the system.
    • Watermark: Image overlay on top of your video contains identifying information about the video.

Video Transcoding Architecture

  1. Preprocessor: Splits videos into smaller chunks (GOP alignment). It has 4 responsibilities.
    • Video splitting: Video stream is split or further split into smaller Group of Pictures (GOP) alignment.
    • It split videos by GOP alignment for old clients.
    • It generates DAG based on configuration files client programmers write.
    • It stores GOPs and metadata in temporary storage in case the encoding fails, the system could use persisted data for retry operations.
  2. DAG Scheduler: Organizes tasks into sequential or parallel stages.
    • It splits a DAG graph into stages of tasks and puts them in the task queue in the resource manager.
    • Stage 1: video, audio, and metadata.
    • The video file is further split into two tasks in stage 2: video encoding and thumbnail.
  3. Resource Manager: Responsible for managing the efficiency of resource allocation. It contains 3 queues and a task scheduler.
    • Task queue: priority queue that contains tasks to be executed.
    • Worker queue: priority queue that contains worker utilization info.
    • Running queue: contains currently running tasks and workers running the tasks.
    • Task scheduler: picks the optimal task/worker, and instructs the chosen task worker to execute the job.
  4. Task Workers: Perform transcoding and other operations.
    • Different task workers may run different tasks
  5. Temporary Storage: Stores intermediate data for retries.
    • The choice of storage system depends on factors like data type, data size, access frequency, data life span, etc.
  6. Output: Transcoded videos ready for distribution.

System Optimizations

Speed Optimizations

  1. Parallel Video Uploads: Split videos into smaller chunks for faster, resumable uploads.
  2. Distributed Upload Centers: Use CDNs as upload hubs close to users.
  3. Parallel Processing: Decouple modules using message queues for high parallelism.

Safety Optimizations

  1. Pre-Signed URLs: Restrict video uploads to authorized users.
  2. Protect Videos:
    • DRM Systems (e.g., Apple FairPlay, Google Widevine).
    • AES Encryption.
    • Watermarking.

Cost-Saving Optimizations

  1. Serve only popular videos via CDN; less popular ones from high-capacity servers.
  2. Encode on-demand for rarely accessed videos.
  3. Regionalize video distribution based on popularity.
  4. Build custom CDNs and partner with ISPs to reduce bandwidth costs.

Error Handling

Recoverable Errors

  • Retry failed uploads, transcoding, or resource allocation tasks.

Non-Recoverable Errors

  • Stop malformed video processing and return error codes.

Google Drive

Picture this

You fix one typo in a 40-page report on your laptop at 11 pm, close the lid, and the next morning your phone already shows the corrected version. Meanwhile a colleague edited the same file at the same moment, and instead of one of you silently losing work, the system shows both copies and lets them choose. Now multiply that by 10 million daily users, each storing up to 10 GB, adding up to 500 PB in total, with a flat rule that losing data is unacceptable. The challenge is to move as few bytes as possible, keep every device in agreement, and never drop a file even when servers, networks or whole regions fail.

1 Macro Structure & Dependency Map

The system is split into two planes: a data plane that moves file bytes as blocks, and a metadata plane that records what exists, which version is current, and who needs to hear about it. Almost every design choice follows from keeping those two planes separate.

  • Block Servers & Cloud Storage — the data plane; files become 4 MB blocks that are stored, synced and deduplicated independently
    • Split into blocks (max 4 MB), each with a unique hash
      • Compressed and encrypted before upload
    • Stored in cloud storage (e.g. S3) with cross-region replication
      • Cold storage (S3 Glacier) for inactive files
    • Delta sync: only changed blocks travel
  • Metadata DB & API Servers — the metadata plane; the source of truth for files, blocks and versions
    • Tables: User, File, Block, File Version
    • API servers handle auth, profiles and every non-upload workflow
      • Metadata cache for hot entries
      • Sharding and replication; promote a replica on failure
    • Upload status: pending → uploaded
  • Notification Service — tells every other device that something changed, so sync can begin
    • Publisher/subscriber over long polling
    • Offline backup queue holds changes for disconnected clients
      • Clients reconnect to another server if one fails
  • Sync & Conflict Resolution — the rules that keep multiple writers from destroying each other's work
    • First processed version wins
    • Losing version saved separately; user merges or overrides
    • Revision history
      • Limit saved revisions; prioritise recent versions

Blocks are the hub of the data plane: delta sync, deduplication, compression and reconstruction all depend on files being chunks with hashes. The metadata DB is the hub of the control plane: it knows which blocks form which version. The notification service links the two by telling clients when to go and fetch. Conflict resolution is what happens when two clients race through that loop at once.

2 Black-Box Cause & Effect Flow

Every file change travels the same loop: bytes go one way, metadata goes another, and a notification closes the loop for other devices.

Client (browser / mobile app)

Input: A local file created or edited by the user.

Output: Two parallel streams: file data toward block servers, file metadata toward API servers.

You post the parcel and, separately, update the shipping register saying a parcel is on its way.

→ feeds into: Block Servers and API Servers

Block Servers

Input: File bytes.

Output: Blocks of up to 4 MB, each hashed, compressed and encrypted, written to cloud storage.

A packing station that cuts a long roll of fabric into labelled squares and seals each in its own envelope.

→ feeds into: Cloud Storage

Cloud Storage (S3) + Cold Storage

Input: Encrypted, compressed blocks.

Output: Durable, cross-region-replicated blocks; a callback when upload completes. Inactive files later migrate to cold storage.

A vault with branches in several cities; rarely touched boxes get moved to a cheaper basement.

→ feeds into: API Servers (completion callback)

API Servers + Metadata DB/Cache

Input: File metadata from the client; completion callback from storage.

Output: File and version records, first with status pending, then uploaded.

The register clerk who first writes "expected" and later ticks "received".

→ feeds into: Notification Service

Notification Service

Input: A change event (add, edit, delete, share).

Output: A message to every online subscriber over long polling; an entry in the offline backup queue for disconnected clients.

A town crier who shouts to everyone in the square and leaves a note on the door of anyone who is away.

→ feeds into: other clients start the download flow

Download Flow (other clients)

Input: A change notification (or queued changes on reconnect).

Output: Updated metadata fetched from API servers, then the needed blocks downloaded and the file reconstructed.

Read the new register entry first, then collect only the envelopes that changed, and stitch the fabric back together.

→ feeds into: an up-to-date local copy

Follow one file edit

  1. You edit a 40 MB presentation on your laptop. Split into 4 MB blocks, it is 10 blocks; your edit touched blocks 2 and 5.
  2. Your client sends the new file metadata to the API servers, which record the new version in the metadata DB with status pending.
  3. The notification service immediately tells your other devices that a change is underway.
  4. In parallel, the client sends the data to the block servers. Using block hashes, they detect that only blocks 2 and 5 changed. Those two are compressed, encrypted and uploaded to cloud storage; the other 8 are untouched (delta sync).
  5. Cloud storage fires a callback to the API servers, which flip the status to uploaded and record which blocks make up the new version.
  6. The notification service pushes "file updated" to your phone, which is holding an open long-poll connection.
  7. Your phone asks the API servers for the new metadata, sees it needs blocks 2 and 5, downloads just those from the block servers, and rebuilds the file.
  8. Your tablet was offline all day. The change waits in the offline backup queue; when the tablet reconnects it pulls the latest changes and runs the same download flow.

3 Purpose & Concept Beacons

Google Drive keeps many devices in agreement about a user's files by moving bytes as small, hashed blocks and coordinating everything through a strongly managed metadata record plus change notifications.

Mental picture

Picture a jigsaw library. Every document is a jigsaw cut into numbered pieces of at most 4 MB (blocks), each stamped with a fingerprint (hash) and sealed in a tamper-proof bag (compression and encryption). The pieces live in a vault with branches in several cities (S3 with cross-region replication), and old puzzles are moved to the cellar (cold storage). A head librarian keeps the master catalogue of which pieces make up which edition of which puzzle (metadata DB via API servers). When a puzzle changes, a messenger runs to every reading room (notification service over long polling), and leaves notes for readers who are out (offline backup queue). Readers then swap only the pieces whose fingerprints changed (delta sync).
