4 Opportunistic Drilling

The marks concentrate on four ideas: the improved architecture, the block model with delta sync, the upload/download choreography, and conflict handling. Everything else (failure handling, storage savings) plugs into these.

From one server to the improved design

The starting point is almost comically simple: one web server, one metadata database, and a drive/ directory containing a namespace folder per user. A file is identified by namespace plus relative path. It works for a demo, but one disk fills up, one server is a single point of failure, and nothing is replicated.

The first fixes are familiar: shard storage by user_id, move files to Amazon S3 with cross-region replication, put a load balancer in front of multiple web servers, and shard and replicate the metadata database. The improved design then separates concerns into distinct services, shown below.

Common trap: sending file bytes through the API servers. API servers handle every workflow except uploading; bytes go through block servers.

Blocks, hashes and delta sync

Block servers cut every file into blocks of at most 4 MB, give each block a unique hash, compress it with an algorithm suited to the file type, encrypt it, and store it independently in cloud storage. The file itself is just an ordered list of block references in the metadata DB, and reconstruction means joining blocks in that order.

This single idea pays off three times. Delta sync: when you edit a file, only blocks whose hashes changed are transferred. Deduplication: identical blocks within an account are stored once. Reliability: a failed block upload can be retried on its own, and a failed block server simply has its pending tasks reassigned.

Gains

Far less bandwidth per edit, faster sync, storage savings from dedup, and fine-grained retries.

Costs

More metadata: a Block table and File Version table must track which blocks make up each version, and clients must reassemble files.

Upload and download choreography

Upload runs two tracks at once. On the metadata track, the client sends file metadata to the API servers, which store it with status pending and trigger a notification that a change is coming. On the data track, the client uploads to block servers, which push blocks to cloud storage. When storage finishes, it calls back the API servers, which set the status to uploaded and trigger a second notification.

Download is the mirror image, triggered by a change elsewhere. An online client hears about it via the notification service; an offline client finds changes waiting when it reconnects. Either way, it fetches metadata from the API servers first, then downloads only the needed blocks and rebuilds the file.

  1. Trigger: notification (online) or queued changes (on reconnect).
  2. Fetch updated metadata via API servers.
  3. Download the changed blocks from block servers.
  4. Reconstruct the file locally.
Common trap: thinking notifications carry the file. They only say "something changed"; the client then pulls metadata and blocks itself.

Sync conflicts and failure handling

When two users modify the same file at the same time, the version the system processes first wins. User 1's update goes through; user 2 gets a sync conflict. Nothing is thrown away: the system presents user 2 with both their local copy and the latest server version, and user 2 chooses to merge them or override one with the other.

Component failsRecovery
Load balancerSecondary load balancer becomes active.
Block serverPending tasks are reassigned to other servers.
Metadata DBPromote a replica (slave) to master; redirect traffic to remaining replicas.
Cloud storageFetch files from another region via cross-region replication.
Notification serviceClients reconnect to alternative servers.

Storage costs are controlled three ways: block-level dedup by hash, limiting the number of saved revisions while favouring recent ones for frequently edited files, and moving rarely accessed files to cold storage such as S3 Glacier.

Test yourself

Answer in the margin with your stylus before you reveal each one.

Why split files into 4 MB blocks instead of storing whole files?

Blocks with hashes enable delta sync (only changed blocks travel), deduplication (identical blocks stored once) and independent retries. Whole-file storage would force re-uploading an entire 10 GB file for a one-byte change.

What does the pending status protect against?

Metadata is written before the bytes have finished uploading. Marking it pending means the file is known but not yet complete; only the cloud storage callback moves it to uploaded, so no client treats a half-uploaded file as ready.

A laptop is offline for two days while files change. What happens when it reconnects?

Change information was kept in the offline backup queue. On reconnecting, the client pulls the latest changes, fetches updated metadata from the API servers, and downloads only the blocks it needs.

Two users save the same file at the same moment. Walk through the outcome.

Whichever update the system processes first wins and becomes the latest version. The other user gets a sync conflict and is shown both their local copy and the server version, then chooses to merge or override.

Compare the roles of block servers and API servers.

Block servers handle file bytes: splitting, hashing, compressing, encrypting and storing blocks. API servers handle everything else: authentication, profiles, and metadata updates in the metadata DB.

Why long polling for the notification service?

Clients hold a connection open so the server can respond as soon as a file is added, edited or deleted, giving near-instant change notification without constant repeated requests.

The primary metadata database dies. What happens?

A replica is promoted to master and traffic is redirected to the remaining replicas, so metadata stays available.

Introduction

Google Drive is a cloud-based file storage and synchronization service that allows users to store, access, and share files from various devices. This chapter discusses designing a scalable system with the following features:

  • File Upload and Download
  • File Sync Across Devices
  • File Sharing
  • File Revision History
  • Notifications for Edits, Deletes, and Shares

Step 1: Understanding the Problem

Key Requirements

Functional Requirements:

  • Upload and download files.
  • Sync files across multiple devices.
  • Maintain file revisions.
  • Enable file sharing with permissions.
  • Send notifications on file edits, deletions, and shares.

Non-Functional Requirements:

  • Reliability: Data loss is unacceptable.
  • Fast Sync Speed: Avoid user impatience with delayed syncing.
  • Bandwidth Efficiency: Minimize unnecessary data usage.
  • Scalability: Handle 10 million daily active users (DAU).
  • High Availability: Operate seamlessly during server failures or network issues.

Constraints and Assumptions

  • Users get 10 GB free space.
  • Maximum file size: 10 GB.
  • Average file upload size: 500 KB.
  • Upload frequency: 2 files per day per user.
  • Total storage required: 500 PB.

Step 2: High-Level Design

Single-Server Setup

A basic setup includes:

  1. Web Server: Handles uploads and downloads.
  2. Metadata Database: to keep track of metadata like user data, login info, files info.
  3. Storage Directory: Holds files organized by namespaces.
  • A web server and a directory called drive/ is set up as the root directory to store uploaded files.
  • Under drive/ directory, there is a list of directories called namespaces.
  • Each namespace contains all the uploaded files for that user.
  • Each file or folder can be uniquely identified by joining the namespace and the relative path.

This design serves as a starting point but is inadequate for scaling.

APIs

  1. Upload a file to Google Drive: Two types of uploads are supported
    • Simple upload: Used when file size is small.
    • Resumable upload:
      • Endpoint: https://api.example.com/files/upload?uploadType=resumable
      • Send the initial request to retrieve the resumable URL.
      • Upload the data and monitor upload state
      • If upload is disturbed, resume the upload.
  2. Download a file from Google Drive: To download a file
    • Endpoint: https://api.example.com/files/download
  3. Get file revisions:
    • Endpoint: https://api.example.com/files/list_revisions

Moving to Distributed Systems

Improvements:

  1. Sharding: Split storage across servers based on user_id.
  2. Amazon S3: Use S3 for scalable and redundant file storage with cross-region replication.
  3. Load Balancer: Distribute traffic across multiple web servers.
  4. Metadata Database Replication: Ensure availability through database sharding and replication.

Sync Conflicts:

For a large storage system like Google Drive, sync conflicts happen from time to time. When two users modify the same file or folder at the same time, a conflict happens.

  • In the example user 1 and user 2 tries to update the same file at the same time, but user 1's file is processed by our system first.
  • User 1's update operation goes through, but, user 2 gets a sync conflict.
  • The system presents both copies of the same file: user 2's local copy and the latest version from the server.
  • User 2 has the option to merge both files or override one version with the other.

Improved design

  1. User Interaction: Users access the application via browser or mobile app.
  2. Block Servers:
    • Files are split into 4 MB blocks (maximum size) and assigned unique hash values.
    • Blocks are stored independently in cloud storage (e.g., Amazon S3).
    • File reconstruction involves joining blocks in a specific order.
  3. Cloud Storage: Blocks are stored in cloud storage for scalability and redundancy.
  4. Cold Storage: Inactive files are moved to cold storage to reduce costs.
  5. Load Balancer: Distributes requests evenly among API servers to ensure efficient operation.
  6. API Servers:
    • Handle user authentication, profile management, and file metadata updates.
    • Manage all non-uploading workflows.
  7. Metadata Database and Cache:
    • Stores metadata for users, files, blocks, and versions.
    • Frequently accessed metadata is cached for faster retrieval.
  8. Notification Service:
    • A publisher/subscriber system that notifies clients about file changes (add, edit, delete).
    • Ensures clients can pull the latest updates.
  9. Offline Backup Queue: Temporarily stores file change information for offline clients to sync when back online.

Step 3: Design Deep Dive

Metadata Database

A highly simplified version is shown below as it only includes the most important tables and fields.

Schema Design:

  • User Table: Stores user profiles and preferences.
  • File Table: Maintains file metadata (e.g., size, name, path).
  • Block Table: Tracks file blocks for reconstructing files.
  • File Version Table: Stores file revision history.

File Upload Flow

  1. File Upload:
    • File is split into blocks, compressed, and encrypted by the block server.
    • Blocks are uploaded to block servers and stored in S3.
  2. Metadata Upload:
    • Client sends metadata to the API server.
    • Metadata is stored in the database with status pending.
  3. Completion:
    • S3 triggers a callback to update the file status to uploaded.
    • Notification service informs relevant users.

File Sync

  1. Delta Sync: Transfer only modified blocks instead of the entire file.
  2. Compression: Blocks are compressed using compression algorithms depending on file types.
  3. Conflict Resolution:
    • First processed version wins.
    • Conflicting versions are saved separately for user resolution.

File Download Flow

Download flow is triggered when a file is added or edited elsewhere. There are two ways a client can know:

  • If client A is online while a file is changed by another client, notification service will inform client A.
  • If client A is offline while a file is changed by another client, data will be saved to the cache. When the offline client is online again, it pulls the latest changes.

Once a client knows a file is changed, it first requests metadata via API servers, then downloads blocks to construct the file.

  1. Trigger: Notification service informs the client of file updates.
  2. Metadata Fetch: Client retrieves updated metadata via API.
  3. Block Download: Client downloads updated blocks from block servers and reconstructs the file.

Notification Service

  1. Purpose: Keeps clients updated about file changes.
  2. Mechanism: Implements long polling for asynchronous notifications.
  3. Example: When a file is added, edited, or deleted, notifications are pushed to all relevant clients.

Storage Optimization

  1. De-duplication: Remove duplicate blocks at the account level using hash-based comparisons.
  2. Versioning Strategy:
    • Limit the number of saved revisions.
    • Prioritize recent versions for frequently edited files.
  3. Cold Storage: Move rarely accessed files to cheaper storage solutions (e.g., Amazon S3 Glacier).

Failure Handling

  1. Load Balancer Failure: Secondary load balancer becomes active.
  2. Block Server Failure: Pending tasks are reassigned to other servers.
  3. Metadata Database Failure:
    • Promote a slave node to master.
    • Redirect traffic to remaining replicas.
  4. Cloud Storage Failure: Use cross-region replication to fetch unavailable files.
  5. Notification Service Failure: Clients reconnect to alternative servers.
16

Proximity Service

Picture this

It is 8 pm on a Friday in downtown San Francisco and you open a map app: "restaurants within 500 m". Your phone sends two numbers, 37.776720 and -122.416730, and within a blink you get a ranked list of nearby places. Out of 200 million businesses on the planet, the system had to find the few dozen inside a small circle around you, while 100 million daily users fire around 5,000 searches per second, spiking in exactly the dense neighbourhoods where businesses cluster. The catch is that databases are brilliant at sorting along one line but clumsy at asking "what is near this point in two dimensions?"

1 Macro Structure & Dependency Map

The system is two services on one database cluster: a read-only Location-Based Service that answers "what is near me" and a Business Service that manages the businesses themselves. The intellectual heart is the geospatial index that turns 2D proximity into a 1D lookup.

  • Geospatial Index — the whole problem is making 2D "nearby" searchable; every other choice follows from which index you pick
    • Hash family: even grid, geohash
      • Geohash: 12 precision levels; shared prefix = nearby
      • Boundary issues → also search 8 neighbours
    • Tree family: quadtree, Google S2, R-tree
      • Quadtree splits until ≤100 businesses per leaf
      • S2: Hilbert curve, geofencing
    • Naive 2D search: lat/long range query (baseline to reject)
  • Location-Based Service (LBS) — the hot, read-only, stateless path that handles ~5,000 QPS
    • GET /v1/search/nearby with latitude, longitude, radius (default 5000 m)
    • Radius → geohash length → own cell + 8 neighbours
    • Parallel Redis calls, then rank by distance
  • Business Service & Data Store — the source of truth for business details and owner edits
    • Business CRUD APIs (GET/POST/PUT/DELETE /v1/businesses)
    • MySQL primary-replica cluster; business table sharded by business ID
      • Geohash index table fits one server: use read replicas, not shards
    • Updates not real-time; batch processed daily
      • Replica lag is acceptable
  • Caching & Deployment — what makes the read path fast and resilient under peaks
    • Cache key = geohash (not raw coordinates)
    • Two Redis caches: geohash → business IDs; business_id → details
    • Multi-region deployment
      • GDPR / CCPA privacy compliance

The geospatial index is the hub because it is what LBS queries, what the cache is keyed on, and what determines whether the data must be rebuilt (quadtree) or simply re-hashed (geohash). LBS and Business Service are split because their traffic shapes differ: LBS is massive, read-only and stateless, while Business Service is lower-volume and owns writes.

2 Black-Box Cause & Effect Flow

A nearby search is a funnel: coordinates become a cell code, the cell code becomes a list of IDs, the IDs become rich details, and the details become a ranked list.

Load Balancer

Input: HTTP requests from clients.

Output: /search/nearby routed to LBS; /businesses/{id} routed to Business Service.

A fork in the road: "looking for places?" goes left, "looking at one place?" goes right.

→ feeds into: LBS or Business Service

LBS: radius to geohash

Input: latitude, longitude, radius.

Output: The user's geohash at the right precision plus its 8 neighbouring geohashes.

Turns "this exact spot and 500 m around it" into "this tile and the eight tiles touching it".

→ feeds into: Geohash Redis

Geohash Redis

Input: A list of 9 geohashes.

Output: Business IDs in each of those cells, fetched with parallel queries.

A set of pigeonholes labelled by tile code; each holds the IDs of businesses located in that tile.

→ feeds into: Business Info Redis

Business Info Redis

Input: Business IDs.

Output: Full details: name, address, reviews, location.

The card catalogue: give it an ID, get the full card.

→ feeds into: LBS ranking

LBS ranking

Input: Candidate businesses with coordinates.

Output: Results sorted by distance from the user, returned to the client.

The tiles gave a rough neighbourhood; ranking measures the real distance and orders the list.

→ feeds into: the client's map

Business Service & DB cluster

Input: Owner create/update/delete requests; customer detail views.

Output: Writes to the MySQL primary, replicated to replicas and synced into the Redis caches, batch processed daily.

The back office that edits the records; the front counter (Redis) gets its copies refreshed on a schedule.

→ feeds into: Redis caches used by LBS

Follow one search

  1. You search for restaurants within 500 m. The client sends latitude 37.776720, longitude -122.416730, radius 500 m to the load balancer.
  2. The load balancer sees /search/nearby and forwards the request to one of the stateless LBS servers.
  3. LBS consults the radius-to-precision table: 500 m maps to geohash length 6. It encodes your coordinates into a 6-character geohash.
  4. Because you might be standing near a cell edge, LBS computes the 8 neighbouring geohashes, giving a list of 9: [my_geohash, neighbor1, ..., neighbor8].
  5. LBS queries the Geohash Redis server for all 9 in parallel. Each returns a list of business IDs, like 9q9hvu → [343, 347, 112].
  6. LBS fetches full details for those IDs from the Business Info Redis server.
  7. LBS computes the distance from you to each business, sorts them, and returns the ranked list.
  8. Later, a restaurant owner updates their hours through Business Service. The write goes to the MySQL primary and is picked up in the daily batch, so up to a day of staleness is expected and harmless.

3 Purpose & Concept Beacons

A proximity service converts two-dimensional location into a one-dimensional key (a geohash or a tree path) so that "what is near me?" becomes a fast, cacheable lookup instead of a scan.

Mental picture

Imagine the Earth covered in nested tiles, like a floor where each tile can be cut into four smaller tiles, and those into four more. Every tile has a postcode spelled out letter by letter, and longer postcodes mean smaller tiles: that postcode is the geohash. To find what is near you, you read your own postcode at the right length for your radius, then peek at the eight tiles touching yours (neighbour search). A pigeonhole wall holds the business IDs for each postcode (Geohash Redis), and a card catalogue holds each business's details (Business Info Redis). A quadtree is the same floor, but tiles are cut only where it is crowded, so a dense downtown gets tiny tiles and a desert gets huge ones.

100M DAU × 5 / 86,400 ≈ 5,000 QPSRead-heavy search load; optimise reads and caching.
200M businessesLarge but the index still fits in memory on one server (GBs).
1D index vs 2D queryA normal DB index speeds only one dimension, so lat/long range queries stay slow.
GeohashInterleaves longitude and latitude bits into one string; 12 precision levels.
Longer shared prefix = closerGeohash's guarantee; the reverse (close implies shared prefix) is not guaranteed.
500 m → length 6Choose the minimal geohash length for the radius (1-2 km → 5; 5-20 km → 4).
Own cell + 8 neighboursThe fix for boundary issues: never trust a single cell.
Quadtree (≤100 per leaf)In-memory tree that splits crowded areas; adapts to density and supports k-nearest.
O(n log n) build, minutesQuadtree servers cannot serve while building, so roll out releases incrementally.
Google S2 / Hilbert curveMaps the sphere to 1D; great for geofencing arbitrary areas with variable cell levels.
Cache key = geohashRaw GPS is noisy and users move; the geohash is a stable key.
Shard business table, replicate indexBusiness data sharded by ID; geohash index fits one server, so add read replicas.

4 Opportunistic Drilling

Almost every question lands on the index: why naive search fails, how geohash works and breaks, when a quadtree wins, and how the final architecture stitches it to Redis. Drill these four and you can reconstruct the rest.

Why naive 2D search fails, and the two index families

The intuitive approach draws a box around the user and asks the database for every business whose latitude is within the radius and whose longitude is within the radius. Without indexes that scans the whole table. With separate indexes on latitude and longitude it is only slightly better: each index returns a huge band (a horizontal strip and a vertical strip spanning the globe), and the database must intersect those two enormous sets.

The root problem is that a database index speeds search in one dimension only. So the better approach maps 2D space into one dimension. Two families do this. Hash-based: the even grid and geohash. Tree-based: quadtree, Google S2 and R-tree.

Common trap: proposing an even grid. Fixed-size cells ignore density: a downtown cell holds thousands of businesses while a rural or ocean cell holds none.

Geohash: postcodes for the planet

Split the world into four quadrants along the prime meridian and the equator, labelling each with two bits. Split each quadrant into four again, and keep going. Each step adds bits, alternating between longitude and latitude, and the resulting bit string is encoded as a short alphanumeric string. There are 12 precision levels; each extra character means a smaller cell.

Choosing precision is a table lookup: take the minimal geohash length that covers the radius. 500 m needs length 6; 1 km and 2 km need length 5; 5 km and 20 km need length 4. The useful property is that a longer shared prefix means two points are closer, so a prefix match finds everything in a cell.

The catch is at the edges. Two places can be metres apart yet share no prefix at all (for example on opposite sides of the equator), and two places can share a long prefix but sit in different cells. The fix is simple and always applied: search your own cell plus its 8 neighbours.

Quadtree: tiles that shrink where it is crowded

A quadtree recursively splits 2D space into four quadrants, and each internal node has exactly four children. It keeps splitting a region until no leaf holds more than a threshold of businesses (100 in the notes). Dense cities therefore get deep, fine-grained branches, while empty areas stop early with large leaves.

It is an in-memory structure built on each LBS server at startup. It needs only GBs of memory, so it fits on one server, but building it is O(n log n) and takes a few minutes for about 200 million businesses. During that time the server cannot serve traffic, so new releases must roll out incrementally to a subset of servers. Adding or updating a business either triggers an incremental rebuild (with lots of cache invalidation) or an on-the-fly update that needs locking.

CriterionGeohashQuadtreeGoogle S2

Updating the indexEasyComplex; may rebuild treeNot covered in the notes
Known weaknessBoundary issuesStartup build time, rebalancingComplexity
Common trap: restarting all quadtree servers at once during a deploy. Each takes minutes to rebuild and cannot serve meanwhile, so an all-at-once rollout means an outage.

Scaling, caching and the final architecture

The business table is sharded by business ID so data spreads evenly. The geohash index table is different: it maps geohash to business ID, one row per business, and it fits on a single server, so sharding adds complexity with no benefit. Read replicas handle the read load instead. The primary-replica setup can briefly serve stale data, which is fine because business information is not updated in real time and changes are batch processed daily.

For caching, raw coordinates make a poor key: GPS readings are imprecise and users move, so almost every request would miss. The geohash is stable, so it becomes the key. Two caches result: geohash → list of business IDs, and business_id → business details.

Gains

Stateless LBS scales horizontally; parallel Redis reads keep latency low; multi-region deployment handles peaks and outages.

Costs

Data is eventually consistent: a business edit is not visible until the daily batch and cache sync.

Test yourself

Jot an answer in the margin with your stylus, then tap to compare.

Why does indexing latitude and longitude separately still perform poorly?

A database index speeds search in only one dimension. Each index returns a huge strip of candidates, and the database must intersect those two large sets. Geospatial indexing solves this by mapping 2D location to a single 1D key.

What happens if LBS searches only the user's own geohash cell?

Businesses just across a cell boundary are missed, even if they are a few metres away, because nearby points need not share a prefix. That is why LBS always adds the 8 neighbouring cells.

A user wants restaurants within 500 m. Which geohash length, and why that one?

Length 6, from the radius-to-precision table. You pick the minimal length whose cells cover the radius, so the cell plus its neighbours captures the search circle without pulling in far too many candidates.

Compare geohash and quadtree for a "find the 5 closest gas stations" query.

Quadtree is better: it supports k-nearest searches and adapts cell size to density. Geohash is built for fixed-radius search and cannot dynamically resize its grid, although it is simpler and easier to update.

Why is the geohash a better cache key than the raw coordinates?

GPS coordinates are imprecise and change as users move, so exact coordinates rarely repeat and would almost always miss the cache. Many nearby users share the same geohash, making it a stable, high-hit-rate key.

Why shard the business table but not the geohash index table?

The business table holds rich details for 200 million businesses and benefits from even distribution by business ID. The geohash index is small enough to fit on one server, so sharding only adds complexity; read replicas handle the read load.

What operational risk does the quadtree introduce, and how is it handled?

Building it at startup takes a few minutes (O(n log n) for about 200 million businesses), during which the server cannot serve traffic. Releases are rolled out incrementally to a subset of servers at a time so capacity remains.

Introduction

A proximity service is designed to find nearby locations, such as restaurants, hotels, gas stations, and other businesses. This functionality is used in applications like Google Maps and Yelp to help users discover places within a defined radius.

Step 1: Understanding the Problem and Establishing Scope

Functional Requirements

  1. Search for businesses based on user location (latitude, longitude) and search radius.
  2. Allow business owners to add, update, or delete businesses (not real-time).
  3. Provide detailed business information when requested.

Non-Functional Requirements

  • Low latency: Users should get quick responses.
  • Data privacy: Compliance with GDPR and CCPA regulations.
  • High availability: Handle peak-hour spikes in busy locations.

Back-of-the-Envelope Estimation

  • 100 million daily active users.
  • 200 million businesses in the system.
  • Search QPS Calculation:
    • Users make 5 searches per day.
    • Search QPS = (100M × 5) / 86,400 ≈ 5,000 QPS.

Step 2: High-Level Design

API Design

Search Nearby Businesses

GET /v1/search/nearby

  • Request Parameters:
    • latitude: User's location latitude.
    • longitude: User's location longitude.
    • radius: Search radius (default: 5000m).

Business APIs

API EndpointDescription
GET /v1/businesses/{id}Fetch detailed business info
POST /v1/businessesAdd a new business
PUT /v1/businesses/{id}Update business details
DELETE /v1/businesses/{id}Remove a business from the system

Data Model

  • Since the read volume is high because two features are very commonly used, a relational database such as MySQL is a good fit.
    • Search for nearby businesses
    • View the detailed information of a business

Data Schema

  • Key Database tables are the business table and the geospatial index table
  • The business table consists the detailed information about a business.

High-Level System Architecture

The system comprises of two parts: Location based service (LBS) and business related service.

  • Location-Based Service (LBS):
    • Processes location-based search queries.
    • Read-heavy service with no write requests.
    • QPS is high especially during peak hours in dense areas and the system is stateless.
  • Business Service: Deals with two types of requests.
    • Business owners create, update or delete businesses.
    • Customers view detailed information about a business.
  • Load Balancer: Routes traffic to LBS and Business service.
  • Database Cluster:
    • Uses primary-replica architecture for read-heavy workloads.
    • There might be some discrepancy between data read b/w data read by LBS and data written by by primary database.
    • This inconsistency is not an issue because the business information is not updated in real-time.

Step 3: Algorithms for Fetching Nearby Businesses

Option 1: Two-Dimensional Search (Naive Approach)

The most intuitive way is to draw a circle with pre-defined radius and find all the businesses within the circle.

SQL Query:

SELECT business_id, latitude, longitude
FROM business
WHERE (latitude BETWEEN :lat - radius AND :lat + radius)
AND (longitude BETWEEN :long - radius AND :long + radius);

Problems:

  • Inefficient: Requires scanning the entire database.
  • Limited by one-dimensional indexes (latitude/longitude).

A potential improvement is to build index on longitude and latitude columns, although this is slightly better but still very slow.

Better Approach

  • The problem with last approach is that the database index can only increase search speed in one dimension.
  • An optimal approach is to represent the two-dimensional data into one dimension using geospatial indexing.
    • Hash: Even grid, Geo Hash
    • Tree: Quadtree, Google S2, RTree

Option 2: Evenly Divided Grid

  • Divides the world into fixed-size grids.
  • Issue: Uneven business distribution (high density in cities, sparse in rural areas).

Option 3: Geohash

  • Divide the planet into four quadrants along with the prime meridian and equator. And then divide each grid into four smaller grids.
  • Each grids can be represented by altering b/w longitude and latitude bit.
  • Repeat this subdivision
  • Encodes latitude and longitude into a single alphanumeric string. It has 12 precisions (levels)
  • Hierarchical grid structure allows for efficient searching.
  • The right precision is chosen by using the minimal geohash length according to the table.
  • Geohash guarantees that the longer a shared prefix is between two geohashes, the closer they are.

Challenges:

  • Boundary issues (businesses close to grid edges may get excluded).
    • Two locations can be very close but have no shared prefix at all (can be on other side of equator)
    • Two locations can have a long shared prefix but belong to different geohashes.
  • Solution: Need to search neighboring grids.

Option 4: Quadtree

A quadtree is a tree data structure that recursively divides a two-dimensional space into four quadrants, with each internal node having exactly four children, representing the four sub-regions of the space.

  • The quadtree is an in-memory data structure and it runs on each LBS server and built on server startup time.
  • The root node is recursively broken down into 4 quadrants until no nodes are left with more than x number of businesses (100 in this case).
  • The quadtree index doesn't take too much memory (typically in GBs) and can easily fit in one server.
  • Since the time complexity to build the tree is nlogn, it might take a few minutes to build the tree.
  • Efficient for k-nearest search queries (e.g., find the closest gas station).

Operational considerations

  • For around 200 million businesses, it might take few minutes to build a quadtree at the server start time.
  • While the quadtree is built it cannot serve traffic, therefore a new release should be rolled out incrementally to a subset of servers.
  • When updating a business or adding a new the easiest approach is to incrementally rebuild the quadtree. (Leading to a lot of cache invalidation)
  • Also possible to update the quadtree on the fly but more complex to implement. (Needs locking mechanism)

Option 5: Google S2

It maps a sphere to a 1D index based on Hilbert curve. Two points that are close to each other on the Hilbert curve are close in 1D space.

  • Divides the earth into small cells using a Hilbert curve.
  • Great for geofencing because it can cover arbitrary areas with varying levels.
  • Geofencing also allows to define parameters that surround the area of interest.
  • Another advantage if instead of having a fixed level of precision, we can specify min,max level and max cells in S2.

Tradeoff Comparison

Geohash

  • Easy to use and implement - No need to build/rebuild a tree
  • Supports fixed radius results
  • Updating the index is easy.
  • Cannot dynamically adjust the grid size based on population density.

Quadtree

  • Slightly harder to implement.
  • Supports fetching k-nearest businesses.
  • Can dynamically adjust the grid size based on population density.
  • Updating the index is more complicated as might need to rebuild the whole tree.

Step 4: Scaling the Database and Caching Strategy

Scaling the Business Table

  • Sharding by business ID ensures even data distribution.
  • We have separate rows for each business in the table.
GeohashBusiness ID
9q9hvu343
9q9hvu347
9q9hvu112

Scaling the Geospatial Index

  • Might not be a good fit for the geohash table. In this case everything can fit in a single server so there's no technical reason for sharding.
  • A better approach is to have read-replicas to help with read loads.

Cache Strategy

The most obvious cache key choice is the location coordinate, however it has a few issues:

  • Location coordinates from gps are not accurate.
  • A user can move causing the location coordinate to change.
  • A better key is the geohash.
Cache KeyCache Value
geohashList of business IDs in that grid
business_idBusiness details (name, address, reviews, etc.)

Step 5: Deployment Strategy and Final Architecture

Region and Availability Zones

  • Deploy LBS and Business Service across multiple regions.

Handling Real-Time Updates

  • Business updates are batch processed daily.

Final System Architecture

This final algorithm looks like this:

Steps to Retrieve Nearby Businesses

  1. User Request:
    • A user searches for restaurants within 500 meters.
    • The client sends latitude (37.776720), longitude (-122.416730), and radius (500m) to the load balancer.
  2. Request Forwarding:
    • The load balancer (LB) forwards the request to the Location-Based Service (LBS).
  3. Geohash Calculation:
    • LBS determines the geohash length matching the radius.
    • Using a reference table, 500m corresponds to geohash length = 6.
  4. Fetching Neighboring Geohashes:
    • LBS calculates neighboring geohashes to include nearby areas.
    • The result is a list: 
      [my_geohash, neighbor1_geohash, neighbor2_geohash, ..., neighbor8_geohash]
  5. Fetching Business IDs from Redis:
    • For each geohash in the list, LBS queries the Geohash Redis server to fetch business IDs.
    • Parallel queries are used to minimize latency.
  6. Retrieving & Ranking Businesses:
    • LBS fetches full business details from the Business Info Redis server.
    • Businesses are sorted by distance from the user's location.
    • The ranked results are sent back to the client.

Key Optimizations

  • Parallel Redis Calls: Reduces response time.
  • Geohash Indexing: Ensures efficient spatial queries.
  • Caching: Speeds up lookup and retrieval of business data.

This method ensures low-latency, scalable retrieval of businesses near a user's location.

Choosing the Best Indexing Method

Indexing MethodProsCons
GeohashEasy to implement, efficient for proximity searchBoundary issues, fixed grid size
QuadtreeDynamically adjusts to density, supports k-nearest queriesMore complex, requires tree rebalancing
Google S2Advanced geofencing, used in Google MapsHarder to implement

References

  1. Geohash Algorithm
  2. Quadtree Indexing
  3. Google S2 Geometry

Nearby Friends

Picture this

It is Saturday evening and ten million phones are awake at once, each one quietly whispering "here I am" to the backend every 30 seconds. Somewhere downtown, you open the app and, within seconds, dots appear: your college roommate is 1.2 miles away, a colleague is 3 miles out, and the dot for your cousin just slid a little closer. Unlike a restaurant finder, where the addresses sit still for years, every dot here is moving, and every move must be relayed to the handful of friends who care. That is roughly 334,000 location updates arriving each second, each fanning out to about 40 online friends. The hard part is not finding friends; it is being a tireless, real-time switchboard at that volume.

1 Macro Structure & Dependency Map

From 10,000 feet this is a fan-out machine: updates come in over persistent connections, get stored briefly, and are broadcast to friends. Read each hub as a load-bearing wall; everything nested under it collapses if the hub is misunderstood.

  • WebSocket servers (stateful, persistent connections) — the only path by which updates reach phones in real time; every other component is fed by or feeds these
    • Periodic location update routine (client sends location every 30s)
      • Other routines: client init, receive update, subscribe / unsubscribe a friend
    • Distance filter: forward only if friend is within the 5-mile threshold
      • Server keeps each connected user's latest location in memory for this math
    • Scaling by "draining" a server in the load balancer before removal
      • REST API servers handle auxiliary work (friends, profiles) and scale trivially
  • Redis Pub/Sub (one channel per user) — the switchboard that routes one user's update to all servers holding that user's friends
    • WebSocket servers subscribe to channels of each connected user's friends
      • Channels are pre-allocated; idle channels consume no memory
    • Distributed cluster sized for CPU: ~14M pushes/s ÷ ~100k per server = 140+ servers
      • Memory need is only ~200GB (2 servers of 100GB would do)
    • Consistent hash ring stored in ZooKeeper / etcd
      • Ring cached in memory on each WebSocket server
  • Redis location cache (latest location + TTL) — the "who is active and where" snapshot that seeds new clients and defines activity itself
    • Maps user_id to lat, long, timestamp
      • TTL expiry = user is inactive (friends disappear after ~10 min)
    • Sharded across several Redis nodes to absorb the write load
  • Durable stores (User DB + Location history DB) — the slow, permanent side: who your friends are, and where everyone has been
    • User DB: users + friendships, sharded by user_id
      • Could be its own service owned by a dedicated team
    • Location history in Cassandra (write-heavy), used for analytics / ML
      • Not on the hot path of the nearby feature

WebSocket servers are the hub because they own the live connection and the distance calculation. Redis Pub/Sub is the second hub because it replaces a brute-force "look up all 400 friends" query with a push-based broadcast. The location cache and durable stores are supporting actors: the cache answers "where is everyone right now" at startup, and the databases hold the slow-changing friend graph and the history nobody reads in real time.

2 Black-Box Cause & Effect Flow

Treat each component as a sealed box: know what goes in and what comes out, and the whole update pipeline becomes a chain of cause and effect.

Mobile client

Input: GPS reading, a 30-second timer.

Output: A location update (lat, long, timestamp) over its persistent WebSocket.

A lighthouse that flashes its position every half minute. Walking speed is slow, so more frequent flashes would waste battery for little gain.

→ feeds into: Load balancer → the client's WebSocket server

WebSocket server (sender side)

Input: The user's location update.

Output: A row in location history, a fresh entry in the location cache, an in-memory copy, and a publish to the user's own Pub/Sub channel.

A post office clerk who files a copy, updates the "last seen" board, and then drops the letter into the user's personal outgoing chute.

→ feeds into: Location history DB, Location cache, Redis Pub/Sub

Redis Pub/Sub channel

Input: One published message on channel user_X.

Output: A copy delivered to every subscriber, i.e. each WebSocket server holding one of X's online friends.

A megaphone with a subscriber list. It does not know who is near whom; it just repeats the message to everyone who signed up.

→ feeds into: Subscribed WebSocket servers

WebSocket server (receiver side)

Input: Friend X's new location, plus its own connected user's last known location held in memory.

Output: Either a pushed update (distance + timestamp) to the phone, or silence if beyond 5 miles.

The bouncer at the door: it calculates the distance and only lets the update through if the friend is close enough to matter.

→ feeds into: Friend's mobile client

Client initialization

Input: A newly opened connection with the user's location.

Output: Friend list fetched, subscriptions to every friend's channel, friends' current locations pulled from cache and sent down.

Walking into a party: you get the guest list, tune into everyone's conversation, and glance at where each person is standing right now.

→ feeds into: Steady-state periodic update loop

Location cache TTL

Input: Silence from a user (no updates).

Output: The cache entry expires; the user is treated as inactive.

A candle that burns out unless someone keeps relighting it. No explicit "logout" is needed.

→ feeds into: Future client initializations (friend no longer shown)

Follow one location update

  1. Maya's phone, 30 seconds after its last ping, sends (37.77, -122.41, t=20:00:30) over its open WebSocket.
  2. The load balancer routes it along the persistent connection to WebSocket server WS-7, which owns Maya's connection.
  3. WS-7 appends the point to the Cassandra location history table (for later analytics).
  4. WS-7 overwrites Maya's entry in the Redis location cache and resets its TTL; it also stores the point in its own memory.
  5. WS-7 hashes the channel name "maya" on the cached consistent-hash ring, finds Pub/Sub server p_3, and publishes.
  6. Maya has 400 friends; about 10% (40) are online. Their WebSocket servers all subscribed to "maya" during init, so p_3 pushes 40 copies out.
  7. On WS-2, friend Leo's last location is in memory: 1.8 miles from Maya. Within 5 miles, so WS-2 pushes "Maya, 1.8 mi, 20:00:30" to Leo's phone.
  8. On WS-9, friend Priya is 11 miles away. WS-9 drops the update silently.
  9. Multiply by 334k updates per second and you get ~14 million pushes per second through the Pub/Sub layer.

3 Purpose & Concept Beacons

Build a real-time fan-out backend that relays each active user's constantly changing location to nearby friends within seconds, tolerating occasional lost points but never falling over.

Mental picture

Imagine a vast radio network. Every user owns a personal radio frequency: that is their Redis Pub/Sub channel. The WebSocket servers are receiving stations that tune in to the frequencies of every friend of the listeners they serve. When you speak your location into your frequency, every tuned-in station hears it, but each station has a filter: it only relays your voice to its listener if you are within 5 miles. The big bulletin board by the door that shows "last heard from, and where" is the Redis location cache, and chalk marks on it fade after a few minutes (TTL). The archive room recording every broadcast forever is the Cassandra location history database.

10M concurrent / 30s = ~334k QPSThe inbound update rate; tells you writes dominate and the refresh interval is the main dial.
400 friends x 10% online = 40Fan-out factor per update; multiplies inbound QPS into ~14M pushes/s.
WebSocketBidirectional persistent connection; lets the server push without polling, but makes servers stateful.
One channel per userPublisher does not need to know who listens; subscribers manage their own interest.
Idle channels cost nothingSo channels can be pre-allocated for every user of the feature; no setup dance when someone comes online.
CPU-bound, not memory-bound200GB memory fits on 2 servers, but ~100k pushes/s per server forces 140+ servers.
TTL = activityExpiry in the cache automatically removes inactive users; memory is naturally capped.
Consistent hashingMaps channels to Pub/Sub servers so adding/removing a server moves only a slice of channels.
ZooKeeper / etcdService discovery holding the hash ring; WebSocket servers cache it locally.
DrainingStop new connections to a WebSocket server before removal; graceful scale-down of stateful nodes.
Eventual consistencyA few seconds of lag between replicas is fine; losing an occasional point is acceptable.
Geohash channelsExtension for "nearby random person": subscribe to your area's channel plus its neighbors.

4 Opportunistic Drilling

Interviews on this problem live or die on three things: the fan-out path, scaling the Pub/Sub cluster, and what state the WebSocket layer holds. Drill those; skim the rest.

The periodic update and fan-out path

The core insight is to flip the question. Instead of each user asking "where are my 400 friends?", each user announces "here I am" once, and the system pushes that announcement to the ~40 friends who are online. Redis Pub/Sub is the lightweight message bus that makes this cheap: one publish, many deliveries.

Notice where the distance check happens: on the receiving WebSocket server, not in Redis. Pub/Sub delivers blindly to every subscriber; the receiving server compares the friend's new point against its own user's in-memory location and decides whether to push. This keeps Redis dumb and fast.

  1. Client sends location to its WebSocket server.
  2. Server writes to location history DB and to the location cache (plus its own memory).
  3. Server publishes to the user's channel.
  4. Pub/Sub broadcasts to every subscribed WebSocket server.
  5. Each receiver computes distance and pushes only if within the threshold.
Common trap: proposing peer-to-peer between phones. The notes reject it: mobile connections are flaky and battery-constrained, so a shared backend acting as a fan-out hub is the practical choice.

Scaling Redis Pub/Sub: a CPU problem in disguise

The memory math is surprisingly small: around 200GB for all channels, which two 100GB servers could hold. But the push rate tells a different story. Roughly 14 million location pushes per second, at about 100k pushes per server, demands at least 140 Redis servers. The bottleneck is CPU, so the cluster must be distributed.

To know which server owns which channel, the channel names are placed on a consistent hash ring stored in a service discovery system (ZooKeeper or etcd). Each WebSocket server caches that ring in memory and hashes a channel name to find its home. When a server is added or removed, consistent hashing ensures only the channels in the affected arc move.

Gains

Horizontal scaling of push throughput; minimal channel movement on resize; lookups are local (cached ring).

Costs

The cluster is effectively stateful: resizing triggers a storm of resubscriptions and may drop some updates, so do it at the daily traffic low, driven by a scheduled job, and overprovision for spikes.

Common trap: sizing the cluster by memory alone and concluding "two servers is enough." Always compute both memory and operations per second; here CPU wins by a factor of 70.

What each store holds, and why Redis twice

Redis appears in two roles and it is easy to blur them. The location cache stores just the latest point per user with a TTL: it answers "where is my friend right now?" during initialization and naturally forgets inactive users. Redis Pub/Sub stores no location at all; it is purely a routing fabric.

StoreHoldsWhy this tech
Redis location cacheuser_id → lat, long, timestampOnly current location matters; built-in TTL eviction
Redis Pub/SubPer-user channels and subscriber listsLightweight bus; idle channels are free
Location history (Cassandra)Same four columns, every pointOptimized for heavy writes; for analytics/ML
User DBUsers and friendshipsRelational or NoSQL, sharded by user_id

Adding or removing a friend is handled by a client callback: the app tells the WebSocket server, which subscribes to or unsubscribes from that friend's channel. "Whale" users with many friends are capped (Facebook's cap is 5000), and their extra load is absorbed by having enough WebSocket servers.

Extension: nearby random people via geohash channels

If the interviewer asks to show strangers nearby, swap "one channel per user" for "one channel per geohash cell." Everyone inside a cell publishes to and subscribes to that cell's channel, so you hear about anyone in your square of the map.

An alternative to Redis Pub/Sub entirely is Erlang: millions of lightweight processes can handle both WebSocket connections and channels in one distributed application. The catch is people, not technology: Erlang is niche and strong developers are hard to hire.

Test yourself

Write your answer in the margin with your stylus before tapping to reveal.

Why is the location refresh interval 30 seconds rather than 1 second?

Human walking speed is slow, so position barely changes in a second. With 10M concurrent users, 30s gives ~334k QPS; 1s would be 10M QPS inbound and 30x the fan-out, with little user-visible benefit and much worse battery drain.

Where does the 5-mile distance check happen, and why there?

On the receiving WebSocket server, which holds its connected user's latest location in memory. Pub/Sub just broadcasts to all subscribers; doing the math at the edge keeps Redis simple and avoids extra lookups.

Memory says 2 Redis servers; why do we need 140+?

The channels fit in ~200GB, but pushing ~14M updates per second at ~100k pushes per server needs at least 140 servers. The workload is CPU-bound, so the cluster size is set by throughput, not storage.

What happens when a Redis Pub/Sub server is added to the cluster?

Some channels move to the new server per the consistent hash ring. WebSocket servers see the updated ring and must resubscribe those channels, causing a burst of resubscription requests and possibly a few missed updates. Consistent hashing limits how many move; doing it at the daily traffic low limits the damage.

How does the system know a friend has gone inactive?

Each location cache entry has a TTL. If a user stops sending updates, the entry expires and they are treated as inactive, so they no longer appear when friends initialize. The TTL also caps the cache's maximum memory.

Compare the Redis location cache with the Cassandra location history table.

Both hold user_id, lat, long, timestamp. The cache keeps only the latest point with a TTL for real-time lookups; Cassandra keeps every point permanently for analytics and machine learning, chosen because it handles heavy write loads well.

Why can Pub/Sub channels be pre-allocated for every user?

Channels that exist but have no activity consume no memory in Redis Pub/Sub. Pre-allocating avoids the complexity of creating a channel when a user comes online and notifying all interested WebSocket servers.

Introduction

This chapter focuses on designing a scalable backend for an application which enables user to share their location and discover friends who are nearby.

The major difference with the proximity chapter is that in this problem, locations constantly change, whereas in that one, business addresses more or less stay the same.

Step 1: Understand the Problem and Establish Design Scope

Some questions to drive the interview:

  • C: How geographically close is considered to be "nearby"?
  • I: 5 miles, this number should be configurable
  • C: Is distance calculated as straight-line distance vs. taking into consideration eg a river in-between friends
  • I: Yes, that is a reasonable assumption
  • C: How many users does the app have?
  • I: 1bil users and 10% of them use the nearby friends feature
  • C: Do we need to store location history?
  • I: Yes, it can be valuable for eg machine learning
  • C: Can we assume inactive friends will disappear from the feature in 10min
  • I: Yes
  • C: Do we need to worry about GDPR, etc?
  • I: No, for simplicity's sake

Functional requirements

  • Users should be able to see nearby friends on their mobile app. Each friend has a distance and timestamp, indicating when the location was updated
  • Nearby friends list should be updated every few seconds

Non-functional requirements

  • Low latency: it's important to receive location updates without too much delay
  • Reliability: Occasional data point loss is acceptable, but system should be generally available
  • Eventual consistency: Location data store doesn't need strong consistency. Few seconds delay in receiving location data in different replicas is acceptable

Back-of-the-envelope

Some estimations to determine potential scale:

  • Nearby friends are friends within 5mile radius
  • Location refresh interval is 30s. Human walking speed is slow, hence, no need to update location too frequently.
  • On average, 100mil users use the feature every day \w 10% concurrent users, ie 10mil
  • On average, a user has 400 friends, all of them use the nearby friends feature
  • App displays 20 nearby friends per page
  • Location Update QPS = 10mil / 30 == ~334k updates per second

Step 2: Propose High-Level Design and Get Buy-In

Before exploring API and data model design, we'll study the communication protocol we'll use as it's less ubiquitous than traditional request-response communication model.

High-level design

At a high-level we'd want to establish effective message passing between peers. This can be done via a peer-to-peer protocol, but that's not practical for a mobile app with flaky connection and tight power consumption constraints.

A more practical approach is to use a shared backend as a fan-out mechanism towards friends you want to reach:

What does the backend do?

  • Receives location updates from all active users
  • For each location update, find all active users which should receive it and forward it to them
  • Do not forward location data if distance between friends is beyond the configured threshold

This sounds simple but the challenge is to design the system for the scale we're operating with.

We'll start with a simpler design at first and discuss a more advanced approach in the deep dive:

  • Load balancer: spreads traffic across rest API servers as well as bidirectional web socket servers
  • Rest API servers: handles auxiliary tasks such as managing friends, updating profiles, etc
  • Websocket servers: stateful servers, which forward location update requests to respective clients. It also manages seeding the mobile client with nearby friends locations at initialization (discussed in detail later).
  • Redis location cache: used to store most recent location data for each active user. There is a TTL set on each entry in the cache. When the TTL expires, user is no longer active and their data is removed from the cache.
  • User database: stores user and friendship data. Either a relational or NoSQL database can be used for this purpose.
  • Location history database: stores a history of user location data, not necessarily used directly within nearby friends feature, but instead used to track historical data for analytical purposes
  • Redis pubsub: used as a lightweight message bus which enables different topics for each user channel for location updates.

In the above example, websocket servers subscribe to channels for the users which are connected to them & forward location updates whenever they receive them to appropriate users.

Periodic location update

Here's how the periodic location update flow works:

  • Mobile client sends a location update to the load balancer
  • Load balancer forwards location update to the websocket server's persistent connection for that client
  • Websocket server saves location data to location history database
  • Location data is updated in location cache. Websocket server also saves location data in-memory for subsequent distance calculations for that user
  • Websocket server publishes location data in user's channel via redis pub sub
  • Redis pubsub broadcasts location update to all subscribers for that user channel, ie servers responsible for the friends of that user
  • Subscribed web socket servers receive location update, calculate which users the update should be sent to and sends it

Here's a more detailed version of the same flow:

On average, there's going to be 40 location updates to forward as a user has 400 friends on average and 10% of them are online at a time.

API Design

Websocket Routines we'll need to support:

  • periodic location update - user sends location data to websocket server
  • client receives location update - server sends friend location data and timestamp
  • websocket client initialization - client sends user location, server sends back nearby friends location data
  • Subscribe to a new friend - websocket server sends a friend ID mobile client is supposed to track eg when friend appears online for the first time
  • Unsubscribe a friend - websocket server sends a friend ID, mobile client is supposed to unsubscribe from due to eg friend going offline

HTTP API - traditional request/response payloads for auxiliary responsibilities.

Data model

  • The location cache will store a mapping between user_id and lat,long,timestamp. Redis is a great choice for this cache as we only care about current location and it supports TTL eviction which we need for our use-case.
  • Location history table stores the same data but in a relational table \w the four columns stated above. Cassandra can be used for this data as it is optimized for write-heavy loads.

Step 3: Design Deep Dive

Let's discuss how we scale the high-level design so that it works at the scale we're targeting.

How well does each component scale?

  • API servers: can be easily scaled via autoscaling groups and replicating server instances
  • Websocket servers: we can easily scale out the ws servers, but we need to ensure we gracefully shutdown existing connections when tearing down a server. Eg we can mark a server as "draining" in the load balancer and stop sending connections to it, prior to being finally removed from the server pool
  • Client initialization: when a client first connects to a server, it fetches the user's friends, subscribes to their channels on redis pubsub, fetches their location from cache and finally forwards to client
  • User database: We can shard the database based on user_id. It might also make sense to expose user/friends data via a dedicated service and API, managed by a dedicated team
  • Location cache: We can shard the cache easily by spinning up several redis nodes. Also, the TTL puts a limit on the max memory we could have taken up at a time. But we still want to handle the large write load
  • Redis pub/sub server: we leverage the fact that no memory is consumed if there are channels initialized but are not in use. Hence, we can pre-allocate channels for all users who use the nearby friends feature to avoid having to deal with eg bringing up a new channel when a user comes online and notifying active websocket servers

Scaling deep-dive on redis pub/sub component

We will need around 200gb of memory to maintain all pub/sub channels. This can be achieved by using 2 redis servers with 100gb each.

Given that we need to push ~14mil location updates per second, we will however need at least 140 redis servers to handle that amount of load, assuming that a single server can handle ~100k pushes per second.

Hence, we'll need a distributed redis server cluster to handle the intense CPU load.

In order to support a distributed redis cluster, we'll need to utilize a service discovery component, such as zookeeper or etcd, to keep track of which servers are alive.

What we need to encode in the service discovery component is this data:

Web socket servers use that encoded data, fetched from zookeeper to determine where a particular channel lives. For efficiency, the hash ring data can be cached in-memory on each websocket server.

In terms of scaling the server cluster up or down, we can setup a daily job to scale the cluster as needed based on historical traffic data. We can also overprovision the cluster to handle spikes in loads.

The redis cluster can be treated as a stateful storage server as there is some state maintained for the channels and there is a need for coordination with subscribers so that they hand-off to newly provisioned nodes in the cluster.

We have to be mindful of some potential issues during scaling operations:

  • There will be a lot of resubscription requests from the web socket servers due to channels being moved around
  • Some location updates might be missed from clients during the operation, which is acceptable for this problem, but we should still minimize it from happening. Consider doing such operation when traffic is at lowest point of the day.
  • We can leverage consistent hashing to minimize amount of channels moved in the event of adding/removing servers

Adding/removing friends

Whenever a friend is added/removed, websocket server responsible for affected user needs to subscribe/unsubscribe from the friend's channel.

Since the "nearby friends" feature is part of a larger app, we can assume that a callback on the mobile client side can be registered whenever any of the events occur and the client will send a message to the websocket server to do the appropriate action.

Users with many friends

We can put a cap on the total number of friends one can have, eg facebook has a cap of 5000 max friends.

The websocket server handling the "whale" user might have a higher load on its end, but as long as we have enough web socket servers, we should be okay.

Nearby random person

What if the interviewer wants to update the design to include a feature where we can occasionally see a random person pop up on our nearby friends map?

One way to handle this is to define a pool of pubsub channels, based on geohash:

Anyone within the geohash subscribes to the appropriate channel to receive location updates for random users:

We could also subscribe to several geohashes to handle cases where someone is close but in a bordering geohash:

Alternative to Redis pub/sub

An alternative to using Redis for pub/sub is to leverage Erlang - a general programming language, optimized for distributed computing applications.

With it, we can spawn millions of small, erlang processes which communicate with each other. We can handle both websocket connections and pub/sub channels within the distributed erlang application.

A challenge with using Erlang, though, is that it's a niche programming language and it could be hard to source strong erlang developers.

Step 4: Wrap Up

We successfully designed a system, supporting the nearby friends features.

Core components:

  • Web socket servers: real-time comms between client and server
  • Redis: fast read and write of location data + pub/sub channels

We also explored how to scale restful api servers, websocket servers, data layer, redis pub/sub servers and we also explored an alternative to using Redis Pub/Sub. We also explored a "random nearby person" feature.

18

Google Maps

Picture this

You are in a rental car at an unfamiliar airport, phone on the dashboard, and you type "Disneyland." Within a second the screen fills with streets, a blue line snakes across the city, and a voice says "42 minutes." Behind that second, the app has turned your words into coordinates, stitched together a route across a road graph built from terabytes of raw data, asked a traffic model how long it will take, and streamed you only the few map squares you can actually see. Now multiply by a billion daily users, all of them also sending their GPS positions back in, and one accident on a freeway that should reroute thousands of drivers at once. That is the problem: a planet-sized map, served as if it were a local file.

1 Macro Structure & Dependency Map

The design stands on three services — location, navigation, map rendering — all resting on one idea: chop the world into tiles. Read the tree top-down; the tiling hub comes first because both rendering and routing borrow it.

  • Tiling the world (geohash, zoom levels) — the core trick that turns a petabyte-scale planet into small, cacheable, addressable squares
    • Map projection: 3D sphere to 2D plane (Google uses Web Mercator)
      • Every projection distorts geometry somewhat
    • Geohash: recursive quadrant subdivision encoded as a string
      • Latitude/longitude as the underlying positioning system
    • Zoom levels: level 0 = one 256x256 tile; each level quadruples tile count
  • Map rendering service — what the user sees; must be smooth and cheap on data and battery
    • Precomputed static tiles served from a CDN (closest POP)
      • World map estimated at ~70PB, after compressing near-identical tiles (e.g. desert)
    • Tile URL from geohash: client-computed or via a small URL API
    • Vector tiles (paths & polygons) rendered on the client
      • Substantial bandwidth savings vs raster images
  • Navigation service — turns "A to B" into an accurate route + ETA; the most algorithmically rich part
    • Geocoding service (address → lat/long), backed by Redis
    • Route planner → shortest-path (A* variant on routing tiles) + ETA (ML on traffic) + ranker (filters)
      • Updater services asynchronously refresh traffic and other DBs
    • Routing tiles: graph of intersections (nodes) and roads (edges), hierarchical levels of detail
      • Built by an offline pipeline, stored as binary adjacency lists in S3
    • Adaptive ETA and rerouting over WebSocket
  • Location service — the feedback loop: user GPS streams feed traffic, ETAs, and road-data improvements
    • Client batches GPS points; POST /v1/locations
    • Cassandra: partition key user_id, clustering key timestamp
    • Kafka streams updates to traffic, ML, routing-tile and analytics consumers
      • ~200k QPS, ~1M QPS at peak (1B DAU x 35 min/week)

Tiling is the root hub: rendering uses image tiles by zoom level, and navigation uses routing tiles with levels of detail — the same "divide into squares, load only what you need" strategy applied twice. The location service is the loop that keeps navigation honest: without live GPS data there is no traffic, and without traffic the ETA is a guess.

2 Black-Box Cause & Effect Flow

Three parallel flows share the same client: tiles flow down, locations flow up, and route requests go round-trip. Here they are as sealed boxes in causal order.

Client tile resolver

Input: Current viewport position and zoom level.

Output: A list of tile URLs (derived from geohash + zoom).

Like knowing a book's shelf number: once you know the geohash and zoom, you know exactly which file to fetch, no server thinking required.

→ feeds into: CDN

CDN with precomputed tiles

Input: Tile URL request.

Output: A static 256x256 tile (image or vector) from the nearest point of presence.

A chain of neighborhood newsstands that each carry the same printed pages, so nobody has to travel to the printing press.

→ feeds into: Client mosaic rendering

Location service

Input: Batched array of (lat, long, timestamp) tuples.

Output: Rows in Cassandra and events on Kafka.

A mail slot that accepts a bundle of postcards at once instead of one knock per postcard.

→ feeds into: Traffic update service, ML, routing-tile processing, analytics

Geocoding service

Input: Address text, e.g. "1600 Amphitheatre Parkway, Mountain View, CA".

Output: Coordinates (37.4224764, -122.0842499) and a place ID.

The translator between how humans name places and how machines locate them.

→ feeds into: Route planner

Shortest-path service

Input: Origin and destination lat/long.

Output: Candidate paths computed with an A* variant over routing tiles.

A hiker who only unfolds the map sections she needs, switching to a coarser regional map for long distances.

→ feeds into: ETA service, Ranker

ETA service + Ranker

Input: Candidate paths, live traffic data, user filters (avoid tolls, freeways).

Output: ML-predicted travel time per path and a ranked best route.

A seasoned taxi driver who knows rush-hour patterns, combined with your preference to skip toll booths.

→ feeds into: Navigation response to client

Adaptive rerouting

Input: A traffic incident on some routing tile + stored in-flight routes.

Output: Affected users identified and pushed new routes/ETAs over WebSocket.

A dispatcher who knows every driver's planned roads and radios the ones heading toward the crash.

→ feeds into: Client (live updates)

Follow one route request

  1. You type "Disneyland" while at 1355 Market Street, SF; the client sends GET /v1/nav?origin=1355+market+street,SF&destination=Disneyland.
  2. The navigation service calls the geocoding service, which looks up both addresses in the Redis-backed geocoding DB and returns lat/long pairs.
  3. The route planner hands the pairs to the shortest-path service, which derives geohashes and thus the origin and destination routing tiles.
  4. Because this trip is hundreds of miles, the algorithm quickly climbs from detailed local tiles to coarser, wide-area tiles, loading them from S3 (heavily cached) and traversing with A*.
  5. The ETA service scores each candidate path with an ML model fed by the traffic DB, which the update-traffic service keeps fresh from location data.
  6. The ranker applies your filters (say, "avoid tolls") and picks the top route; the response includes distance, duration, polyline, and turn-by-turn HTML instructions.
  7. Meanwhile, your phone fetches only the visible map tiles from the nearest CDN POP, and every few seconds uploads a batch of GPS points to the location service.
  8. Twenty minutes in, an accident blocks a tile on your path. The rerouting check sees your stored tile chain covers it and pushes a faster route over your WebSocket.

3 Purpose & Concept Beacons

Serve a planet-scale map and accurate, traffic-aware directions to a billion users while spending as little of each phone's data and battery as possible — by precomputing and tiling everything that does not change, and streaming only what does.

Mental picture

Think of the world as a giant atlas cut into numbered pages at many magnifications. The printed pages are the precomputed map tiles, and the newsstands on every corner that stock them are the CDN's points of presence. A second, hidden atlas shows only roads as dots and lines: those are the routing tiles, with a detailed city edition and a coarse highway edition, stored in the library basement (S3). A librarian who converts street addresses to page coordinates is the geocoding service, and the navigator who plans a trip by flipping between editions is the shortest-path service. Finally, millions of travelers mailing back postcards of where they are is the location service, and the analyst reading those postcards to mark jams in red is the traffic update pipeline feeding the ETA service.

Map tile (256x256)The unit of rendering; the whole world at zoom 0 is one tile.
Zoom +1 = 4x tilesTile count quadruples per level; explains the ~70PB storage estimate.
GeohashString encoding of a recursive quadrant; lets a client name the tile it needs.
Web MercatorGoogle's chosen map projection; a distortion trade-off for a flat display.
Static tiles + CDNPrecompute once, cache everywhere; dynamic tile generation would crush servers and defeat caching.
Vector tilesSend paths and polygons, render on the device; big bandwidth savings.
Nodes = intersections, edges = roadsRoad network as a graph so Dijkstra / A* variants can run on it.
Routing tileA small subgraph with references to neighbors; load only the tiles your trip touches.
Hierarchical routing tilesSeveral levels of detail (fine local to coarse long-distance); long trips use coarse tiles.
Client-side batchingGPS points sent in groups; cuts request count, still ~200k QPS (1M peak).
Cassandra (user_id, timestamp)Write-heavy, availability over consistency; partition by user, sort by time.
Kafka fan-outOne location stream feeds traffic, ML, routing-tile and analytics consumers independently.

4 Opportunistic Drilling

The payoff lies in four places: how routing scales with hierarchical tiles, how the navigation pipeline decomposes, why tiles are static on a CDN, and how adaptive rerouting avoids scanning every driver.

Routing tiles and hierarchy: making A* work on a planet

Pathfinding cost grows with the size of the graph, so running A* on the entire world's road network is hopeless. The fix mirrors map rendering: cut the road graph into routing tiles, each a small subgraph that holds references to its neighbors. The algorithm starts at the origin tile and pulls in adjacent tiles only as it explores, stitching together a bigger graph on the fly.

For a cross-country drive, even stitching small tiles is too slow and memory hungry. So there are tiles at several levels of detail, from fine-grained local streets up to coarse tiles that span wide areas. The algorithm uses the appropriately detailed tiles based on where you are headed.

These tiles are produced by a periodic offline pipeline that converts unstructured raw road data (TBs from many sources, improved by user location data) into graphs. They need no database features, so they live in S3 as compressed binary adjacency lists, cached aggressively.

Common trap: putting routing tiles in a relational or NoSQL database. Nothing queries inside them; the service just loads a whole tile by its geohash, which is exactly what object storage plus caching does best.

The navigation pipeline, box by box

Navigation is not one service but a small assembly line. Knowing the order and what each station reads is what interviewers probe.

StationReadsProduces
GeocodingGeocoding DB (Redis: frequent reads, rare writes)Lat/long for each address
Shortest pathRouting tiles in S3Candidate paths (A* variant)
ETATraffic DBML-predicted travel time
RankerUser filtersOrdered best routes
UpdatersLocation stream (Kafka)Fresh traffic and road data, asynchronously

Note the requirement shape: a little latency is fine, but accuracy matters. The route need not be the mathematically fastest, but it must never send you the wrong way.

Rendering: static tiles, CDN, and the geohash URL

Generating tiles on demand for a billion users would put enormous load on servers and make caching nearly impossible, since every response would be unique. Instead, all tiles are precomputed for every zoom level, stored at an origin, and served from CDN points of presence closest to the user.

Client computes tile URL from geohash

No extra API hop; tiles fetched straight from the CDN.

But you are locked in

The tile-naming scheme lives in shipped app code; forcing clients to update is hard. A small server API that returns tile URLs keeps flexibility at the cost of one extra call.

New tiles are fetched when the user zooms or pans, or while navigating into a new tile. Sending vector data instead of raster images lets the client draw the map itself, which the notes call a substantial bandwidth saving — directly serving the data-and-battery requirement.

Adaptive ETA and rerouting without scanning everyone

To reroute drivers when an accident occurs, the system stores each navigating user's route as the list of routing tiles they will pass through. When a tile has an incident, find every user whose list contains it and recompute. The naive list, however, can be very long.

The clever compression: store only the origin tile and then its successively coarser "super" tiles until one contains the destination: user_1, r_1, super(r_1), super(super(r_1)), .... Now the question "is this user affected?" becomes "does the user's final, largest tile contain the accident tile?"

Updates are delivered over WebSocket: mobile push notifications have tiny payloads and do not work for web apps, long-polling costs more server compute, and SSE is one-way, while WebSocket's two-way channel also suits future features like last-mile delivery.

Test yourself

Sketch or jot your answer in the margin first, then tap to check.

Why are map tiles precomputed and served from a CDN rather than generated per request?

Dynamic generation would put a huge load on servers and make caching hard. Static tiles keyed by geohash and zoom can be cached at CDN points of presence near users, minimizing latency and server work.

How does the number of tiles change as you zoom in, and what does the lowest zoom level look like?

At the lowest zoom the whole world is one 256x256 tile. Each additional zoom level quadruples the number of tiles, which is why total storage reaches roughly 70PB even after compressing near-identical tiles.

What problem do hierarchical routing tiles solve?

For long routes, stitching together many small, detailed tiles is slow and memory hungry. Coarser tiles (e.g. highway level) let the algorithm cover long distances with far fewer nodes, using detailed tiles only near origin and destination.

Compare client-side tile URL calculation with a tile URL API.

Client-side calculation avoids an extra network call but locks the tiling scheme into app code that is hard to force-update. A URL API adds a hop but lets the server change the scheme freely.

Why Cassandra for user location data, and what are its keys?

The workload is extremely write-heavy and prefers availability over consistency, since locations go stale quickly anyway. user_id is the partition key to fetch all of a user's updates, and timestamp is the clustering key to keep them time-sorted.

What happens when an accident occurs on a routing tile?
