It's worth noting that addressing data inconsistencies across microservices is a challenging problem, which raise the system complexity. It is good to consider whether the cost is worth it, given our more pragmatic approach of encapsulating dependent operations within the same relational database.

Step 4: Wrap Up

We presented a design for a hotel reservation system.

These are the steps we went through:

  • Gathering requirements and doing back-of-the-envelope calculations to understand the system's scale
  • We presented the API Design, Data Model and system architecture in the high-level design
  • In the deep dive, we explored alternative database schema designs as requirements changed
  • We discussed race conditions and proposed solutions - pessimistic/optimistic locking, database constraints
  • Ways to scale the system via database sharding and caching
  • Finally we addressed how to handle data consistency issues across multiple microservices
23

Distributed Email Service

Picture this

Monday, 8:59 a.m. A billion inboxes wake up at once. Every second, 100,000 new emails leave the building, some carrying 20 MB slide decks, while strangers' mail servers knock on your door with messages that must land in the right inbox, pass spam checks, appear on screen instantly, and be searchable the moment they arrive. Nothing can ever be lost, because a missing email might be a job offer or a contract. That is a distributed email service like Gmail: a planet-scale post office that never closes, never loses a letter, and remembers every word you have ever received.

1 Macro Structure & Dependency Map

At a distance the system is two conveyor belts (sending and receiving) feeding a set of specialized stores, all partitioned by user. Read each hub as a question the design must answer.

  • Protocols & the mail ecosystem — you must speak the outside world's language before you can build anything
    • SMTP between servers; HTTP/REST for our webmail clients
    • DNS MX records tell senders which server accepts mail for a domain
      • POP downloads and deletes; IMAP keeps mail on the server
      • Attachments base64-encoded, ~25 MB limit
  • Async send & receive pipelines — queues absorb 100k emails/sec and slow remote servers
    • Send: load balancer → web servers → outgoing queue → SMTP outgoing workers
    • Receive: SMTP load balancer → SMTP servers → incoming queue → mail processing workers
      • Error queue; exponential backoff when recipient server is down
    • Real-time servers push new mail via WebSockets
      • Long-polling fallback for older browsers
  • Metadata DB partitioned by user_id — almost every operation touches one user's mailbox only
    • Tables: folders, emails (timeuuid email_id), attachments
    • Denormalized read / unread email tables
      • Thread reconstruction via Message-Id, In-Reply-To, References headers
    • Consistency chosen over availability
      • Custom DB at Gmail scale (BigTable); multi-DC leader-follower failover
  • Supporting stores — each data shape gets a store suited to it
    • Attachment store: object storage (e.g. S3)
    • Distributed cache: recent emails in Redis
    • Search store: Elasticsearch partitioned by user_id, updated async via Kafka
      • Custom engine built on LSM trees as an alternative
  • Deliverability — sending is easy; landing in the inbox, not spam, is hard
    • Dedicated IPs, separate marketing mail, IP warm-up over 2-6 weeks
    • Ban spammers fast, ISP feedback loops, SPF / DKIM authentication

Protocols set the boundary with the outside world, and the pipelines are how mail crosses that boundary without overwhelming anything. Once mail is inside, the user_id partitioning of the metadata DB is the organizing idea that lets search, cache and storage scale by user. Deliverability is the one hub that depends on reputation rather than engineering alone.

2 Black-Box Cause & Effect Flow

Follow the boxes along the send path and then the receive path. Each takes a message in one state and hands it on in a safer or more useful state.

Load balancer + web servers

Input: POST /v1/messages from the webmail client (To, Cc, Bcc, body, attachment references).

Output: A validated email on the outgoing queue, or on the error queue if validation fails.

The post office counter: it rate-limits people mailing in bulk, weighs the parcel (size check), runs a spam check, and hand-delivers mail addressed to someone in the same domain without sending it out.

→ feeds into: outgoing message queue

Outgoing queue + SMTP outgoing workers

Input: Queued emails; attachments are references into the object store.

Output: Mail delivered via SMTP to the recipient's server (found through its MX record); a copy in the Sent folder.

Couriers who take parcels off the loading dock, scan them for viruses, and drive them to the right town. If the town's post office is closed, they come back later, waiting longer each time.

→ feeds into: the remote mail server (or our own receive path)

SMTP load balancer + SMTP servers

Input: Inbound SMTP connections from other mail servers.

Output: Accepted mail on the incoming queue; invalid mail discarded; large attachments placed in the object store.

The receiving dock with a bouncer: obviously bad deliveries are turned away at the gate before they take up any space inside.

→ feeds into: mail processing workers

Mail processing workers

Input: Accepted incoming mail.

Output: Mail written to the metadata DB, cache and object store, and handed to real-time servers.

Sorters who stamp each letter, file a copy in the right mailbox, put recent ones on the "just arrived" shelf, and ring the recipient's doorbell.

→ feeds into: storage layer and real-time servers

Storage layer (metadata DB, attachment store, cache, search)

Input: Email metadata, bodies, attachments and indexing events.

Output: Durable, user-partitioned mailboxes; fast recent reads; full-text search.

A filing room where each user's drawer lives on one cabinet (one shard), heavy parcels go to the warehouse (S3), and a card catalogue (Elasticsearch) indexes every word.

→ feeds into: GET /v1/folders, GET /v1/folders/{id}/messages, search

Real-time servers

Input: New-mail notifications for online users.

Output: Pushes over WebSockets (long-polling for old browsers); offline users fetch via HTTP later.

The doorbell. If you are home, it rings instantly; if you are away, the mail simply waits in your box.

→ feeds into: the user's open webmail tab

Follow one email

  1. Alice, a user of our service, writes to Carol at another provider, attaches a 2 MB PDF, and presses Send. The attachment is uploaded to the object store and the email references it.
  2. The load balancer checks Alice is not sending excessively and routes the request to a web server.
  3. The web server runs a spam check and basic validation (size well under the ~25 MB limit). Carol's domain differs from Alice's, so there is no internal short-circuit. The email goes onto the outgoing queue.
  4. An SMTP outgoing worker pulls it, runs spam and virus checks, looks up the MX record for Carol's domain in DNS, and delivers via SMTP. A copy is stored in Alice's Sent folder.
  5. Suppose Carol's server is down: the email stays queued and is retried with exponential backoff. A growing outgoing queue is a monitoring signal to investigate or add consumers.
  6. Carol replies. Her server resolves our MX record and connects to our SMTP load balancer; an SMTP server applies the acceptance policy and places the mail on the incoming queue.
  7. A mail processing worker checks it, then writes metadata to the emails and unread tables in Alice's partition (keyed by user_id, with a timeuuid email_id), caches it in Redis, and stores any large attachment in the object store.
  8. An indexing event is published to Kafka, and Elasticsearch updates Alice's index asynchronously.
  9. Alice has webmail open, so a real-time server pushes the reply over her WebSocket and it appears in her inbox, grouped into the thread via its In-Reply-To header.

3 Purpose & Concept Beacons

Reliably move and store email for a billion users, with no data loss, instant delivery and per-user search, by decoupling everything with queues and partitioning everything by user.

Mental picture

Imagine a national postal service for a country of a billion people. Counters in every town accept outgoing letters and weigh them (web servers with validation), then drop them on a loading dock (outgoing queue) where couriers drive them to other countries' post offices listed in a global directory (SMTP workers using DNS MX records). Incoming trucks arrive at a guarded receiving dock (SMTP servers with acceptance policy), and sorters file each letter into one private drawer per citizen (metadata DB partitioned by user_id), sending bulky parcels to a warehouse (S3 attachment store). A doorbell rings when you are home (WebSocket push), and each citizen has a personal card catalogue of every letter they have ever received (per-user Elasticsearch index).

1 bil users x 10 sent/day → 100k emails/secA write firehose; signals queues and horizontally scaled workers.
730 PB/yr metadata, 1,460 PB/yr attachmentsAttachments dominate storage; put them in an object store, not the metadata DB.
MX recordDNS entry naming a domain's mail server; how any sender finds where to deliver.
SMTP vs HTTPSMTP between mail servers; HTTP/REST for our own clients because it is flexible and extensible.
Outgoing queue sizeA growing queue means a dead recipient server (retry with backoff) or too few consumers.
Partition key = user_idAll of one user's mail on one shard; operations rarely cross users.
timeuuid email_idClustering key that sorts emails by creation time for free.
read / unread tablesDenormalization because Cassandra-style stores cannot filter on non-key columns.
Consistency over availabilityDuring failover, affected users briefly cannot sync rather than see wrong mailbox state.
Email search is write-heavyEvery email reindexes, but users rarely search; optimize the write path.
LSM treeBuffer writes in memory, flush and merge to disk sequentially; used by Cassandra, BigTable, RocksDB.
IP warm-up (2-6 weeks)New sending IPs must build reputation slowly or mail goes to spam.

4 Opportunistic Drilling

The pipelines and the metadata data model carry most of the interview weight; search and deliverability are where you show depth. Drill these four.

Why traditional mail servers break, and the queue-based pipelines that replace them

Classic mail servers stored each email as a separate file in a local directory per user. That is fine for one server and a few users, but at scale disk I/O becomes the bottleneck, and a single damaged disk or dead server loses mail, violating reliability and availability.

The distributed design puts a queue in the middle of both directions. On the send side, the web server only validates and enqueues, so a slow or unreachable recipient server never blocks the user's click. On the receive side, SMTP servers only accept or reject and enqueue, and mail processing workers do the heavy lifting of storing, caching and notifying.

Common trap: Forgetting to monitor the outgoing queue. If it grows, either the recipient server is unavailable (retry with exponential backoff) or you need more consumers.

The metadata database: partition by user, denormalize for queries

Email metadata has a telling shape: headers are small and read often, bodies can be large but are usually read once, nearly every operation is scoped to one user, recent mail is read far more than old mail, and loss is unacceptable. Relational DBs are tuned for small rows, object stores cannot efficiently support "mark as read" or search, and Gmail's BigTable is not open source. So the notes describe the characteristics of the ideal store instead: single-digit MB columns, strong consistency, low disk I/O, high availability and easy incremental backups.

The primary key has two halves. The partition key (user_id) decides which shard holds the data, so one user's mailbox lives in one place. The clustering key (such as a timeuuid email_id) decides the sort order inside that partition, so "newest first" is free.

The catch: in a Cassandra-style store you cannot filter on a column that is not part of the key, so "show unread emails" cannot be a simple WHERE is_read = false. Fetching all and filtering in memory does not scale. The answer is to denormalize into separate read and unread tables, and move a row between them when its state changes.

Gains

Every common query is a single-partition key lookup; users never contend with each other; strong consistency keeps mailbox state correct.

Costs

Sharing one email across multiple users is not supported; denormalized tables duplicate writes; during failover or partition, affected users briefly cannot sync.

Search: Elasticsearch or a custom LSM-based engine

Email search is not web search. Its scope is one mailbox, results are sorted by attributes like date rather than relevance, and indexing must be quick and accurate. It is also write-heavy: every arriving, moved or deleted email triggers reindexing, yet users rarely open the search box.

Google searchEmail search
ScopeThe whole internetUser's own mailbox
SortingRelevanceAttributes (time, date, etc.)
AccuracyIndexing takes time; not instantIndexing quick, results accurate

The off-the-shelf option is Elasticsearch partitioned by user_id so a user's documents sit on one node. Writes (reindexing) flow asynchronously through Kafka; searches are synchronous. The custom option builds the index on an LSM tree: writes accumulate in memory and, past a threshold, are merged into the next layer on disk, so the disk only sees fast sequential writes.

Gains

Elasticsearch is ready-made and handles full-text email search well. A custom engine can be tuned for email, scale further, and can be the datastore itself.

Costs

Elasticsearch is another cluster to run and keep in sync with the metadata store, and scales only so far. A custom engine needs significant engineering effort.

Deliverability and availability

Spinning up a server that sends mail is trivial; getting that mail into inboxes instead of spam folders is not. Recipient providers judge you by reputation. Use dedicated sending IPs, keep marketing mail on separate servers so it does not taint important mail, warm up new IPs gradually over 2 to 6 weeks, ban spammers quickly, process ISP feedback on complaint rates, and authenticate mail with SPF and DKIM.

For availability, most components scale independently because users rarely interact at the data level. A multi-data-center setup with leader-follower failover keeps the service alive when a whole DC fails.

Test yourself

Answer in the margin with your stylus before you peek.

Why does the send path put a queue between web servers and SMTP workers?

It decouples the user's request from delivery to remote servers, which may be slow or down. Users get a fast response, workers scale independently, and failed deliveries are retried with exponential backoff.

What happens if the outgoing queue keeps growing?

Either a recipient server is unavailable, so mail is waiting on retries, or there are not enough consumers. Investigate the remote server or scale out SMTP workers.

Why partition the metadata DB by user_id, and what does it cost?

Almost every operation touches only one user's mailbox, so each query hits one shard and users do not interfere. The cost is that an email cannot be shared across users in this model, which is not required here.

How do you fetch unread emails when the store cannot filter on is_read?

Denormalize into separate read and unread tables, keyed the same way, and move rows between them when the state changes. Filtering all emails in memory does not scale.

Compare email search with web search.

Email search covers one mailbox, sorts by attributes like date, and needs fast, accurate indexing. Web search covers the whole internet, sorts by relevance, and tolerates indexing delay. Email search is also write-heavy.

Why does an LSM tree suit a write-heavy search index?

It buffers writes in memory and flushes them to disk as sequential merges, avoiding slow random writes. The same idea powers Cassandra, BigTable and RocksDB.

Why might mail from a brand-new server land in spam, and how do you fix it?

Recipient providers do not trust unknown IPs. Use dedicated IPs, warm them up over 2 to 6 weeks, separate marketing mail, ban spammers fast, process ISP feedback, and authenticate with SPF and DKIM.

Introduction

We'll design a distributed email service, similar to Gmail in this chapter.

In 2020, Gmail had 1.8bil active users, while Outlook had 400mil users worldwide.

Step 1: Understand the Problem and Establish Design Scope

  • C: How many users use the system?
  • I: 1bil users
  • C: I think following features are important - auth, send/receive email, fetch email, filter emails, search email, anti-spam protection.
  • I: Good list. Don't worry about auth for now.
  • C: How do users connect \w email servers?
  • I: Typically, email clients connect via SMTP, POP, IMAP, but we'll use HTTP for this problem.
  • C: Can emails have attachments?
  • I: Yes

Non-functional requirements

  • Reliability - we shouldn't lose data
  • Availability - We should use replication to prevent single points of failure. We should also tolerate partial system failures.
  • Scalability - As userbase grows, our system should be able to handle them.
  • Flexibility and extensibility - system should be flexible and easy to extend with new features. One of the reasons we chose HTTP over SMTP/other mail protocols.

Back-of-the-envelope estimation

  • 1bil users
  • Assuming one person sends 10 emails per day -> 100k emails per second.
  • Assuming one person receives 40 emails per day and each email on average has 50kb metadata -> 730pb storage per year.
  • Assuming 20% of emails have storage attachments and average size is 500kb -> 1,460pb per year.

Step 2: Propose High-Level Design and Get Buy-In

Email knowledge 101

There are various protocols used for sending and receiving emails:

  • SMTP - standard protocol for sending emails from one server to another.
  • POP - standard protocol for receiving and downloading emails from a remote mail server to a local client. Once retrieved, emails are deleted from remote server.
  • IMAP - similar to POP, it is used for receiving and downloading emails from a remote server, but it keeps the emails on the server-side.
  • HTTPS - not technically an email protocol, but it can be used for web-based email clients.

Apart from the mailing protocol, there are some DNS records we need to configure for our email server - the MX records:

Email attachments are sent base64-encoded and there is usually a size limit of 25mb on most mail services. This is configurable and varies from individual to corporate accounts.

Traditional mail servers

Traditional mail servers work well when there are a limited number of users, connected to a single server.

  • Alice logs into her Outlook email and presses "send". Email is sent to Outlook mail server. Communication is via SMTP.
  • Outlook server queries DNS to find MX record for gmail.com and transfers the email to their servers. Communication is via SMTP.
  • Bob fetches emails from his gmail server via IMAP/POP.

In traditional mail servers, emails were stored on the local file system. Every email was a separate file.

As the scale grew, disk I/O became a bottleneck. Also, it doesn't satisfy our high availability and reliability requirements. Disks can be damaged and server can go down.

Distributed mail servers

Distributed mail servers are designed to support modern use-cases and solve modern scalability issues.

These servers can still support IMAP/POP for native email clients and SMTP for mail exchange across servers.

But for rich web-based mail clients, a RESTful API over HTTP is typically used.

Example APIs:

  • POST /v1/messages - sends a message to recipients in To, Cc, Bcc headers.
  • GET /v1/folders - returns all folders of an email account

Example response:

[{id: string        Unique folder identifier.
  name: string      Name of the folder.
                    According to RFC6154 [9], the default folders can be one of
                    the following: All, Archive, Drafts, Flagged, Junk, Sent,
                    and Trash.
  user_id: string   Reference to the account owner
}]
  • GET /v1/folders/{:folder_id}/messages - returns all messages under a folder \w pagination
  • GET /v1/messages/{:message_id} - get all information about a particular message

Example response:

{
  user_id: string                      // Reference to the account owner.
  from: {name: string, email: string}  // <name, email> pair of the sender.
  to: [{name: string, email: string}]  // A list of <name, email> paris
  subject: string                      // Subject of an email
  body: string                         //  Message body
  is_read: boolean                     //  Indicate if a message is read or not.
}

Here's the high-level design of the distributed mail server:

  • Webmail - users use web browsers to send/receive emails
  • Web servers - public-facing request/response services used to manage login, signup, user profile, etc.
  • Real-time servers - Used for pushing new email updates to clients in real-time. We use websockets for real-time communication but fallback to long-polling for older browsers that don't support them.
  • Metadata db - stores email metadata such as subject, body, from, to, etc.
  • Attachment store - Object store (eg Amazon S3), suitable for storing large files.
  • Distributed cache - We can cache recent emails in Redis to improve UX.
  • Search store - distributed document store, used for supporting full-text searches.

Here's what the email sending flow looks like:

  • User writes an email and presses "send". Email is sent to load balancer.
  • Load balancer rate limits excessive mail sends and routes to one of the web servers.
  • Web servers do basic email validation (eg email size) and short-circuits outbound flow if domain is same as sender. But does spam check first.
  • If basic validation passes, email is sent to message queue (attachment is referenced from object store)
  • If basic validation fails, email is sent to error queue
  • SMTP outgoing workers pull messages from outgoing queue, do spam/virus checks and route to destination mail server.
  • Email is stored in the "Sent Emails" folder

We need to also monitor size of outgoing message queue. Growing too large might indicate a problem:

  • Recipient's mail server is unavailable. We can retry sending the email at a later time using exponential backoff.
  • Not enough consumers to handle the load, we might have to scale the consumers.

Here's the email receiving flow:

  • Incoming emails arrive at the SMTP load balancer. Mails are distributed to SMTP servers, where mail acceptance policy is done (eg invalid emails are directly discarded).
  • If attachment of email is too large, we can put it in object store (s3).
  • Mail processing workers do preliminary checks, after which mails are forwarded to storage, cache, object store and real-time servers.
  • Offline users get their new emails once they come back online via HTTP API.

Step 3: Design Deep Dive

Let's now go deeper into some of the components.

Metadata database

Here are some of the characteristics of email metadata:

  • headers are usually small and frequently accessed
  • Body size ranges from small to big, but is typically read once
  • Most mail operations are isolated to a single user - eg fetching email, marking as read, searching.
  • Data recency impacts data usage. Users typically read only recent emails
  • Data has high-reliability requirements. Data loss is unacceptable.

At gmail/outlook scale, the database is typically custom made to reduce input/output operations per second (IOPS).

Let's consider what database options we have:

  • Relational database - we can build indexes for headers and body, but these DBs are typically optimized for small chunks of data.
  • Distributed object store - this can be a good option for backup storage, but can't efficiently support searching/marking as read/etc.
  • NoSQL - Google BigTable is used by gmail, but it's not open-sourced.

Based on above analysis, very few existing solutions seems to fit our needs perfectly. In an interview setting, it's infeasible to design a new distributed database solution, but important to mention characteristics:

  • Single column can be a single-digit MB
  • Strong data consistency
  • Designed to reduce disk I/O
  • Highly available and fault tolerant
  • Should be easy to create incremental backups

In order to partition the data, we can use the user_id as a partition key, so that one user's data is stored on a single shard. This prohibits us from sharing an email with multiple users, but this is not a requirement for this interview.

Let's define the tables:

  • Primary key consists of partition key (data distribution) and clustering key (sorting data)
  • Queries we need to support - get all folders for a user, display all emails for a folder, create/get/delete an email, fetch read/unread email, get conversation threads (bonus)

Legend for tables to follow:

Here is the folders table:

emails table:

  • email_id is timeuuid which allows sorting based on timestamp when email was created

Attachments are stored in a separate table, identified by filename:

Supporting fetchin read/unread emails is easy in a traditional relational database, but not in Cassandra, since filtering on non-partition/clustering key is prohibited. One workaround to fetch all emails in a folder and filter in-memory, but that doesn't work well for a big-enough application.

What we can do is denormalize the emails table into read/unread emails tables:

In order to support conversation threads, we can include some headers, which mail clients interpret and use to reconstruct a conversation thread:

{
  "headers" {
     "Message-Id": "<7BA04B2A-430C-4D12-8B57-862103C34501@gmail.com>",
     "In-Reply-To": "<CAEWTXuPfN=LzECjDJtgY9Vu03kgFvJnJUSHTt6TW@gmail.com>",
     "References": ["<7BA04B2A-430C-4D12-8B57-862103C34501@gmail.com>"]
  }
}

Finally, we'll trade availability for consistency for our distributed database, since it is a hard requirement for this problem.

Hence, in the event of a failover or network parititon, sync/update actions will be briefly unavailable to impacted users.

Email deliverability

It is easy to setup a server to send emails, but getting the email to a receiver's inbox is hard, due to spam-protection algorithms.

If we just setup a new mail server and start sending mails through it, our emails will probably end up in the spam folder.

Here's what we can do to prevent that:

  • Dedicated IPs - use dedicated IPs for sending emails, otherwise, recipient servers will not trust you.
  • Classify emails - avoid sending marketing emails from the same servers to prevent more important email to be classified as spam
  • Warm up your IP address slowly to build a good reputation with big email providers. It takes 2 to 6 weeks to warm up a new IP
  • Ban spammers quickly to not deteriorate your reputation
  • Feedback processing - setup a feedback loop with ISPs to keep track of complaint rate and ban spam accounts quickly.
  • Email authentication - use common techniques to combat phishing such as Sender Policy Framework, DomainKeys Identified Mail, etc.

You don't need to remember all of this. Just know that building a good mail server requires a lot of domain knowledge.

Search

Searching includes doing a full-text search based on email contents or more advanced queries based on from, to, subject, unread, etc filters.

One characteristic of email search is that it is local to the user and it has more writes than reads, because we need to re-index it on each operation, but users rarely use the search tab.

Let's compare google search with email search:

ScopeSortingAccuracy
Google searchThe whole internetSort by relevanceIndexing takes some time, so not instant results.
Email searchUser's own email boxSort by attributes eg time, date, etcIndexing should be quick and results accurate.

To achieve this search functionality, one option is to use an Elasticsearch cluster. We can use user_id as the partition key to group data under the same node:

Mutating operations are async via Kafka in order to decouple services from the reindexing flow. Actually searching for data happens synchronously.

Elasticsearch is one of the most popular search-engine databases and supports full-text search for emails very well.

Alternatively, we can attempt to develop our own custom search solution to meet our specific requirements.

Designing such a system is out of scope. One of the core challenges when building it is to optimize it for write-heavy workloads.

To achieve that, we can use Log-Structured Merge-Trees (LSM) to structure the index data on disk. Write path is optimized for sequential writes only. This technique is used in Cassandra, BigTable and RocksDB.

Its core idea is to store data in-memory until a predefined threshold is reached, after which it is merged in the next layer (disk):

Main trade-offs between the two approaches:

  • Elasticsearch scales to some extent, whereas a custom search engine can be fine-tuned for the email use-case, allowing it to scale further.
  • Elasticsearch is a separate service we need to maintain, alongside the metadata store. A custom solution can be the datastore itself.
  • Elasticsearch is an off-the-shelf solution, whereas the custom search engine would require significant engineering effort to build.

Scalability and availability

Since individual user operations don't collide with other users, most components can be independently scaled.

To ensure high availability, we can also use a multi-DC setup with leader-folower failover in case of failures:

Step 4: Wrap Up

Additional talking points:

  • Fault tolerance - Many parts of the system could fail. It is worthwhile how we'd handle node failures.
  • Compliance - PII needs to be stored in a reasonable way, given Europe's GDPR laws.
  • Security - email encryption, phishing protection, safe browsing, etc.
  • Optimizations - eg preventing duplication of the same attachments, sent multiple times by different users.
24

S3-like Object Storage

Picture this

Somewhere a company is pouring 100 petabytes a year into your service: nightly database backups, millions of tiny thumbnails, and 200 MB video masters. They never edit any of it; they write it once and read it back, sometimes years later, and they expect every byte to still be there even if a whole rack catches fire. Meanwhile each spinning hard disk manages only 100 to 150 random seeks per second and fails at a steady, predictable rate. Designing an S3-like object store means building a warehouse of nearly unlimited size on top of unreliable shelves, cheaply, while promising six nines of durability.

1 Macro Structure & Dependency Map

The whole design follows from one split: metadata (what and where) is stored separately from data (the bytes). Read the map as "the split", then "how each half works", then "how we keep bytes alive".

  • Separate metadata from data — the UNIX inode idea; lets each side scale independently
    • Object = immutable key-value pair: URI is the key, bytes are the value
    • Write once, read many (~95% of operations are reads)
      • Block vs file vs object storage comparison
      • Flat namespace; "folders" simulated by name prefixes
  • Data store — where bytes physically live, addressed by object UUID
    • Data routing service (stateless), placement service (virtual cluster map, Paxos/Raft), data nodes
    • Small objects packed into large WAL-style files; object_mapping table in SQLite on each node
      • Files pinned to CPU cores to avoid write-lock contention
    • Primary replicates to two secondaries before replying (strong consistency)
  • Durability — the promise the whole product is sold on
    • Replicate across failure domains (rack, DC, network)
    • 3-copy replication vs 8+4 erasure coding
    • Checksums per file and per object to catch silent corruption
      • HDD annual failure rate 0.81% → 3 copies give 6 nines
  • Metadata store — maps names to UUIDs and answers listing and versioning queries
    • Bucket table (small, one server) and object table (sharded by hash(bucket_name, object_name))
    • Listing by prefix via a denormalized table sharded by bucket ID
    • Versioning via TIMEUUID object_version; delete markers
      • Per-user bucket limits keep the bucket table small
  • Lifecycle operations — getting big files in and dead bytes out
    • Multipart upload with upload ID and per-part ETags
    • Garbage collection via compaction
      • Lazy deletion, orphan parts, corrupted data

Everything hangs off the metadata/data split: the data store only ever deals with opaque UUIDs and bytes, while the metadata store only deals with names, buckets and versions. Durability is a property of the data store, and listing, versioning and sharding are properties of the metadata store. Lifecycle operations touch both, which is why they come last.

2 Black-Box Cause & Effect Flow

An upload passes through a gatekeeper, a bytes path and a names path. Keep the two paths distinct in your head and the rest falls into place.

Load balancer + API service

Input: RESTful HTTP requests such as PUT /bucket-to-share/script.txt.

Output: Orchestrated calls to IAM, the data store and the metadata store; an HTTP response.

The warehouse front office. It never touches boxes itself; it checks your paperwork and tells the loading crew and the records clerk what to do.

→ feeds into: IAM

IAM

Input: The caller's identity and the requested action on a bucket.

Output: Allow or deny (authentication, authorization, access control).

The security desk that checks your badge before you enter any aisle.

→ feeds into: data store (on writes) or metadata store (on reads)

Data routing + placement service

Input: Object bytes to store, or a UUID to fetch.

Output: The right primary data node, chosen from the virtual cluster map via consistent hashing.

A dispatcher with a live map of every shelf, which it keeps current by listening to heartbeats; it points each box to a replication group.

→ feeds into: data nodes

Data nodes

Input: Object bytes.

Output: Bytes appended to a large file, a row in the local object_mapping table (object_id, filename, file_offset, object_size), copies on two secondaries, and a UUID.

The shelves. Small parcels are packed tightly into big crates, a small ledger records which crate and position each parcel sits at, and two other shelves get identical copies.

→ feeds into: API service (returns the UUID)

Metadata store

Input: bucket_id, object_name, object_id (UUID), version and other metadata.

Output: Name-to-UUID lookups, prefix listings, version history.

The card catalogue. It does not hold the parcels; it tells you which UUID a name refers to, which the shelves then locate.

→ feeds into: every download (name → UUID → bytes)

Garbage collector

Input: Deleted, orphaned or corrupted objects inside data files.

Output: Compacted files with only live objects and an updated object_mapping table.

The night crew that repacks half-empty crates into full ones and throws out the empties.

→ feeds into: reclaimed disk space on primaries, replicas or all 12 erasure-coded nodes

Follow one upload

  1. A user sends HTTP PUT to create a bucket named "bucket-to-share". The API service asks IAM whether the user may write, then creates a bucket entry in the metadata store and returns success.
  2. Next, PUT /bucket-to-share/script.txt arrives with Content-Length: 4567 and a custom header x-amz-meta-author: Alex. The load balancer routes it to a stateless API service replica.
  3. IAM confirms the user's identity and write permission on the bucket.
  4. The API service streams the 4,567 bytes to the data store. The data routing service consults the placement service, and consistent hashing deterministically picks this object's replication group.
  5. The primary data node appends the bytes to the end of its current data file, say "/data/c", and inserts a row into its SQLite object_mapping table: object_id, filename /data/c, the starting offset, and size 4567.
  6. The primary replicates to two secondary data nodes and replies only after they succeed, choosing strong consistency over lower latency. A UUID is returned to the API service.
  7. The API service writes a metadata row: bucket_id, object_name script.txt, object_id (the UUID), plus other metadata. The client gets a success response.
  8. Later, GET /bucket-to-share/script.txt reverses the route: IAM checks read permission, the metadata store maps the name to the UUID, and the data store looks up filename and offset and streams back 4,567 bytes.

3 Purpose & Concept Beacons

Store huge volumes of immutable objects cheaply and durably by separating names from bytes, packing bytes efficiently on disk, and spreading redundancy across failure domains.

Mental picture

Picture a vast automated warehouse. At the front, a card catalogue maps each item's name to a barcode (metadata store: name to UUID), while the shelves out back only understand barcodes (data store). A dispatcher with a live floor plan decides which aisle a new box goes to (placement service with the virtual cluster map), and small parcels are packed into shipping crates with a packing list taped inside (WAL-style data files plus the object_mapping table). Every box is either photocopied onto shelves in three different buildings (replication) or split into puzzle pieces with spare pieces stored across aisles, so any few lost pieces can be rebuilt (8+4 erasure coding). A tamper seal on every crate reveals rot (checksums), and a night crew repacks crates to reclaim space (compaction).

100 PB/year, 6 nines durability, 4 nines availabilityDurability is the headline requirement; it shapes replication and erasure coding choices.
100-150 IOPS per HDDDisk seeks are scarce; pack small objects together and read sequentially.
0.68 bil objects, 0.68 TB metadataAt 1 KB each, metadata is tiny compared to data; store it separately.
Object immutabilityNo in-place updates, only replace or delete; enables append-only files and versioning.
Metadata vs data splitLike a UNIX inode and its blocks; scale each store independently.
Placement service (5 or 7 nodes, Paxos/Raft)Critical brain of the data store; a 7-node cluster tolerates 3 failures.
object_mapping in SQLitePer-node lookup of (filename, offset, size); local, so no network hop.
Replication: 200% overhead, 6 ninesFast reads and simple; the choice for latency-sensitive data.
Erasure coding 8+4: 50% overhead, 11 ninesCheaper and more durable, but slower reads and more computation.
Failure domainRack, DC or network that can fail together; copies must span them.
hash(bucket_name, object_name)Object table shard key; avoids hot buckets but makes listing hard.
TIMEUUID object_version + delete markerVersions sort by time; deleting adds a version that returns 404.

4 Opportunistic Drilling

The data store internals and the durability math are where this design is won or lost; metadata sharding and multipart uploads are the most common follow-ups.

Inside the data store: routing, placement and nodes

The data store has three parts. The data routing service is stateless: it asks the placement service where to put or find data, then reads from or writes to data nodes. The placement service holds the virtual cluster map, a picture of the physical topology, and prunes nodes that stop sending heartbeats. Data nodes hold the bytes, and each runs a daemon that reports how many drives it manages and how full each one is.

Because placement is critical, it runs as a 5- or 7-node cluster synchronized by Paxos or Raft; 7 nodes survive 3 failures. Given an object's UUID, consistent hashing deterministically selects its replication group. The primary writes locally, replicates to two secondaries, and only then replies, so every successful write is already on three nodes at the price of higher latency.

Gains

Waiting for all replicas means any later read from any replica sees the object: strong consistency.

Costs

Write latency grows with the slowest replica.

How bytes are organized on disk

The naive approach, one file per object, collapses with many small objects. Each file consumes at least a whole disk block (typically 4 KB), wasting space on tiny objects, and millions of files mean millions of inodes, which operating systems handle poorly and cap at a maximum.

The fix is to append many objects into one big file, WAL style. Appends to a single file must be serialized, so cores would queue behind each other; confining each file to a specific core removes that contention. To find an object again, each node keeps an object_mapping table of object_id, filename, file_offset and object_size.

Where should that table live? A shared database cluster would need aggressive scaling and add a network hop to every read. Since each node only cares about its own objects, a lightweight relational DB, SQLite, runs inside each data node. Relational wins over RocksDB here because the access pattern is low write, high read.

Common trap: Proposing a central lookup database for object locations. The notes favour a local SQLite per node because data nodes only need their own mappings.

Durability: replication vs erasure coding

Hardware fails, and disasters take out whole racks or data centers at once. So copies must be spread across failure domains, not just across disks. With a typical HDD annual failure rate of 0.81%, three copies yield six nines of durability.

Erasure coding takes a different approach. Data is split into chunks and extra parity chunks are computed; if some chunks are lost, the rest can rebuild them. With 8+4, eight data chunks and four parity chunks are spread across failure domains, and up to four can be lost. Think of it as tearing a letter into eight strips and writing four clever summary strips, any eight of which rebuild the letter.

3-copy replication8+4 erasure coding
Storage overhead200%50%
Durability6 nines11 nines
Read speedFast; read one copySlower; collect chunks from many locations
ComputeLowHigher; compute and store parities
ImplementationSimpleMuch harder
Best forLatency-sensitive dataCost efficiency and durability

Whole-disk failures are obvious; partial corruption is not. So checksums (hashes of the contents) are stored for every file and every object, and verified on read. With 8+4 erasure coding, each of the 8 data pieces is fetched and its checksum verified separately.

Metadata: sharding, listing and versioning

The bucket table is small (users have a bucket limit) and fits one server, scaled for reads with replicas. The object table does not fit. Sharding by bucket_id creates hotspots because a single bucket can hold billions of objects. The chosen key is hash(bucket_name, object_name), since most queries look up an object by bucket and name.

That choice makes listing hard: "all objects under abc/ in bucket 123" is scattered across every shard. You could query every shard and merge, but pagination breaks because each shard returns different result counts and needs its own limit and offset. Since object stores are not optimized for listing anyway, the answer is a separate denormalized listing table sharded by bucket ID, so a listing hits one instance.

Versioning adds an object_version column of type TIMEUUID so versions sort by time, and each new version gets a new object_id. Deleting does not erase anything: it adds a new version with a special delete marker, and a GET for that name returns 404.

Multipart upload and garbage collection

Uploading a multi-gigabyte file in one request means one network hiccup restarts everything. Multipart upload splits the file into chunks that travel independently.

  1. Client initiates a multipart upload; the data store returns an upload ID.
  2. Client splits the file into parts and uploads each one with that upload ID.
  3. For each part, the data store returns an ETag, an MD5 checksum of that part.
  4. Client sends "complete multipart upload" with the upload ID, part numbers and all ETags.
  5. The data store reassembles the object, which can take a few minutes, then returns success.

Leftover parts become garbage, alongside lazily deleted objects and data that failed checksum verification. The garbage collector reclaims space by compaction: it copies live objects from an old file such as "data/b" into a new file "data/d", then updates the object_mapping table in one database transaction. Compaction runs only on files past a size threshold to avoid creating lots of small files, and deletions must reach every copy: primary and replicas, or all 12 nodes under 8+4 erasure coding.

Test yourself

Work each one out in the margin with your stylus, then reveal to check.

Why separate the metadata store from the data store?

Like a UNIX inode and its data blocks, names and locations are small and query-heavy while bytes are large and opaque. Splitting them lets each store be scaled and optimized independently.

What goes wrong if every object is stored as its own file?

Small objects waste most of a 4 KB block, and millions of files create millions of inodes, which operating systems handle poorly and cap. Packing objects into large append-only files fixes both.

Compare 3-copy replication with 8+4 erasure coding.

Replication costs 200% extra storage for 6 nines and gives fast, simple reads. Erasure coding costs 50% extra for 11 nines but needs more computation, is harder to build, and reads are slower because chunks come from many places.

What happens if a portion of a disk silently corrupts an object?

A whole-disk failure would be noticed, but partial corruption would not. Checksums stored per file and per object detect the mismatch on read, and the corrupted data becomes garbage to collect.

Why is listing objects by prefix slow, and how is it fixed?

The object table is sharded by hash(bucket_name, object_name), so one prefix's objects are scattered across shards and pagination across shards is awkward. A denormalized listing table sharded by bucket ID keeps a listing on one instance.

How does deleting a versioned object work?

A new version is added with a special object_id acting as a delete marker. Requests for the object then return 404, while older versions remain in the history.

Why does the placement service run on 5 or 7 nodes with Paxos or Raft?

It is critical: every write needs its cluster map. A consensus cluster keeps replicas in sync and survives failures; 7 nodes tolerate 3 failures.

Introduction

In this chapter, we'll be designing an object storage service, similar to Amazon S3.

Storage systems fall into three broad categories:

  • Block storage
  • File storage
  • Object storage

Block storage are devices, which came out in 1960s. HDDs and SSDs are such examples. These devices are typically physically attached to a server, although they can also be network-attached via high-speed network protocols. Servers can format the raw blocks and use them as a file system or it can hand control of them to servers directly.

File storage is built on top of block storage. It provides a higher level of abstraction, making it easier to manage folders and files.

Object storage sacrifices performance for high durability, vast scale and low cost. It targets "cold" data and is mainly used for archival and backup. There is no hierarchical directory structure, all data is stored as objects in a flat structure. It is relatively slow compared to other storage types. Most cloud providers have an object storage offering - Amazon S3, Google GCS, etc.

Block StorageFile StorageObject Storage
Mutable ContentYYN (has object versioning）
CostHighMedium to highLow
PerformanceMedium to high, very highMedium to highLow to medium
ConsistencyStrong consistencyStrong consistencyStrong consistency [5]
Data accessSAS/iSCSI/FCStandard file access, CIFS/SMB, and NFSRESTful API
ScalabilityMedium scalabilityHigh scalabilityVast scalability
Good forVirtual machines (VM), databasesGeneral-purpose file system accessBinary data, unstructured data

Some terminology, related to object storage:

  • Bucket - logical container for objects. Name is globally unique.
  • Object - An individual piece of data, stored in a bucket. Contains object data and metadata.
  • Versioning - A feature keeping multiple variants of an object in the same bucket.
  • Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) - each resource is uniquely identified by a URI.
  • Service-level Agreement (SLA) - contract between service provider and client.

Amazon S3 Standard-Infrequent Access storage class SLAs:

  • Durability of 99.999999999% across multiple Availability Zones
  • Data is resilient in the event of entire Availability Zone being destroyed
  • Designed for 99.9% availability

Step 1: Understand the Problem and Establish Design Scope

  • C: Which features should be included?
  • I: Bucket creation, Object upload/download, versioning, Listing objects in a bucket
  • C: What is the typical data size?
  • I: We need to store both massive objects and small objects efficiently
  • C: How much data do we store in a year?
  • I: 100 petabytes
  • C: Can we assume 6 nines of data durbility (99.9999%) and service availability of 4 nines (99.99%)?
  • I: Yes, sounds reasonable

Non-functional requirements

  • 100 PB of data
  • 6 nines of data durability
  • 4 nines of service availability
  • Storage efficiency. Reduce storage cost while maintaining high reliability and performance

Back-of-the-envelope estimation

Object storage is likely to have bottlenecks in disk capacity or IO per second (IOPS).

Assumptions:

  • we have 20% small (less than 1mb), 60% mid-size (1-64mb) and 20% large objects (greater than 64mb),
  • One hard disk (SATA, 7200rpm) is capable of doing 100-150 random seeks per second (100-150 IOPS)

Given the assumptions, we can estimate the total number of objects the system can persist.

  • Let's use median size per object type to simplify calculation - 0.5mb for small, 32mb for medium, 200mb for large.
  • Given 100PB of storage (10^11 MB) and 40% of storage usage results in 0.68bil objects
  • If we assume metadata is 1kb, then we need 0.68tb space to store metadata info

Step 2: Propose High-Level Design and Get Buy-In

Let's explore some interesting properties of object storage before diving into the design:

  • Object immutability - objects in object storage are immutable (not the case in other storage systems). We may delete them or replace them, but no update.
  • Key-value store - an object URI is its key and we can get its contents by making an HTTP call
  • Write once, read many times - data access pattern is writing once and reading many times. According to some Linkedin research, 95% of operations are reads
  • Support both small and large objects

Design philosophy of object storage is similar to UNIX - when we save a file, it creates the filename in a data structure, called inode and file data is stored in different disk locations. The inode contains a list of file block pointers, which point to different locations on disk.

When accessing a file, we first fetch its metadata from the inode, prior to fetching the file contents.

Object storage works similarly - metadata store is used for file information, but contents are stored on disk:

By separating metadata from file contents, we can scale the different stores independently:

High-level design

  • Load balancer - distributes API requests across service replicas
  • API service - Stateless server, orchestrating calls to metadata and object store, as well as IAM service.
  • Identity and access management (IAM) - central place for auth, authz, access control.
  • Data store - stores and retrieves actual data. Operations are based on object ID (UUID).
  • Metadata store - stores object metadata

Uploading an object

  • Create a bucket named "bucket-to-share" via HTTP PUT request
  • API service calls IAM to ensure user is authorized and has write permissions
  • API service calls metadata store to create a bucket entry. Once created, success response is returned.
  • After bucket is created, HTTP PUT is sent to create an object named "script.txt"
  • API service verifies user identity and ensures user has write permissions
  • Once validation passes, object payload is sent via HTTP PUT to the data store. Data store persists it and returns a UUID.
  • API service calls metadata store to create a new entry with object_id, bucket_id and bucket_name, among other metadata.

Example object upload request:

PUT /bucket-to-share/script.txt HTTP/1.1
Host: foo.s3example.org
Date: Sun, 12 Sept 2021 17:51:00 GMT
Authorization: authorization string
Content-Type: text/plain
Content-Length: 4567
x-amz-meta-author: Alex

[4567 bytes of object data]

Downloading an object

Buckets have no directory hierarchy, buy we can create a logical hierarchy by concatenating bucket name and object name to simulate a folder structure.

Example GET request for fetching an object:

GET /bucket-to-share/script.txt HTTP/1.1
Host: foo.s3example.org
Date: Sun, 12 Sept 2021 18:30:01 GMT
Authorization: authorization string
  • Client sends an HTTP GET request to the load balancer, ie GET /bucket-to-share/script.txt
  • API service queries IAM to verify the user has correct permissions to read the bucket
  • Once validated, UUID of object is retrieved from metadata store
  • Object payload is retrieved from data store based on UUID and returned to the client

Step 3: Design Deep Dive

Data store

Here's how the API service interacts with the data store:

The data store's main components:

The data routing service provides a RESTful or gRPC API to access the data node cluster. It is a stateless service, which scales by adding more servers.

It's main responsibilities are:

  • querying the placement service to get the best data node to store data
  • reading data from data nodes and returning it to the API service
  • Writing data to data nodes

The placement service determines which data nodes should store an object. It maintains a virtual cluster map, which determines the physical topology of a cluster.

The service also sends heartbeats to all data nodes to determine if they should be removed from the virtual cluster.

Since this is a critical service, it is recommended to maintain a cluster of 5 or 7 replicas, synchronized via Paxos or Raft consensus algorithms. Eg a 7 node cluster can tolerate 3 nodes failing.

Data nodes store the actual object data. Reliability and durability is ensured by replicating data to multiple data nodes.

Each data node has a daemon running, which sends heartbeats to the placement service.

The heartbeat includes:

  • How many disk drives (HDD or SSD) does the data node manage?
  • How much data is stored on each drive?

Data persistence flow

  • API service forwards the object data to data store
  • Data routing service sends the data to the primary data node
  • Primary data node saves the data locally and replicates it to two secondary data nodes. Response is sent after successful replication.
  • The UUID of the object is returned to the API service.

Caveats:

  • Given an object UUID, it's replication group is deterministically chosen by using consistent hashing
  • In step 4, the primary data node replicates the object data before returning a response. This favors strong consistency over higher latency.

How data is organized

One simple approach to managing data is to store each object in a separate file.

This works, but is not performant with many small files in a file system:

  • Data blocks on HDD are wasted, because every file uses the whole block size. Typical block size is 4kb.
  • Many files means many inodes. Operating systems don't deal well with too many inodes and there is also a max inode limit.

These issues can be addressed by merging many small files into bigger ones via a write-ahead log (WAL). Once the file reaches its capacity (typically a few GB), a new file is created:

The downside of this approach is that write access to the file needs to be serialized. Multiple cores accessing the same file must wait for each other. To fix this, we can confine files to specific cores to avoid lock contention.

Object lookup

To support storing multiple objects in the same file, we need to maintain a table, which tells the data node:

  • object_id
  • filename where object is stored
  • file_offset where object starts
  • object_size

We can deploy this table in a file-based db like RocksDB or a traditional relational database. Since the access pattern is low write+high read, a relational database works better.

How should we deploy it? We could deploy the db and scale it separately in a cluster, accessed by all data nodes.

Downsides:

  • we'd need to aggressively scale the cluster to serve all requests
  • there's additional network latency between data node and db cluster

An alternative is to take advantage of the fact that data nodes are only interested to data related to them, so we can deploy the relational db within the data node itself.

SQLite is a good option as it's a lightweight file-based relational database.

Updated data persistence flow

  • API Service sends a request to save a new object
  • Data node service appends the new object at the end of a file, named "/data/c"
  • A new record for the object is inserted into the object mapping table

Durability

Data durability is an important requirement in our design. In order to achieve 6 nines of durability, every failure case needs to be properly examined.

First problem to address is hardware failures. We can achieve that by replicating data nodes to minimize probability of failure. But in addition to that, we also ought to replicate across different failure domains (cross-rack, cross-dc, separate networks, etc). A critical event can cause multiple hardware failures within the same domain:

Assuming annual failure rate of a typical HDD is 0.81%, making three copies gives us 6 nines of durability.

Replicating the data nodes like that grants us the durability we want, but we could also leverage erasure coding to reduce storage costs.

Erasure coding enables us to use parity bits, which allow us to reconstruct lost bits in the event of a failure:

Imagine those bits are data nodes. If two of them go down, they can be recovered using the remaining four ones.

There are different erasure coding schemes. In our case, we could use 8+4 erasure coding, split across different failure domains to maximize reliability:

Erasure coding enables us to achieve a much lower storage cost (50% improvement) at the expense of access speed due to the data routing service having to collect data from multiple locations:

Other caveats:

  • Replication requires 200% storage overhead (in case of 3 replicas) vs. 50% via erasure coding
  • Erasure coding gives us 11 nines of durability vs 6 nines via replication
  • Erasure coding requires more computation to calculate and store parities

In sum, replication is more useful for latency-sensitive applications, whereas erasure coding is attractive for storage cost efficiency and durability. Erasure coding is also much harder to implement.

Correctness verification

If a disk fails entirely, then the failure is easy to detect. This is less straightforward in the event part of the disk memory gets corrupted.

To detect this, we can use checksums - a hash of the file contents, which can be used to verify the file's integrity.

In our case, we'll store checksums for each file and each object:

In the case of erasure coding (8+4), we'll need to fetch each of the 8 pieces of data separately and verify each of their checksums.

Metadata data model

Table schemas:

Queries we need to support:

  • Find an object ID by name
  • Insert/delete object based on name
  • List objects in a bucket sharing the same prefix

There is usually a limit on the number of buckets a user can create, hence, the size of the buckets table is small and can fit into a single db server. But we still need to scale the server for read throughput.

The object table will probably not fit into a single database server, though. Hence, we can scale the table via sharding:

  • Sharding by bucket_id will lead to hotspot issues as a bucket can have billions of objects
  • Sharding by bucket_id makes the load more evenly distributed, but our queries will be slow
  • We choose sharding by hash(bucket_name, object_name) since most queries are based on the object/bucket name.

Even with this sharding scheme, though, listing objects in a bucket will be slow.

Listing objects in a bucket

In a single database, listing an object based on its prefix (looks like a directory) works like this:

SELECT * FROM object WHERE bucket_id = "123" AND object_name LIKE `abc/%`

This is challenging to fulfill when the database is sharded. To achieve it, we can run the query on every shard and aggregate the results in-memory. This makes pagination challenging though, since different shards contain a different result size and we need to maintain separate limit/offset for each.

We can leverage the fact that typically object stores are not optimized for listing objects, so we can sacrifice listing performance. We can also create a denormalized table for listing objects, sharded by bucket ID. That would make our listing query sufficiently fast as it's isolated to a single database instance.

Object versioning

Versioning works by having another object_version column which is of type TIMEUUID, enabling us to sort records based on it.

Each new version produces a new object_id:

Deleting an object creates a new version with a special object_id indicating that the object was deleted. Queries for it return 404:

Optimizing uploads of large files

Uploading large files can be optimized by using multipart uploads - splitting a big file into several chunks, uploaded independently:

  • Client calls service to initiate a multipart upload
  • Data store returns an upload ID which uniquely identifies the upload
  • Client splits the large file into several chunks, uploaded independently using the upload id
  • When a chunk is uploaded, the data store returns an etag, which is a md5 checksum, identifying that upload chunk
  • After all parts are uploaded, client sends a complete multipart upload request, which includes upload_id, part numbers and all etags
  • Data store reassembles the object from its parts. The process can take a few minutes. After that, success response is returned to the client.

Old parts, which are no longer useful can be removed at this point. We can introduce a garbage collector to deal with it.

Garbage collection

Garbage collection is the process of reclaiming storage space, which is no longer used. There are a few ways data becomes garbage:

  • lazy object deletion - object is marked as deleted without actually getting deleted
  • orphan data - eg an upload failed mid-flight and old parts need to be deleted
  • corrupted data - data which failed checksum verification

The garbage collector is also responsible for reclaiming unused space in replicas. With replication, data is deleted from both primaries and replicas. With erasure coding (8+4), data is deleted from all 12 nodes.

To facilitate the deletion, we'll use a process called compaction:

  • Garbage collector copies objects which are not deleted from "data/b" to "data/d"
  • object_mapping table is updated once copying is complete using a database transaction
  • To avoid making too many small files, compaction is done on files which grow beyond a certain threshold

Step 4: Wrap Up

Things we covered:

  • Designing an S3-like object storage
  • Comparing differences between object, block and file storages
  • Covered uploading, downloading, listing, versioning of objects in a bucket
  • Deep dived in the design - data store and metadata store, replication and erasure coding, multipart uploads, sharding
25

Real-time Gaming Leaderboard

Picture this

It is the last evening of the monthly tournament. Five million daily players are grinding out matches, and every win nudges someone up the ladder. Mary, currently sitting in position 361, finishes a game, taps "Leaderboard", and expects to see herself climb right now, not after a nightly batch job. Behind that single tap sits a hard question: how do you keep tens of millions of scores permanently sorted, let thousands of them change every second, and still answer "what is my exact rank?" in milliseconds?

1 Macro Structure & Dependency Map

From 10,000 feet, this system is a pipe that carries trusted wins into one always-sorted data structure, plus a few side tables that give names to the numbers. Read the map top-down: each hub is a decision the others lean on.

  • Trusted score ingestion — if scores can be forged, every rank downstream is meaningless
    • Game service validates the win, then calls the leaderboard service
      • POST /v1/scores takes user_id and points; only game servers may call it
    • Rejected alternative: client writes its own score
      • Open to man-in-the-middle; a player with a proxy edits their score
    • Optional message queue between game and leaderboard services
      • Only worth it if other services consume game results; not required here
  • Redis sorted set — the always-sorted core that makes rank queries cheap
    • Hash map (user_id → score) + skip list (scores in order)
      • Skip list = sorted linked list with multi-level express indexes
    • Four commands: ZADD, ZINCRBY, ZREVRANGE, ZREVRANK
      • O(log N) updates and rank; O(log N + M) range fetch
    • One key per monthly tournament, e.g. leaderboard_feb_2021
      • Old months move to historical storage
  • Supporting relational storage — turns user IDs into names and provides the rebuild source
    • MySQL user profile table (username, display name)
      • Cache the top 10 players' details; they are read constantly
    • MySQL game-result table (who won, when)
      • Used to reconstruct the leaderboard after an infrastructure failure
    • Redis replica + Redis persistence for crash safety
  • Scaling strategy — what happens when one Redis node is no longer enough
    • Range (fixed) partitioning by score — author's preference
      • user_id → shard mapping kept in application code (MySQL or a cache)
    • Hash partitioning via Redis Cluster
      • Top 10 needs scatter-gather; rank has no easy answer
    • NoSQL alternative (DynamoDB) with write sharding
      • Exact rank is hard; fall back to percentiles computed by a cron job
  • Hosting model — who runs the boxes
    • Self-managed: Redis + MySQL (+ optional profile cache)
    • Serverless: AWS API Gateway routing to AWS Lambda
      • Recommended by the author for a game built from the ground up

The sorted set is the gravitational center: the API shape, the storage estimate, the scaling debate and even the NoSQL comparison all orbit around "how do we keep scores sorted and rankable?" Trusted ingestion sits upstream because a fast leaderboard of fake scores is worthless. Relational storage and hosting are supporting cast: they name the players and keep the lights on, but they never answer a rank query themselves.

2 Black-Box Cause & Effect Flow

Treat each component as a sealed box: something goes in, something comes out. Two flows share the same core — the write path (a win becomes a score) and the read path (a tap becomes a ranked list).

Game client

Input: A finished match on the player's device.

Output: A "match finished" signal to the game service (or nothing at all, if the server runs the game logic itself).

The client is the witness, not the judge. It reports that something happened but never gets to write the verdict.

→ feeds into: Game service

Game service

Input: Match result from the client or from its own game logic.

Output: A validated POST /v1/scores call with user_id and points.

This is the referee who checks the scoreboard before announcing a winner. Because only game servers may hit the score API, a player with a proxy cannot inflate their own number.

→ feeds into: Leaderboard service

Leaderboard service

Input: Score updates from game servers; read requests (GET /v1/scores, GET /v1/scores/{user_id}) from players.

Output: ZINCRBY writes to Redis; JSON responses with user_id, user_name, rank and score.

A thin translator: it turns HTTP calls into sorted-set commands and stitches the returned IDs together with human-readable names.

→ feeds into: Redis sorted set (scores) and MySQL / cache (names)

Redis sorted set (leaderboard_<month>)

Input: ZINCRBY for wins; ZREVRANGE and ZREVRANK for reads.

Output: Updated score, ordered slices of (user, score), or a user's position.

A self-sorting shelf. Every time a book (player) gets thicker (more points), it slides into its correct slot automatically in O(log N) steps, so reading the top shelf is always instant.

→ feeds into: Leaderboard service response

MySQL tables + top-10 cache

Input: User IDs to resolve; win records to persist.

Output: Usernames and display names; a durable history of wins.

The filing cabinet next to the scoreboard: it knows who "mary1934" really is, and it keeps receipts so the board can be rebuilt if Redis burns down.

→ feeds into: Leaderboard response; recovery script after outages

Recovery path (MySQL WAL / game-result table)

Input: A large-scale Redis outage.

Output: A rebuilt sorted set, replayed by an ad-hoc script.

If the scoreboard is wiped, you replay every stored win in order and the board redraws itself.

→ feeds into: Redis sorted set

Follow one score update

  1. Mary (user_id mary1934) wins a match in February 2021. Her client tells the game service the match ended.
  2. The game service checks the win is legitimate, then calls POST /v1/scores with user_id=mary1934 and points=1.
  3. The leaderboard service runs ZINCRBY leaderboard_feb_2021 1 'mary1934'. If she had no entry, her score starts from zero and becomes 1; otherwise it grows by one. Cost: O(log N).
  4. The win is also recorded in MySQL, giving a durable trail the leaderboard can be reconstructed from later.
  5. Mary taps "Leaderboard". The service runs ZREVRANGE leaderboard_feb_2021 0 9 WITHSCORES and gets back the top 10 (user, score) pairs in descending order.
  6. The service resolves those 10 IDs to names — ideally from a cache, since the top 10 are the hottest profiles in the game.
  7. For Mary's own row, ZREVRANK returns her position, say 361.
  8. For the bonus "four above, four below" view, the service runs ZREVRANGE leaderboard_feb_2021 357 365 and returns her neighbourhood.
  9. At month's end a new key (leaderboard_mar_2021) starts fresh, and February's board moves to historical storage.

3 Purpose & Concept Beacons

A real-time leaderboard is fundamentally a "keep it sorted on every write" problem: pay a small O(log N) cost per update so that top-K and rank queries never have to scan or re-sort millions of rows.

Mental picture

Imagine a giant stadium scoreboard with an army of ushers. The referees on the field (game service) are the only people allowed to radio in a point; a fan shouting from the stands (the client) is ignored. The scoreboard itself (the Redis sorted set) is a magical ladder where every player's plaque slides to its correct rung the instant a point arrives, guided by express elevators that skip whole floors (the skip-list indexes). A clerk's office under the stands (MySQL) holds everyone's real name and the paper receipts for every point, so if lightning fries the board, the clerks can replay the receipts and rebuild it. When the stadium outgrows one board, you split it into sections by score range (range partitioning), so the VIP section with the top scores can still be read in one glance.

Sorted setRedis structure = hash map + skip list; signals "rank and top-K are cheap, reads never re-sort".
Skip listSorted linked list with layered indexes; 64 nodes take 11 hops instead of 62 — logarithmic search.
ZINCRBYIncrement a user's score (starts at 0 if new), O(log N); the whole write path in one command.
ZREVRANGE 0 9Top 10 in descending order, O(log N + M); the leaderboard page.
ZREVRANKA user's position, O(log N); the query SQL struggles with.
500 QPS / 2,500 peakScore-update load at 5M DAU × 10 games; comfortably within one Redis server.
~650 MB26 bytes × 25M MAU; even doubled for skip-list overhead, it fits in memory easily.
Server-authoritative scoringOnly game servers call POST /v1/scores; defeats proxy-based score tampering.
Range partitioningShard by score band; top 10 lives in one shard, rank = local rank + counts of higher shards.
Scatter-gatherQuery every shard, merge in the app; the price of hash partitioning and write sharding.
Write shardingAppend user_id % num_partitions to the partition key to cool a hot DynamoDB month partition.
Percentile rankWhen exact rank is too costly (sharded NoSQL), tell users "top 10%" from a periodic cron job.

4 Opportunistic Drilling

Three ideas carry most of the interview weight: why the sorted set beats SQL, how to shard it when it outgrows one box, and what the NoSQL alternative gives up. Master those and the rest is detail.

Why a sorted set beats a relational table

In MySQL, a leaderboard is a table of (user_id, score). A win is an easy UPDATE ... SET score = score + 1, and the top 10 can be made tolerable with an index on score plus LIMIT 10. The trouble starts when Mary, deep in the middle of the pack, asks "what is my rank?" The relational answer is a nested query that counts every row with a score greater than or equal to hers — effectively a scan that grows with the player base.

The Redis sorted set sidesteps this by paying the sorting cost up front. It keeps two structures in lockstep: a hash map for "what is mary1934's score?" and a skip list that keeps everyone in score order. A skip list is a sorted linked list with extra "express lane" levels on top; searching starts on the fastest lane and drops down level by level, like taking an express train to the right neighbourhood and then walking the last block.

OperationRelational DBRedis sorted set
Add a pointUPDATE score = score + 1ZINCRBY, O(log N)
Top 10Index on score + ORDER BY ... LIMIT 10ZREVRANGE 0 9, O(log N + M)
A given user's rankNested COUNT(*) over higher scores — does not scaleZREVRANK, O(log N)
DurabilityBuilt inNeeds replica + persistence, MySQL as rebuild source
Common trap: Treating Redis as the only copy of truth. The notes pair it with a MySQL table of wins precisely so the board can be rebuilt (via the MySQL WAL and an ad-hoc script) after a large outage.

Sizing: why one Redis node is enough — until it is not

Start with the arithmetic. 5 million daily users spread over 24 hours is about 50 users per second on average; uneven traffic pushes peak online users to about 250 per second. Each player averages 10 matches a day, so score updates run at about 500 QPS, peaking at 2,500. Top-10 reads, assuming one look per user per day, are only about 50 QPS.

Storage is equally modest. Worst case, all 25 million monthly users play: a 24-character ID plus a 16-bit score is 26 bytes, so about 650 MB. Double it for skip-list overhead and it still fits comfortably. 2,500 writes per second is well within a single Redis server's capability.

The picture changes if the game explodes. At 500 million DAU the notes estimate 65 GB of storage and 250,000 QPS — now sharding is mandatory, and the interesting design debate begins.

Common trap: Jumping to sharding before doing the math. The strongest answer states that the baseline fits on one node, then explains exactly which growth figures force a change.

Sharding the leaderboard: range vs hash partitioning

With range (fixed) partitioning, each shard owns a band of scores — for example [900–1000] on one node, lower bands on others. The application keeps a user_id → shard mapping (in MySQL or a cache). The top 10 is simply the top of the highest band. A user's rank is their rank within their own shard plus the number of users in every higher shard, and that count is an O(1) lookup via the info keyspace command.

With hash partitioning via Redis Cluster, users are spread across nodes by a hash of their key (similar to, but not exactly, consistent hashing). Writes spread nicely, but every leaderboard read becomes a scatter-gather: ask every shard for its top 10, then merge in the application.

ConcernRange partitioningHash partitioning (Redis Cluster)
Top 10Read one shard (the highest band)Scatter-gather across all shards, merge in app
User rankLocal rank + O(1) counts of higher shardsNo straightforward approach
Large top-KMostly localLatency rises: lots of data from every shard
More partitionsManageableLatency grows with partition count
Extra bookkeepinguser_id → shard mapping in appHandled by the cluster

The author therefore leans toward fixed range partitions. Two operational tips round it out: give write-heavy Redis nodes twice the memory they need so snapshots have room, and use Redis-benchmark to make data-driven sizing decisions.

The NoSQL alternative and the percentile escape hatch

A NoSQL store optimized for heavy writes and for sorting within a partition — DynamoDB, Cassandra or MongoDB — is a valid alternative. The notes walk through DynamoDB. A first chess-leaderboard table works but cannot query by score, so score becomes the sort key. That creates a new problem: partitioning by month makes the current month a hotspot, hammered while older months sit idle.

The fix is write sharding: append a partition number, computed as user_id % num_partitions, to the key. Writes now spread out, but reads must scatter-gather across every sub-partition. That is the core tradeoff.

Gains

More partitions means higher write scalability, and a fully managed database with global secondary indexes for fields outside the primary key.

Costs

More partitions means reads must hit more of them to aggregate results, and exact rank becomes hard to compute. The right partition count needs benchmarking.

When exact rank is impractical at that scale, reframe the product: tell users their percentile. A cron job periodically analyses the score distribution (e.g. 10th percentile = score < 100, 90th percentile = score < 6500) and each user is placed in a bucket.

Common trap: Forgetting that write sharding and hash partitioning share the same weakness — scatter-gather reads that slow down as you add partitions.

Security, hosting and the finishing touches

The design rejects letting clients post their own scores because a player can put a proxy in the middle and rewrite the number. Only game servers call POST /v1/scores, and for server-run games the server records wins automatically. A message queue between game and leaderboard services is a reasonable extension only if other consumers need game results.

For hosting, you can run Redis and MySQL yourself, or put AWS API Gateway in front of AWS Lambda functions that run only when called and scale automatically. The author recommends the serverless route for a game built from scratch.

  1. Faster retrieval: cache user objects in a Redis hash (user_id → user object).
  2. Breaking ties: equal scores share a rank by default; to break ties, order by the last played game.
